In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surah Maryam**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾ ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya,﴾ ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair, and I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord.">﴾

We have already discussed the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at the beginnings of the surahs, such as His saying here, ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1], in Surah Hud, so there is no need to repeat it here.

His saying, ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 2], is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is a mention of the mercy of your Lord." It has also been said that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "What is recited to you is a mention of the mercy of your Lord." The first view is more evident. The view that it is a predicate of His saying ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ is clearly untenable, because there is no connection between the two.

His saying, ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾: the word "mention" (dhikr) is a verbal noun (masdar) with its object added to it, and the word "mercy" (rahmah) is a verbal noun with its agent added to it, namely "your Lord." His saying "His servant" (abdahu) is the direct object of the verbal noun "mercy," which is added to its agent, in accordance with the saying of Ibn Malik in the Khulasah (the Alfiyyah):

*"After its genitive, the one to which it is added, complete its function with the accusative or the nominative."*

His saying "Zakariyya" is either a substitute (badal) for "His servant," or an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to it.

In this verse, He, may He be exalted, has made clear that what is recited at the beginning of this noble surah is the mention of Allah's mercy with which He showed mercy to His servant Zakariyya when he called upon Him with a secret call, that is, he supplicated in privacy and in hidden humility. His praise of him, may He be exalted, for making his supplication secret indicates that concealing supplication is better than displaying and proclaiming it. This meaning, which is understood from this verse, is stated explicitly in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Who rescues you from the darknesses of the land and the sea, when you call upon Him in humility and in secret?"﴾ [al-An'am: 63], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Call upon your Lord in humility and in secret. Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾ [al-A'raf: 55]

Concealment is better than display because it is closer to sincerity (ikhlas) and further from showing off (riya'). As for the statement of those who say that the reason he concealed his supplication was that he feared his people would blame him for asking for a child, in a situation where a child was normally impossible given his advanced age and his wife's age and her barrenness; and the statement of those who say that he concealed it because it was a request for a worldly matter, so that if Allah answered his supplication he would obtain what he wanted, and if He did not answer it no one would know; and other statements besides these: all of these are not the most evident. The most evident view is that the secret of his concealment is what we have mentioned, namely that concealment is better than public declaration in supplication.

Allah did not specify the place or the time of this supplication of Zakariyya in this passage, but He alluded to it in Surah Al 'Imran in His saying: ﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found provision with her. He said: "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said: "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37–38]. So His saying "there" (hunalika) means: in that place where he found that provision with Maryam.

Some have said: "There" (hunalika) means: at that time, on the basis that "there" (huna) may sometimes refer to time.

His saying in this supplication: ﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened﴾ [Maryam: 4], meaning: they have become weak. Weakness (wahn) is feebleness. He mentioned the weakness of the bone because it is the pillar of the body, the thing on which its structure depends, and the foundation of its construction. When it weakens, this indicates the weakness of the whole body, because it is the strongest and hardest part of it, so its weakening necessitates the weakening of the rest of the body.

*Al-Harf al-Munir / Sihr / Adwa' al-Bayan vol. 4, from p. 204 to p. 212*

His saying: ﴿and the head has glistened with grey hair﴾. The alif and lam in "the head" (ar-ra's) stand in the place of the possessive pronoun, since the intended meaning is: "my head glistened with grey hair." The intended meaning of the glistening of the head with grey hair is the spreading of the whiteness of greyness throughout it. Az-Zamakhshari said in his Kashshaf: "He likened the greying to the flame of fire in its whiteness, its brightness, and its spreading throughout the hair and its pervading of it, and its taking hold of it in every way, to the burning of fire. Then he brought it out as a metaphor (isti'arah). Then he attributed the glistening to the place of the hair and its root, which is the head, and he brought out the greyness as a specification (tamyiz). He did not add the head to a pronoun, being satisfied with the addressee's knowledge that it is the head of Zakariyya. For this reason this sentence is eloquent and is attested to be eloquent." End of his quotation. In our view, as we have explained many times, the evident meaning is that this kind of expression, describing the spreading of the whiteness of grey hair in the head by "the head glistening with grey," is one of the styles of classical Arabic that the Qur'an came with. From it is the saying of the poet:

*"I have lost my resolve in distancing hope, and I did not refrain, and the greyness has made my head glisten."*

From this same category is the saying of Ibn Duraid in his Maqsurah:

*"And the white hair glistened on its pillow, like the blazing of fire in dry ghada wood."*

His saying "grey hair" (shayban) is a specification (tamyiz) transferred from the subject, according to the most evident of the grammatical analyses. This is in contrast to those who claimed that it is the substitute for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) from His saying "glistened," because it means "greyed," so "grey hair" would be a verbal noun derived from it in meaning. Also, those who claimed that it is an indefinite verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

What Allah mentions here about Zakariyya in his supplication, of displaying weakness and old age, occurs in other places, such as His saying here: ﴿and I have reached extreme old age﴾ [Maryam: 8], and His saying in Al 'Imran: ﴿and old age has reached me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40]. What he mentions here of displaying weakness indicates that it is fitting for the one who supplicates to display weakness, fear, and humility in his supplication.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿and I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾ [Maryam: 4], meaning: "I have never been unblessed in my supplicating to You," that is, You never disappointed my supplication whenever I called upon You. He means: You have accustomed me to answering in the past. The Arabs say: "He became unblessed (shaqiya) by that" if he exerted himself in it and did not achieve his goal. They sometimes use "unhappiness" (shaqa') for exhaustion, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not drive you both out of Paradise, lest you become miserable (fatashqa)﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117]. Most often it is used for the opposite of happiness (sa'adah). There is no doubt that the answering of supplication is part of happiness, so not having it answered is part of unhappiness.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir,﴾ ﴿who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing.﴾

The meaning of His words ﴿I fear the mawali﴾ [Maryam: 5] is: I feared my relatives, my paternal cousins and my kinsmen, that they would neglect the religion after me and would not uphold the religion of God as it should be upheld. So grant me a son who will uphold the religion after me as it should be upheld. From this interpretation you know that the meaning of His words ﴿who will inherit from me﴾ is that it is an inheritance of knowledge, prophethood, the call to God, and upholding His religion, not an inheritance of wealth. Two matters support this:

The first: His words ﴿and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾ [Maryam: 5]. It is well known that the family of Ya'qub died out long ago, so what is inherited from them can only be knowledge, prophethood and religion.

The second matter: the evidence that the prophets, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them, do not leave wealth as an inheritance, but only knowledge and religion are inherited from them. Among this evidence is what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their two Sahihs from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity." Also among it is what al-Shaykhan also recorded from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he said to 'Uthman, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, al-Zubayr, Sa'd, 'Ali and al-'Abbas, may God be pleased with them: "I adjure you by God, by Whose permission the heavens and the earth stand, do you know that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity'?" They said: "Yes." [p. 362] Also among it is what al-Shaykhan also recorded from 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, that when the Prophet's wives (ﷺ) had passed away, they wished to send 'Uthman to Abu Bakr to ask him for their inheritance. 'A'isha said: "Did not the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'What we leave is charity'?" Also among it is what al-Shaykhan also recorded from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "My heirs shall not divide a dinar; what I leave after the maintenance of my wives and the provision of my workers is charity." In a wording in Ahmad: "My heirs shall not divide a dinar or a dirham." Also among it is what Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi recorded and authenticated, from Abu Hurayrah, that Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, said to Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him: "Who will inherit from you when you die?" He said: "My children and my family." She said: "Why then do we not inherit from the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed a prophet is not inherited from.' But I will support those whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to support, and I will spend on those on whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to spend."

These hadiths and their like clearly show that wealth is not inherited from the prophets, but rather knowledge and religion are. If it is said: this is specific to him (ﷺ), because his saying "We do not leave inheritance" refers to himself, just as 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said in the authentic hadith referred to above: "I adjure you by God, by Whose permission the heavens and the earth stand, do you know that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity'?" meaning the Messenger of God (ﷺ) himself. The group said: "He did say that hadith." In this authentic hadith, 'Umar said that the intention of the Prophet (ﷺ) by his words "We do not leave inheritance" was himself, and the group mentioned in it confirmed him. This is evidence of specificity. So is there then no obstacle to the inheritance from Zakariyya in the verse we are discussing being wealth? The answer is in several respects:

The first: the apparent form of the plural noun includes all the prophets, so it is not permissible to depart from this apparent meaning except by evidence from the Book or the Sunnah. 'Umar's statement cannot be used to specify a text of the Sunnah, because according to the verification of the scholars of usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence), texts cannot be specified by the statements of the Companions, as is established in the principles.

The second respect: 'Umar's statement "he (ﷺ) means himself" does not preclude the ruling including other prophets, because it is possible that his intention was that he (ﷺ) meant himself, for he is not inherited from. 'Umar did not say that the wording did not include others, and his meaning himself does not preclude that other prophets are also not inherited from.

The third respect: the hadiths that explicitly state the general absence of material inheritance among all the prophets. We will mention some of them here, God willing.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, the text of which is: "As for what is widely known in the books of the usul scholars and others with the wording 'We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from,' a group of imams has denied it, and that is so with regard to the specific wording 'we' (nahnu). But al-Nasa'i recorded it through the chain of Ibn 'Uyaynah from Abu al-Zinad with the wording 'Indeed we, the company of prophets, are not inherited from...' (the hadith)." He recorded it also from Muhammad ibn Mansur, from Ibn 'Uyaynah, from him. It is also so in the Musnad of al-Humaydi from Ibn 'Uyaynah, and he is among the most precise of Ibn 'Uyaynah's companions in this. Al-Haytham ibn Kulayb included it in his Musnad from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq with the wording mentioned. al-Tabarani recorded it in al-Awsat in approximately the same wording. al-Daraqutni recorded it in al-'Ilal through the narration of Umm Hani' from Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq with the wording: 'Indeed the prophets are not inherited from.'" End of the relevant point from Ibn Hajar's words. I have seen in it these chains in which there is explicit statement of the generality of the prophets. Ibn Hajar also said: the denial of the mentioned hadith is not accepted except with regard to the specific wording "we" (nahnu), and these narrations to which he pointed support one another. It is established in the principles that clarification (bayan) is valid by anything that removes the difficulty, even a contextual indicator or other means, as we have explained at length in the introduction to this blessed book. Accordingly, these hadiths we have mentioned show that the intention of his words in the agreed-upon hadith "We do not leave inheritance" is that he meant himself, as 'Umar said, and all the prophets, as the mentioned narrations indicate. Clarification is guidance and indication, and it is valid by anything that removes ambiguity from the text, whether a text, an action, a contextual indicator, or otherwise. In Maraqi al-Su'ud, in defining clarification and what clarification is achieved by, he said:

"Making the difficult clear from the evident, which is obligatory upon the Prophet when its understanding is intended, and it is by whatever evidence in general that clears the blindness."

From what we have established you know that His words here ﴿who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾ mean the inheritance of knowledge and religion, not wealth. Likewise His words ﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾ [al-Naml: 16], that inheritance is also an inheritance of knowledge and religion. The word inheritance (al-wirathah) is in the Book and the Sunnah sometimes applied to the inheritance of knowledge and religion, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from Our servants﴾ [Fatir: 32], and His saying: ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book after them are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾ [al-Shura: 14], and His saying: ﴿Then there succeeded them successors who inherited the Book﴾ [al-A'raf: 169], and other verses.

From the Sunnah on this subject is what Abu al-Darda', may God be pleased with him, related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets," and it is in the Musnad and the Sunan. The author of Tamyiz al-Tayyib min al-Khabith (Distinguishing the Good from the Bad) concerning what circulates on people's tongues of hadith said: It was narrated by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others from Abu al-Darda', raised to the Prophet, with the addition: "Indeed the prophets did not leave a dinar or a dirham as inheritance, but they left knowledge as inheritance." Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and others authenticated it. End of his words verbatim. The author of Kashf al-Khafa wa Muzil al-Ilbas 'amma ishtahara min al-ahadith 'ala alsinat al-nas (Removing Obscurity and the Confusion concerning what is widely known of hadiths on people's tongues) said: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets" was narrated by Ahmad and the four and others from Abu al-Darda', raised, with the addition: "Indeed the prophets did not leave a dinar or a dirham as inheritance, but they left knowledge as inheritance" (the hadith). Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and others authenticated it. Hamzah al-Kinani graded it as hasan, and others graded it as weak because of the irregularity (idtirab) of its chain. However, it has supporting narrations (shawahid), and for this reason the Hafiz said: it has chains by which it is known that the hadith has a basis. al-Daylami narrated it from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib with the wording of the chapter. End of the relevant point from it. The apparent position is that this hadith is fit to be used as evidence, because some of its chains reinforce others.

When you know what we have mentioned of the indication of these proofs that the inheritance mentioned in the verse is an inheritance of knowledge and religion, not an inheritance of wealth, then know that the scholars have three opinions on this: The first is what we have mentioned. The second is that it is an inheritance of wealth. The third is that, with regard to the family of Ya'qub in His words ﴿and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾, it is an inheritance of knowledge and religion.

This is the choice of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. He mentioned that whoever said that his inheritance from Zakariyya was an inheritance of wealth cited a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) in this regard, that he said: "May God have mercy on Zakariyya, what he had of his heirs," meaning: what harmed him was the inheritance of his heirs of his wealth. It is known that this was not established from the Prophet (ﷺ). What appears to us to be the more likely view is what we have mentioned, that it is an inheritance of knowledge and religion, because of the proofs we have mentioned and others that indicate this. Ibn Kathir in his tafsir mentioned here what supports this in several respects. He said, may God have mercy on him, in explaining His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me﴾ [Maryam: 5]: The reason for his fear was that he feared they would conduct affairs among the people after him in a bad manner, so he asked God for a son who would be a prophet after him, to govern them through his prophethood by what would be revealed to him. He was answered in this. It was not that he feared their inheriting his wealth, for the Prophet is greater in rank and more exalted in status than to be anxious about his wealth to such a degree, or to be too proud to accept the inheritance of his agnatic relatives, and to ask that he have a son to take his inheritance to the exclusion of them. This is one respect.

The second: it is not mentioned that he had wealth; rather he was a carpenter who ate from the earnings of his hands, and such a person does not accumulate wealth, especially the prophets, for they were the most detached from this world.

The third: it is established in the two Sahihs through several chains that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity." In a narration in al-Tirmidhi with a sound chain: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from." On this basis, it is determined that His words ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit from me﴾ [Maryam: 5–6] refer to the inheritance of prophethood. This is why He said ﴿and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾, like His saying ﴿and Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾ [al-Naml: 16], meaning in prophethood. For if it were in wealth, He would not have singled him out from among his brothers for this, and there would have been no great benefit in reporting it, since it is a known and established matter in all the laws and religions that a son inherits from his father. Therefore, unless it were a special inheritance, it would not have been reported. All of this is confirmed and established by what is authentically related in the hadith: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave is charity." End of the relevant point from Ibn Kathir's words. Then after this he cited the chains of the hadith we pointed to: "May God have mercy on Zakariyya and what he had of his wealth's heirs" (the hadith). Then he said concerning its chains: "These are mursal narrations that do not conflict with the sound ones."

Know that the wording "We, the company of prophets" and the wording "Indeed we, the company of prophets" have the same meaning, except that "inna" entered upon "nahnu," replacing the word "nahnu," which is the subject (mubtada'), with the word "na," which is suitable for the accusative case. The sentence is the same, except that in one of the two wordings it is emphasized by "inna," as is not hidden.

His words, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ mean by this heir specifically a son, not any other of the heirs, by the evidence of His words, exalted is He, in the same story: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying: My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring﴾ [Al 'Imran: 38]. He also indicated that it is a son with His words: ﴿And Zakariyya, when he called to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 89]. So His words "do not leave me alone" mean: without a son, one alone.

Al-Shinqiti's commentary on the verse, from his tafsir Adwa' al-Bayan (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, in this noble verse, concerning Zakariyya: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me﴾, meaning: after my death, that they will change the religion. We have already mentioned that *al-mawali* (the heirs and kinsmen) are the relatives and the 'asaba (agnatic kin, those who inherit through male lineage). Among this is His saying: ﴿And for each We have made heirs (mawali) of what is left by the parents and the nearest relatives﴾ [An-Nisa: 33]. In the language of the Arabs, *al-mawla* (a word meaning a protector, ally, or kinsman, here in the sense of one bound to another) is applied to anyone with whom you have a bond that makes him your ally and you his ally by it. It is very often used in the language of a paternal cousin (ibn al-amm), because a paternal cousin is an ally of his cousin through agnatic kinship. From this is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-Abd:

*Know with a knowledge that is not mere supposition: when a man's mawla is humiliated, he is humiliated.*

He means: when his paternal cousins are humiliated, he is humiliated. And the saying of al-Fadl ibn al-Abbas ibn Utba ibn Abi Lahab:

*Gently, O cousin of ours, gently, O our mawali! Do not dig up between us what was buried.*

As for His saying, in this noble verse: ﴿And my wife has been barren﴾, it is apparent that she was barren in the time of her youth. *Al-'aqir* is the barren woman who does not bear children, and it is applied to both male and female. Its application to the female is in this verse, and His saying concerning Zakariyya also: ﴿And indeed old age has overtaken me, and my wife is barren﴾ [Ali Imran: 40]. Its application to the male is in the saying of Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

*Wretched is the young man if I am one-eyed, barren, and a coward; what excuse would I have before every gathering?*

Allah has indicated that He removed the barrenness from her and set her right, making her fertile after she had been barren, in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So We responded to him and granted him Yahya, and We set right for him his wife﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 90]. This setting-right is her becoming able to bear children after she had been barren. As for the saying of one who said that her setting-right mentioned here is making her good-natured after she had been bad-natured, it does not contradict what has been mentioned, since it is permissible that both matters be granted to him concerning her. Moreover, that the setting-right is making her fertile after barrenness is the apparent meaning of the context. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and others. The second view is narrated from Ata.

As for His saying, in this noble verse, concerning Zakariyya: ﴿And make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾ [Maryam: 6], meaning: one who is pleasing to You and to Your creation in his character, sayings, deeds, and religion. *Radiyy* is on the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive).

As for His saying, in this noble verse: ﴿So grant me from Yourself﴾, meaning: from Your presence (min 'indika).

As for His saying, Majestic and Exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾ [Maryam: 6], Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i recited the *tha'* (ث) of the two verbs with sukun (silent), meaning ﴿yarithuni wa yarithu min ali Ya'qub﴾. In this reading, both verbs are *majzum* (in the jussive mood) because of the response to the imperative (jawab al-talab) which is "hab li" (grant me). What is established among the scholars of Arabic grammar is that the *mudari'* (present-tense verb) in the jussive after an imperative is jussive by an implied condition indicated by the imperative verb. Its implied form in this verse, which is our present subject, is: "If You grant me from Yourself a guardian who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub." The rest of the readers recited ﴿yarithuni wa yarithu min ali Ya'qub﴾ with *raf'* (nominative), taking the two verbs as a clause describing *waliyyan* (a guardian): i.e., a guardian who is my heir, and an heir from the family of Ya'qub, as he said in al-Khulasa (Ibn Malik's summary of grammar):

*And they described the indefinite with a clause, so it is given what a predicate is given.*

The reading of the majority with *raf'* of the two verbs is clearer in meaning. Ibn Kathir recited the *ya'* (ي) in His saying: ﴿min wara'i wa kanat imra'ati﴾ with a fatha, and the rest with sukun.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from Asim recited "Zakariyya" without a hamza after the alif. The rest recited "Zakariyya'" with a hamza after the alif. From this you know that the elongation (madd) in His saying "wa Zakariyya'u idh nada" (And Zakariyya, when he called out) is separated (munfasil) according to the reading of Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs, and connected (muttasil) according to the reading of the rest. The second hamza, according to the reading of the majority, which is the hamza of *idha*, is softened (musahhalah) in the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr, and fully pronounced (muhaqqaqah) in the reading of Ibn Amir and Shu'ba from Asim.

The reading ﴿khiftu al-mawaliya﴾ with a fatha on the *kha'* and a shadda on the *fa'*, in the form of a past-tense verb, meaning that his mawali became few (khaffu, i.e., decreased), is a shadhdh (irregular, non-canonical) reading, and recitation with it is not permissible, even though it is narrated from Uthman ibn Affan, Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, and others, may Allah be pleased with them.

As for the wife of Zakariyya mentioned here, al-Qurtubi said: she was Ishaa bint Faqudh ibn Qabil, and she was the sister of Hinna bint Faqudh. This is what al-Tabari said. Hinna was the mother of Maryam. Al-Qutabi said: the wife of Zakariyya was Ishaa bint Imran. According to this view, Yahya is literally the cousin of Isa, peace be upon them both. According to the first view, Yahya is the cousin of Isa's mother. In the hadith of the Night Journey, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Then I met my two maternal cousins, Yahya and Isa," which is evidence for the first view. The apparent indication of the hadith supports the second view, not the first, contrary to what he (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not given to any before [him] a namesake.﴾

In this noble verse there is an ellipsis (hadhf) which the context indicates, and its implied meaning is: "So Allah answered his supplication, and he was called: ﴿O Zakariyya﴾ ..." to the end of the verse [Maryam: 7]. Allah, Exalted and Most High, clarified in another place what He had stated briefly here, explaining that the one who called him was some of the angels, and that the call mentioned occurred while he was standing praying in the mihrab (prayer niche). This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the angels called him while he was standing in prayer in the mihrab: "Indeed, Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and noble, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39]. As for His saying, ﴿So the angels called him﴾, some scholars said: He used the word "the angels" and meant Jibril (Gabriel). One of the scholars of usul al-fiqh cited this as an example of a general term (al-'amm) intended in a specific sense (al-khusus), saying: by the generality of "the angels" He meant the specific one, Jibril. The attribution of the verb to a group while only some of them are meant has been explained by us many times before.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿whose name is Yahya﴾, it indicates that Allah is the One who named him, and did not leave his naming to his father. In this there is a great honour for Yahya.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿We have not given to any before [him] a namesake﴾, know first that the word samiy (namesake) is used in the Arabic language in two senses. The first is the saying: "So-and-so is the samiy of so-and-so," meaning: named with his name. Thus whoever shares his name, each of them is the samiy of the other, i.e., named with his name.

The second: samiy is used in the sense of musamiy, i.e., one equal in loftiness, elevation and nobility (p-368), and it is on the pattern fa'il in the meaning of mufa'il, from al-sumuww meaning height, elevation and rank. It is common in the language for fa'il to come in the meaning of mufa'il, like qa'id and jalis in the meaning of muqa'id and mujalis, and akil and sharib in the meaning of mu'akil and musharib. Likewise samiy in the meaning of musamiy, i.e., one equal in loftiness. Once you know this, know that His saying here: ﴿We have not given to any before [him] a namesake﴾ [Maryam: 7] means: We have not made before him anyone named with his name; so he is the first whose name was Yahya. As for the view of one who said its meaning is: "We have not made for him a samiy, i.e., an equal in loftiness and elevation," it is not correct, because he is not superior to Ibrahim, Musa and Nuh. So the first view is the correct one. Among those who held it are Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Aslam and others. The second view is also related from Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas. Once you know that the correct meaning of His saying ﴿We have not given to any before [him] a namesake﴾ is: We have not named anyone with his name before him, then know that His saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, so worship Him and be steadfast in His worship. Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ [Maryam: 65] means: He, Exalted is He, has no equal or peer who matches Him in height, greatness and perfection in reality. Some scholars said: it is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ means: Do you know of anyone named with His name, al-Rahman, Exalted and Most High? And knowledge is with Allah, Exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "My Lord, how will I have a boy when my wife has been barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾.

In this noble verse, Exalted and Majestic is He, mentions that when Zakariyya was given the good news of Yahya, he said: ﴿My Lord, how will I have a boy when my wife has been barren and I have reached extreme old age?﴾ [Maryam: 8]. What he is mentioned here as having said, he is also mentioned as having said in Al 'Imran, in His saying: ﴿He said, "My Lord, how will I have a boy when old age has already overtaken me and my wife is barren?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40]. As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿and I have reached extreme old age (utiyyan)﴾ [Maryam: 8], Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, from 'Asim, read "'itiyyan" with a kasra on the ʿayn, following the kasra that comes after it and for harmony with the yā'. The rest read "'utiyyan" with a damma, according to the original form. The meaning of His saying, ﴿and I have reached extreme old age (utiyyan)﴾, is that he had reached the utmost limit of old age in years, to the point that his bones had become thin and dry. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: He means, "I have become withered (ʿattawtu) from old age, so that I have become a man with thin, dry bones." It is said of a dry stick: ʿūdun ʿātin wa ʿāsin (a dry, stiff stick). One says of it: ʿataa yaʿtū ʿutuwwan wa ʿitiyyan, and ʿasā yaʿsū ʿisiyyan wa ʿusuwwan. Everything that reaches an extreme limit in old age, corruption or disbelief is called ʿātin and ʿāsin.

* *

(p-369) Note

If it is asked: what is the reason for Zakariyya's question in His saying, ﴿how will I have a boy?﴾, given that he knew Allah's power over everything?

The answer has three aspects, which we have mentioned in our book (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'inda Ayat al-Kitab) in the surah of Al 'Imran, and one of them has a weakness, although it is narrated from ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi and others.

The first: Zakariyya's question was a question of inquiry and seeking information, because he did not know whether Allah would bring him a child from the wife of an old woman, despite their advanced age, by way of breaking the customary course, or would command him to marry a young woman, or would return them both to youth. So he asked about the reality in order to know it. There is no difficulty in this, and it is the clearest of them.

The second: his question was a question of wonder at the perfection of Allah's power, Exalted is He.

The third, which we said has a weakness, is what Ibn Jarir reported from ʿIkrimah and al-Suddi: that when the angels called to Zakariyya while he was standing praying in the sanctuary, that Allah gives you good news of Yahya, Satan said to him: "This is not the call of the angels; it is the call of Satan." So doubt entered Zakariyya that the call was from Satan, and at that doubt, arising from Satan's whispering, before he was certain that it was from Allah, he said: ﴿How will I have a boy?﴾ [Maryam: 8]. For this reason he asked Allah for a sign concerning that, by his saying: ﴿My Lord, make for me a sign﴾ [Maryam: 10]. We said that this view has a weakness because the call of the angels would not be confused for Zakariyya with the call of Satan.

As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿ʿitiyyan﴾, its original form is ʿutuwwan, then the waw was changed to a yā'. From the use of ʿitiyy for extreme old age is the poet's saying:

"A youth is only excused, and one who has been in the age of ʿitiyy is not excused."

The reading "ʿisiyyan" with a sīn is irregular, and it is not permissible to recite with it. Al-Qurtubi said: Ibn ʿAbbas recited with it, and it is likewise in the codex of Ubayy.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "So it is. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and I had already created you before, when you were nothing.'"﴾

What Allah, may He be exalted, mentions in this noble verse He also mentions in Al 'Imran in His saying: ﴿He said, "So it is; Allah does what He wills."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40]. Regarding His saying in this noble verse, "kadhalika" (so it is), the scholars have several views on its i'rab (grammatical analysis):

(p-370) The first: it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and its implied sense is: "The matter is so, and there is no doubt that you will bear the boy mentioned." It was also said: "The matter is so: you are old in years and your wife is barren." On this view, His saying ﴿He said, "Your Lord says"﴾ [Maryam: 9] is the start of a new statement.

The second: "kadhalika" is in the accusative position (mahall nasb) governed by "qala" (he said). On this view, the demonstrative "dhalika" refers to something vague which is explained by His saying ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. A parallel to this view is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We conveyed to him that decree, that the last remnant of those would be cut off by morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. The other aspects of its i'rab besides these two we have omitted because they are not clear to us. His saying ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ means: it is light and simple.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿and I had already created you before, when you were nothing﴾ means: the One who created you when you were nothing is able to grant you the mentioned child, as is clear. What He says here to Zakariyya, that He created him when he was nothing, He also refers to in relation to mankind in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Does not man consider that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ [Maryam: 67], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worthy of mention?﴾ [al-Insan: 1].

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿when you were nothing﴾ is evidence that the non-existent is not a thing. A parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ [al-Nur: 39]. This is the correct view, contrary to the Mu'tazila, who say that a non-existent that is possible to exist is a thing, and who use as evidence His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. They said: Allah has named it a thing before He says to it "Be, and it is," and this indicates that it is a thing before its existence. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said, in his tafsir of this verse: "Because the non-existent is not a thing, or is not a thing worth considering, like their saying: 'I am amazed at nothing,' and the saying of the poet:

"The earth became so constricted that his fugitive, when he saw something other than a thing, thought it was a man."

Because his meaning by "something other than a thing" is: when he saw a trivial thing not worth considering, as if it were nothing because of its insignificance, he thought it was a man. For "something other than a thing" in an absolute sense cannot be the object of sight. The correct view is what this verse and similar verses in the Qur'an indicate: that the non-existent is not a thing. As for their argument from the verse, the answer is: when the will has become attached to bringing that non-existent into being, its certain occurrence becomes like its actual occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], and His saying: ﴿and the Horn is blown﴾ [al-Kahf: 99], and His saying: ﴿And the earth shines with the light of its Lord, and the Book is placed, and the prophets and the witnesses are brought﴾ [al-Zumar: 69], (p-371) and His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved are driven﴾ [al-Zumar: 71], and His saying: ﴿And those who feared their Lord are driven﴾, and similar. All these past-tense verbs, which indicate an event that has actually occurred in the past, are used to mean the future, because the certainty of the occurrence of what is mentioned makes it like what has actually occurred. Likewise, calling it a thing before its existence is due to the certainty of its existence by the will of Allah, may He be exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿and I had already created you﴾ was read by the majority of the Seven, except Hamza and al-Kisa'i, as "khalaqtuka" with the pronoun of the first person (ta' al-mutakallim) with a dammah. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it as "wa-qad khalaqnaka," with a nun after which is an alif, and the plural form in it is for magnification (ta'zim).

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 10:**

Allah's words: ﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, while being sound."﴾

The word *āyah* here means a sign, i.e., "appoint for me a sign by which I may know the occurrence of what I was given good news of, namely the child." Some scholars of knowledge said: he asked for a sign in order that his reassurance regarding the fulfilment of what he was given good news of might be complete. A parallel to this view is Allah's words about Ibrahim: ﴿Ibrahim said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. It has also been said that he meant by the sign that he might know the beginning of his wife's pregnancy, since pregnancy is hidden in its early period.

As for His words in this noble verse, ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people,﴾ meaning: your sign of the occurrence of that is that you will not speak to the people, that is, you will be prevented from speech so that you cannot manage it for three nights with their days, while you are sound, that is, sound in creation and whole in your limbs, with no muteness or dumbness in you. Rather, you are prevented from speech by way of breaking the customary course (*kharq al-ʿādah*, a departure from ordinary custom), as we previously mentioned in Āl ʿImrān. As for the remembrance of Allah, he is not prevented from it, by the evidence of His words in Āl ʿImrān: ﴿And remember your Lord much and glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning.﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 41]. The view of one who said that the meaning of His words, ﴿three nights while being sound,﴾ is "three consecutive nights," is not correct. Rather its meaning is what we previously mentioned: that the restraint of his tongue from speaking to his people was not due to any cause or illness that befell him, but by the power of Allah the Exalted. Allah the Exalted said here, ﴿three nights,﴾ and did not mention their days with them, but He mentioned the days in Āl ʿImrān, in His words: ﴿He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 41]. Thus the two verses indicate that they are three nights with their days.

As for His words in this verse, ﴿You will not speak to the people,﴾ it means except by gesture or writing, as is indicated by His words here: ﴿So he conveyed to them, "Glorify [Allah] in the morning and the evening."﴾ [Maryam: 11], and His words in Āl (p-372) ʿImrān: ﴿He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 41]. This is because *al-ramz* is a gesture and signalling with the lips and eyebrow, and the *īḥāʾ* in His words, ﴿So he conveyed to them that they should glorify [Allah],﴾ and so on, some scholars said it is a gesture, and this is the more evident view, by the evidence of His words, ﴿except by gesture,﴾ as previously mentioned. Among those who said that the revelation (*waḥy*) in the verse is a gesture were Qatadah, al-Kalbi, Ibn Munabbih, and al-ʿUtbi, as al-Qurtubi and others transmitted from them. And from Mujahid and al-Suddi, regarding ﴿So he conveyed to them,﴾ that he wrote for them in the earth. And from Ikrimah: he wrote for them in a book. The word *waḥy* in the language of the Arabs is applied to every rapid and hidden communication, and for this reason it is applied to inspiration, as in His words: ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee…﴾ [al-Naḥl: 68], and to a gesture, as is apparent in His words: ﴿So he conveyed to them that they should glorify [Allah]…﴾ [Maryam: 11], and it is applied to writing, as is the other view regarding this noble verse. The application of *waḥy* to writing is well known in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of Labid ibn Rabiʿah in his Muʿallaqah:

*The channels of al-Rayyān, their traces effaced and worn away, like the writing whose pages were preserved by the scribes.*

So his words *al-wuḥiyy* (with a *ḍamma* on the wāw, a *kasra* on the ḥāʾ, and a shadda on the yāʾ) is the plural of *waḥy*, meaning writing.

And the saying of ʿAntarah:

*Like the writings of pages from the era of Kisra, which he sent to a non-Arab who speaks unclearly.*

And the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Except the four dark ones, which seem as if they were the remnant of writing in the folds of pages.*

And the saying of Jarir:

*As if the one who writes the writing were inscribing a kāf and a lām in its dwellings.*

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 11 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche (mihrab) and signaled to them, saying: Glorify [Allah] morning and evening.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, exalted in majesty, mentions that Zakariyya came out to his people from the mihrab and gestured to them, or wrote to them, that they should glorify Allah at the beginning of the day and at its end. Al-bukrah ("morning") is the beginning of the day, and al-ʿashiyy ("evening") is its end. In Surat Ali ʿImran, Allah has also made clear that what Zakariyya commanded his people, by gesture or writing, of glorification morning and evening, Allah had commanded Zakariyya himself as well, in His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord much, and glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 41]. The apparent meaning is that this mihrab from which he came out to his people is the same mihrab in which he was given the good news of a son while he was standing in prayer, as mentioned in His saying: (p-373) ﴿And the angels called him while he was standing in prayer in the mihrab﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 39]. Abu ʿAbdullah al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: "The mihrab is the highest place and the most honorable seat, and they used to make mihrabs in what was raised from the ground." End of quote. Al-Jawhari said in his Sihah: Al-Farra' said: "al-maharib are the fronts of gatherings, and from this the niche (mihrab) of the mosque is named; and al-mihrab is the upper chamber." Wadda' al-Yaman said:

؎ A lady of a chamber; when I come to her I do not reach her, nor do I climb a ladder.

From this meaning is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 37], and so on.

* *

Note (tanbih)
Some scholars derived from this noble verse the legitimacy of the imam being raised above the followers in prayer, since the mihrab was the place of Zakariyya's prayer, as indicated by His saying: ﴿while he was standing in prayer in the mihrab﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 39], and the mihrab is higher than other places; so this shows what has been mentioned. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: This verse indicates that the raising of their imam above the followers was lawful among them. The jurists of the major cities have differed on this question. Imam Ahmad and others permitted it, holding to the story of the minbar, while Malik forbade a great height but not a slight one, and his companions justified the prohibition by fear of pride on the part of the imam.

I say: This requires examination. The best of what is said on this is what Abu Dawud narrated from Hammam: that Hudhayfah led the people in prayer at al-Mada'in standing on a raised platform (dukkan), and Abu Mas'ud seized his shirt and pulled him down. When he finished his prayer he said: "Do you not know that they used to forbid this?" or "That was forbidden?" He said: "Yes, I remembered that when you pulled me." It is also narrated from ʿAdi ibn Thabit al-Ansari, who said: "A man narrated to me that he was with ʿAmmar ibn Yasir at al-Mada'in, and the prayer was established, and ʿAmmar ibn Yasir went forward and stood on a platform praying while the people were below him. Hudhayfah came forward and took hold of his hands, and ʿAmmar followed him until Hudhayfah brought him down. When ʿAmmar finished his prayer, Hudhayfah said to him: 'Did you not hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "When a man leads people in prayer, he should not stand in a place higher than their standing place"' or something similar? ʿAmmar said: 'For that I followed you when you took hold of my hands.'"

I say: These are three of the Companions who reported the prohibition of that, and none of them argued against the other with the hadith of the minbar, which indicates that it was abrogated. Among what indicates its abrogation is that it involves an extra action in the prayer, namely descending and ascending, so it was abrogated just as speech and greeting in prayer were abrogated. This is more appropriate than (p-374) what our companions gave as an excuse, that "the Prophet ﷺ was protected from pride," since many imams are found to have no pride in them. Some of them gave the reason that the height of the minbar was slight. And Allah knows best. End of al-Qurtubi's words, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, said: We will discuss here, if Allah the Exalted wills, the hadiths mentioned, and we will explain the statements of the scholars on this question, their evidences, and what appears to us to be preferred by evidence.

As for the two reports which al-Qurtubi mentioned from Abu Dawud, Abu Dawud related them in his Sunan: "Ahmad ibn Sinan and Ahmad ibn al-Furat Abu Mas'ud al-Razi related to us, the wording being his, saying: Ya'la related to us, al-A'mash related to us from Ibrahim from Hammam: that Hudhayfah led the people in prayer at al-Mada'in on a platform..." to the end of the hadith. Then Abu Dawud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Ahmad ibn Ibrahim related to us, Hajjaj related to us from Ibn Jurayj, Abu Khalid informed me from ʿAdi ibn Thabit al-Ansari: a man narrated to me that he was with ʿAmmar ibn Yasir at al-Mada'in..." to the end of the hadith. It is not hidden that this last report is weak, since the narrator in it from ʿAmmar is a man who is not known, as you see. As for the first report, several have authenticated it, and it was also narrated explicitly as marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ). Ibn Hajar said in al-Talkhis, in discussing the aforementioned report and hadith: "It is opposed by what Abu Dawud narrated through the route of Hammam: that Hudhayfah led the people in prayer at al-Mada'in on a platform, and Abu Mas'ud seized his shirt and pulled him, and when he finished his prayer he said: 'Do you not know that they used to forbid that?' He said: 'Yes.' Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim authenticated it, and in a narration of al-Hakim there is explicit mention of its being marfu'. Abu Dawud also narrated it by another route, in which the imam was ʿAmmar ibn Yasir and the one who pulled him was Hudhayfah, and it is marfu', but in it there is an unknown narrator; the first is stronger. It is strengthened by what al-Daraqutni narrated by another route from Hammam from Abu Mas'ud: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade that the imam stand above something while the people are behind him below him.'" End quote from al-Talkhis.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, in discussing the hadith of Hudhayfah's prayer on the platform and Abu Mas'ud's pulling him, mentioned: "It was related by al-Shafi'i, Abu Dawud, al-Bayhaqi, and countless major hadith scholars and compilers, and its chain is sound. It is said jadhaba and jabadha are two well-known dialects." End quote from him.

As for the story of the minbar, to which al-Qurtubi referred, saying it is the proof of those who permit the imam to be raised above the follower: it is the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd that "the Prophet ﷺ sat on the minbar on the first day it was placed, and he said takbir while on it, then bowed, then descended backwards and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. Then he returned until he finished. When he turned, he said: 'O people, I only did this so that you would follow me and learn my prayer.'" Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim).

As for the statements of the imams on this (p-375) question: the position of al-Shafi'i on it is that it is disliked for the imam to be higher than the follower, and likewise the reverse, unless that is for a valid need, such as the imam being raised in order to teach ignorant people the prayer, as the Prophet ﷺ did in his prayer on the minbar, and he explained that he did it for the purpose of teaching; and the follower being raised so that he may convey the imam's takbirs to other followers. If the raising of either of them is for such a purpose, it is recommended for him to raise himself to achieve that purpose.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: "This is our position, and it is a narration from Abu Hanifah. And there is another narration from him that he dislikes raising absolutely. This is also the view of Malik and al-Awza'i. Shaykh Abu Hamid related from al-Awza'i that he said the prayer is invalidated by it."

As for the position of Malik on the question, it contains a distinction between the imam being higher than the follower and the reverse. The follower being higher is permissible in his view, though he returned to disliking it, and some of his companions remained on his earlier view of its permissibility. The imam being higher does not please him. In al-Mudawwanah Malik said: "There is no harm, outside of Friday, for a man to pray with the imam's prayer on the roof of the mosque while the imam is inside the mosque," then he disliked it. Ibn al-Qasim adopted his first statement. End of the quote transmitted through al-Mawwaq in commenting on Khalil ibn Ishaq's words in his Mukhtasar, coupling it with what is permitted: "and the follower's being higher even on a roof." Also in al-Mudawwanah Malik said: "If the imam prays with people on the roof of the mosque while the people are behind him below that, I do not like it." End quote, also through al-Mawwaq. His saying "I do not like it" is clearly disapproval, and some understood it as prohibition. Regarding the obligation to repeat the prayer, there are two opinions.

The point of disagreement is when the one who is raised does not intend by his raising to show pride over the people. If he intends that, his prayer is invalid according to them, whether he is imam or follower. This question is mentioned by Khalil ibn Ishaq in his Mukhtasar in his words: "the follower's being higher even on a roof, not the reverse, and by seeking, with the intention of an imam or follower, pride, except by a shibr (span)," and his words "except by a shibr" mean: except that the raising is by a span; and a shibr, or something near it, is the length of the forearm bone according to them. The place of permissibility of the slight raising mentioned is when it is not intended for pride. So his words "except by a shibr" are an exception from his words "not the reverse," not from the question of intending pride, in which the prayer is invalid according to them absolutely. Al-Mawwaq said in his commentary on Khalil's words cited from al-Mudawwanah: "Malik and others disliked that the imam pray on something higher than what those behind him pray on, such as a platform in the niche and the like. Ibn al-Qasim said: If he does so, they must repeat it forever, because they are playing around, unless that platform is of slight height, like what we had in Egypt, in which case the prayer suffices for them. Abu Muhammad said: like a span and the length of the forearm bone..." to where he said: "Consider if the follower does likewise, meaning on a raised place, intending pride over equality with the imam." Ibn Bashir said: "his prayer too is invalid." End of the relevant point. Ibn al-Qasim's words "because they are playing around" mean by raising that structure on which the imam prays, as Allah the Exalted said of His Prophet Hud addressing his people ʿAd: ﴿Do you build on every high place a monument, playing?﴾ ﴿And you take fortresses, perhaps you will live forever?﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 128-129]. If a group of those praying is raised with the imam above the rest of the people, meaning they are not among the nobles and notables of the people, then there is a disagreement among them on whether this removes the dislike; and Khalil indicated this in his Mukhtasar with his words: "Is it permissible if there is with the imam a group like the others? It is uncertain." This is the summary of Malik's position on this question.

As for the position of Abu Hanifah on this question: the raising of either the imam or the follower above the other is disliked. al-Tahawi said: the follower's being higher than the imam is not disliked. The place of dislike for the Hanafis is in raising that is not slight, and there is no dislike among them for the slight. The measure of raising that causes dislike according to them is the height of a man standing, and there is no harm in less than that; al-Tahawi mentioned this, and it is narrated from Abu Yusuf. It was said that it is determined by the amount that makes a distinction apparent, and it was said: determined by the length of a cubit, by analogy with the sutrah (screen). The author of Tabyin al-Haqa'iq said: "and upon this reliance is placed." If there is with the imam in his raised place a congregation, and the rest of the followers are below them, that is not disliked according to the correct view among them. End of the meaning of Tabyin al-Haqa'iq, Sharh Kanz al-Daqa'iq.

As for the position of Imam Ahmad on this question: it is a distinction between the imam being higher than the follower, which is disliked according to the well-known view of Ahmad's school, and the follower being higher than the imam, which is permitted. Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: "The well-known view in the school is that it is disliked for the imam to be higher than the followers, whether he intends to teach them the prayer or not. This is also the view of Malik, al-Awza'i and the people of opinion. A narration from Ahmad indicates that it is not disliked." End of the relevant point. He also said in al-Mughni: "If the imam prays in a place higher than the followers, Ibn Hamid said: their prayer is not valid, and this is the view of al-Awza'i, because the prohibition necessitates the invalidity of what is forbidden. al-Qadi said: it is not invalidated, and this is the view of the people of opinion." End of the relevant point.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 11 (part 2 of 2):

Having come to know the positions of the four Imams on this question, know that the argument of those who disliked, or prohibited, the imam being elevated above the congregation (ma'mum) is what we have already mentioned in the story of Abu Mas'ud pulling Hudhayfah when he led the people in prayer and stood praying on a raised platform (dukkan), the hadith mentioned earlier. We have already explained the statements of the scholars regarding the said hadith.

The argument of those who permitted this for the purpose of teaching is the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), concerning the Prophet's ﷺ prayer upon the pulpit (minbar) (p-377). The answer of those who oppose his praying on the pulpit is that it was a slight elevation, and that this is not objectionable; or that it was abrogated, as mentioned earlier in the words of al-Qurtubi.

The argument of those who permitted the ma'mum to be above the imam is what is narrated from Abu Hurayrah: that he prayed with the prayer of the imam while he was on the roof of the mosque.

Ibn Hajar said in "al-Talkhis": Al-Shafi'i narrated it from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad, who said: Salih, the freedman of al-Tawamah, told me that he saw Abu Hurayrah praying above the roof of the mosque with the prayer of the imam in the mosque. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it from the hadith of al-Qa'nabi, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Salih. Sa'd ibn Mansur also narrated it, and al-Bukhari mentioned it as a mu'allaq (suspended) report. End of the relevant part of his words. You have thus seen the positions of the scholars on the question and their evidences.

The one who recorded these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: What appears to be the case, and Allah the Most High knows best, is the obligation of reconciling the mentioned evidences: that the elevation of the imam is disliked for the reason already mentioned, and it is reconciled with the story of the prayer on the pulpit by its being permitted for the purpose of teaching and no other. This is indicated by his ﷺ report that when he rose up they could see him, and when he descended none could see him except those closest to him. Some scholars reconciled it by saying that his elevation on the pulpit was a slight elevation, which is excused. As for the elevation of the ma'mum, analogy conflicts with the action of Abu Hurayrah, because analogy requires the disliking of the ma'mum's elevation by analogy with the elevation of the imam, and this is a clear analogy. When analogy conflicts with the statement of a Companion, some usuliyyun (jurists of legal theory) hold that analogy takes precedence, which is the position of Malik and a group, while others hold that the statement of the Companion takes precedence. There is no doubt that the more cautious course is to avoid the elevation of either the imam or the ma'mum above the other. And knowledge is with Allah the Most High.

As for "an" in His words, ﴿So He revealed to them that glorify [Allah]﴾ [Maryam: 11], it is the explanatory "an" (mufassirah), and the meaning is that what follows it explains the revelation mentioned before it. Thus what He indicated to them is the command to glorify Allah morning and evening. This is the correct view. It is possible that it is the verbal-noun "an" (masdariyyah), based on the view that the masdariyyah "an" comes with imperative verbs; in that case the meaning is: He revealed to them, that is, He signaled to them, to glorify, that is, with glorification; or He wrote that to them, based on the view that what is meant is writing. That it is explanatory is the correct view, and knowledge is with Allah the Most High.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination.﴾ ﴿And We gave him judgment while he was a boy,﴾ ﴿and compassion from Us and purity. And he was devout,﴾ ﴿and dutiful to his parents, and he was not domineering or disobedient.﴾ ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.﴾

(p-378) Know first that we mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that among the kinds of exposition (bayan) it contains is that Allah mentions a thing together with some of its attributes, while it has other attributes mentioned in another place, and we clarify those. Many examples of this have passed, most of them concerning described things that are common nouns (asma' al-ajnas) rather than proper names (al-a'lam). Sometimes we have mentioned this with the attributes of proper names, as here. Once you know this, know that in this noble verse Allah mentions some of Yahya's attributes, and He has also mentioned some of his attributes in other places. We will clarify, if Allah wills, the meaning of what is mentioned here and what is mentioned elsewhere.

Know that here He described him as one to whom He said: ﴿O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination﴾ [Maryam: 12]. He described him by His saying: ﴿And We gave him judgment﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾. So His saying ﴿O Yahya, take the Scripture﴾ is the object of an omitted saying, meaning: and We said to him, ﴿O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination.﴾ The Scripture (al-Kitab) is the Torah, meaning: take the Torah with determination, that is, with earnestness and striving. This is by first understanding its meaning so that he grasps it correctly, then acting upon it in all respects: holding to its creed, permitting what it permits, prohibiting what it prohibits, adopting its manners, heeding its admonitions, and the rest of the aspects of acting upon it. Most of the exegetes hold that the meaning of the Scripture here is the Torah, and more than one has reported consensus (ijma') on this. It has been said that it is a book sent down to Yahya; it has been said that it is a generic noun (ism jins) that includes the earlier books; and it has been said that it is the scrolls of Ibrahim. The most evident view is the view of the majority, that it is the Torah, as we have stated.

His saying in this noble verse, ﴿And We gave him judgment﴾, meaning: We gave him judgment (hukm). The scholars have several close views regarding the meaning of judgment, all returning to one thing: that Allah gave him understanding of the Scripture, that is, grasping what is in it and acting upon it while he was a boy. Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: ﴿And We gave him judgment while he was a boy﴾, meaning: understanding, knowledge, earnestness, resolve, turning toward goodness, devoting oneself to it, and striving in it while he was young and a youth. ‘Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: Ma'mar said: The boys said to Yahya ibn Zakariyya: "Come, let us go and play." He said: "We were not created for play." So Allah sent down: ﴿And We gave him judgment while he was a boy.﴾ Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this noble verse: ﴿And We gave him judgment while he was a boy﴾, Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: We gave him understanding of the Book of Allah in his childhood, before he reached the age of men. Ahmad ibn Mani' narrated to us, saying: 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, saying: Ma'mar informed me, without attributing it to anyone, concerning this verse: ﴿And We gave him judgment while he was a boy,﴾ he said: It reached me that the boys said to Yahya: "Come, let us go and play." He said: (p-379) "We were not created for play," so Allah sent down: ﴿And We gave him judgment while he was a boy.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: ﴿And We gave him judgment﴾, meaning: wisdom (al-hikmah). From this is the saying of Nabigha Dhubyani:

"And judge as the judgment of the girl of the tribe when she looked at doves swift, coming to the watering pond."

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr in his tafsir of this verse: Judgment (al-hukm) is prophethood, or the judgment of the Book, or wisdom, or knowledge of the rulings, or intellect, which is reason, or the manners of service, or true insight; these are views.

The one who restricts it (i.e., the author), may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me is that judgment is knowledge that benefits and acting upon it; this is through understanding the heavenly Book correctly and acting upon it in truth. This includes all the views of the scholars regarding the noble verse. The original meaning of "hikam" is restraint, and beneficial knowledge together with acting upon it restrains words and deeds from defect, corruption, and deficiency.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿boy (sabiyyan)﴾, meaning: one who had not reached maturity, and this is the apparent meaning. It has been said: "sabiyyan" means a young man who had not reached the age of middle age (kuhulah), mentioned by Abu Hayyan and others, but the first is the apparent meaning. It has been said he was three years old, it has been said seven, and it has been said two years. And Allah knows best.

His saying in this noble verse ﴿and compassion (hanan)﴾ is coordinated with "judgment," meaning: and We gave him compassion from Us. Hanan is what he was created with of mercy, tenderness, and kindness. The use of hanan for mercy and tenderness is well known in Arabic speech, and from it is the saying: "Hananaka wa hananayka ya Rabb," meaning: Your mercy. From this meaning is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"O daughter of al-Harith, the king, son of 'Amr, to whom belongs the kingdom of Iraq up to 'Oman."

"And the sons of Shamaja ibn Jarm grant her their she-goats, your compassion, O Possessor of compassion."

He means: Your mercy, O Merciful. And the saying of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd:

"O Abu Mundhir, you have destroyed us, so spare some of us. Your compassion (hanaynka)! Some evil is easier than some."

And the saying of Mundhir ibn Dirham al-Kalbi:

"And the newest meeting from Umayna is a glance, on the edge of al-'Alya, when I am standing."

"She said: 'Hanan! What brought you here? Are you one with lineage, or are you a knower of the tribe?'"

So his saying "hanan" means: my affair is hanan, that is, mercy to you, tenderness and compassion toward you. (p-380) And the saying of al-Hutay'a or another:

"Be compassionate toward me, may the King guide you, for every situation has its speech."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from Us﴾, meaning: from Our presence. The most correct interpretation of his saying "and purity (zakah)" is that it is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: or We gave him purity, that is, cleansing from the filth of sins and disobedience through obedience and drawing near to Allah by what pleases Him. We have already mentioned, in the chapter of "al-Kahf," the verses that indicate the use of zakah in the Qur'an in the sense of purity, so that suffices and need not be repeated here.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: "And purity (zakah)": zakah is purification, blessing, and growth in good matters, meaning: We made him blessed for people, guiding them. It has been said the meaning is: We purified him with good praise of him, as witnesses purify a person. It has been said: "zakah" is charity for his parents. This was said by Ibn Qutayba. End of al-Qurtubi's words. This is contrary to the verification of the meaning of the verse. The verification, if Allah wills, is what we have mentioned: that the meaning is: and We gave him zakah, that is, purity from sins and disobedience through Our enabling him to act by what pleases Allah, exalted is He. The statement of whoever among the scholars said that what is meant by zakah in the verse is righteous deeds returns to what we have mentioned, because righteous deeds are that by which one is purified from sins and disobedience.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And he was devout (taqiyyan)﴾, meaning: one who complies with the commands of his Lord, avoiding everything He forbade. For this reason he never committed any sin and did not approach it. This was said by al-Qurtubi and others on the authority of Qatada and others. There are raised (marfu') hadiths of this sort, but apparently none of them is established as raised, either because of a break in the chain (inqita'), or because of 'an'anah of a mudallis (concealing narrator), or because of weakness in a narrator, as Ibn Kathir and others indicated. We have already mentioned the meaning of "taqwa" many times, and the origin of its root in the Arabic language.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and dutiful to his parents﴾ [Maryam: 14]. Barr, with a fatha, is the agent of birr, with a kasra, in abundance. That is, We made him abundantly dutiful to his parents, meaning: beneficent to them, gentle with them, and humble toward them. His saying "barran" is coordinated with his saying "taqiyyan." His saying: ﴿and he was not domineering (jabbaran) or disobedient (asiyyan)﴾, meaning: he was not arrogant toward obedience to his Lord or obedience to his parents, but was obedient to Allah and humble toward his parents. This was said by Ibn Jarir. The jabbar is one who frequently compels (jabr), that is, forces people and oppresses them. Everyone who is arrogant toward people and wrongs them is a jabbar. It is used in the Qur'an for one of fierce violence, in His saying: ﴿And when you strike, you strike as jabbarin﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 130], and for one who repeatedly kills, in (p-381) His saying: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday? You intend only to be a jabbar in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 19], and the verse. The apparent view is that His saying "asiyyan" is the pattern fa'ul, in which the waw was changed to ya' and assimilated into the ya', according to the well-known morphological rule that Ibn Malik codified in the Khulasa with his saying:

"If a preceding waw or ya' is quiescent and joined, and not from an extended vowel, then change the waw to ya' and assimilate it."

"And the irregular 'mu'tan' (i.e., 'mu'tan') other than what has been written."

So the origin of "asiyyan," according to this, is "asawiyyan," like "sabur." That is, one who frequently disobeys. It may be that its origin is the pattern fa'il, which is also among the intensive forms, as Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 15]. Ibn Jarir said: "And peace is upon him," meaning: security for him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: What appears to me is that it is the customary greeting, and it is more noble than security, because security is attained for him by the negation of disobedience from him, which is the least of his ranks. The nobility lies in Allah greeting him and extending peace to him in the situations in which a person is in the utmost weakness and need, little resource, and poverty before Allah, the Great, the Mighty.

End of Ibn 'Atiyya's words as transmitted through al-Qurtubi in his tafsir of this verse. The two views return to one thing, because the meaning of "salam" is greeting, security, and safety from what is disliked. The statement of whoever said it is security means that this security is from Allah, and the greeting from Allah means security and safety from what is disliked. The apparent and immediate meaning is that His saying ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born﴾ is a greeting from Allah to Yahya, and its meaning is security and safety. His saying ﴿And peace is upon him﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and what justified beginning with it though it is indefinite (nakirah) is that it has the sense of supplication (du'a'). He singled out these three times for peace, which are the time of his birth, the time of his death, and the time of his resurrection, in His saying ﴿the day he was born and the day he dies﴾ and the verse, because they are more lonely than others. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: A person is most lonely in three situations: the day he is born, when he sees himself removed from what he was in; the day he dies, when he sees people he had not seen; and the day he is raised, when he sees himself in a great gathering. He said: So Allah honored Yahya ibn Zakariyya in them, singling him out with peace upon him in them. This was transmitted from him by Ibn Jarir and others.

Al-Tabari reported in his tafsir of this verse, with his chain, from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: When 'Isa and Yahya met, 'Isa said to him: "Ask forgiveness for me, for you are better than me." The other said: "Ask forgiveness for me, for you are better than me." 'Isa said: "You are better than me. I greeted myself, and Allah greeted you." Al-Qurtubi transmitted this statement that Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him. Then he said: Some scholars drew from this verse, regarding the greeting, the superiority of 'Isa, by saying that his self-assurance (idlal) (p-382) in greeting himself, and his station with Allah, the Exalted, which required that, when it was decreed and recounted in the Revealed Book, is greater in rank than that he should greet him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Each has its aspect. End of al-Qurtubi's words. The apparent meaning is that Allah's peace upon Yahya in His saying ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born﴾ [Maryam: 15] is greater than 'Isa's peace upon himself in his saying ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 33], as is evident.

**Warning (tanbih)**

The *fatha* in His words ﴿the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 15] may be a *fatha* of i'rab (grammatical inflection) in the accusative on the three adverbs of time (*zarfiyyah*). It may also be a *fatha* of binā' (indeclinability, fixed final vowel), since such adverbs may be indeclinable. The better view is that the *fatha* in ﴿the day he was born﴾ is a *fatha* of binā', while the *fatha* in ﴿and the day he dies and the day he is raised﴾ is a *fatha* of naṣb (accusative i'rab). This is because a time-adverb preceding a past verb is better indeclinable than inflected, while one preceding a present verb or a nominal sentence is better inflected than indeclinable, as Ibn Mālik (*al-Khulāṣa*, his versified grammar) fixed it in his words:

؎ Make it indeclinable or inflect what is like *idh* when it is made to act; and choose indeclinability for the one that precedes a verb built (on a fixed vowel).

؎ And before an inflected verb or a subject, inflect; whoever builds it, will not be refuted.

The cases in such a construction are four.

The first: the mentioned time-adverb is added to a verbal clause whose verb is indeclinable by original construction, which is the past tense, as in the words of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī:

؎ At a time when I rebuked white hair for (my) youth, and I said, "Has it not yet (ceased)? I am awake, and the white hair is a deterrent."

So the indeclinability of the adverb in such a case is better, though its inflection is permissible.

The second: the mentioned time-adverb is added to a verbal clause whose verb is indeclinable by accidental construction, such as the present tense built because it is joined to the feminine plural *nūn*, as in the words of another:

؎ I will certainly draw my heart away from them by dreaming, at a time when they make every gentle person lose his patience.

The ruling for this is as for the previous case.

The third: it is added to a verbal clause whose verb is inflected, as in the words of Abū Ṣakhr al-Hudhalī:

؎ When I say this at a time when I forget, the breeze of the east wind stirs me, from where the dawn rises.

So the inflection of such a case is better, and its indeclinability is permissible.

The fourth: the mentioned time-adverb is added to a nominal clause, as in the words of the poet:

؎ Do you not know, O ʿAmra, by God, that I am noble at a time when noble people are few?

And the words of another:

؎ He remembered what he remembered of Sulaymā, at a time of contact, unmindful of the (one who) is close.

The ruling for this is as for the previous cases. Know that these modes apply only to the indefinite past time-adverb.
