As for an indefinite time-adverb with future meaning, as in His words ﴿and the day he dies and the day he is raised﴾, it is added only to verbal clauses and not to nominal ones. So the three modes mentioned apply to it, but not the fourth. Ibn Mālik permitted its addition to a nominal clause rarely, as in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿the day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 13], and in the words of Sawād ibn Qārib:

؎ Be for me an intercessor on a day when no one with intercession will avail (even) a thread for Sawād ibn Qārib.

Because the time-adverb in the verse and the verse of poetry mentioned is future, not past. As for His words, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾, Abū Ḥayyān said: in it is an indication that he is one of the martyrs, because of His words, may He be exalted, concerning them: ﴿Nay, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 169].

The one who wrote these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The basis of this deduction is that the *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier) is a restriction on its governing word and a description of its referent. Accordingly, his being raised is restricted to his being alive, and that is the life of the martyrs. But this is not entirely evident, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

This is the summary of what Allah the Exalted mentioned in this noble surah of the attributes of Yaḥyā. He mentioned some of his attributes in another place, as in His words in "Āl ʿImrān": ﴿So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: "Allah gives you good news of Yaḥyā, confirming a word from Allah, and a noble leader, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 39]. The meaning of his being ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾ is that he confirms ʿĪsā. ʿĪsā was called a word because Allah brought him into being by a word, which is His saying "Be," and he was. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Maryam, is only the Messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Maryam﴾ (the verse) [al-Nisāʾ: 171], and He said: ﴿When the angels said, "O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good news of a word from Him"﴾ (the verse) [Āl ʿImrān: 45]. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes regarding the meaning of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿confirming a word from Allah﴾. It has been said that the intended "word" is the Book, meaning: confirming the Book of Allah. The word "kalimah" in the Qur'an is applied to a meaningful statement, as in His words: ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled in goodness﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 137], and His words: ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-Anʿām: 115], and His words: ﴿No! It is a word he is saying﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 100], and so on through other verses.

We have omitted the remaining opinions because of the evident weakness of them, and the correct view, if Allah wills, is what we have mentioned.

His words ﴿and a noble leader (sayyid)﴾: the morphological pattern of *sayyid* is *fayʿil*. Its root is (s-w-d). The *yāʾ* of the augmented *faʿīl* pattern became quiescent before the *wāw* that occupies the position of the middle radical, so the *wāw* was changed to *yāʾ* according to the morphological rule referred to in the *Khulāṣa* by his words:

؎ If a *wāw* or *yāʾ* that precedes it becomes quiescent…

(the two verses mentioned earlier). Its origin is from *al-sawād*, which is a large multitude of people. So the *sayyid* is one whom a large multitude of people obey and follow. The proof that the middle radical of the root is *wāw* is that you say of it *sāda yasūdu* with *wāw*, and you say *sawwadūhu* when they make him a leader. Doubling (the middle radical) restores it to its original form. From this is the saying of ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl al-ʿĀmirī:

؎ Though I am the son of the leader of ʿĀmir and its famous horseman in every gathering.

؎ ʿĀmir did not make me a leader by inheritance; God refused that I should be elevated by a mother or a father.

Another said:

؎ Indeed there are people who made you a leader out of need for a leader, if only they could find a (true) leader.

The fame of such usage suffices instead of explaining it. The verse contains evidence for applying *sayyid* to whoever leads among people. It has come in the two *Ṣaḥīḥs* and others that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Indeed this son of mine is a sayyid," the hadith. He (ﷺ) also said, when Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, may Allah be pleased with him, came to pass judgment concerning the Banū Qurayẓa: "Stand up for your sayyid."

The verification of the meaning of His words ﴿and chaste (ḥaṣūr)﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 39] is that he is the one who restrained himself from women while having the ability to approach them, out of devotion (tabattul) and detachment for the worship of Allah. That was permissible in his law. As for the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ), it is marriage and not tabattul. As for the statement of one who said that *ḥaṣūr* is *faʿūl* in the sense of *mafʿūl*, and that he is "restricted from women" because he is impotent and unable to approach them, this is not correct, because impotence is a defect and deficiency in men, and it is not from his own action so that he be praised for it. So the correct view, if Allah wills, is what we have mentioned, and many scholars have chosen it. As for the statement of one who said that *ḥaṣūr* is the one who does not join the people in gambling, as al-Akhṭal said:

؎ And a drinker who gave me delight with the cup, not one who is restrained, nor one who has no part in it (i.e., gambling).

This is a statement that is not correct regarding the meaning of the verse. Rather its meaning is what we have mentioned, although applying *ḥaṣūr* to that is linguistically valid.

As for His words ﴿and a prophet (nabiyyan)﴾ according to the reading of Nāfiʿ with the *hamzah*, its meaning is clear. It is *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl*, from *al-naba'*, which is news of importance, because revelation is news of importance that Allah informs him of. As for the reading with a doubled *yāʾ*, some scholars said its meaning is the same as the reading of Nāfiʿ, except that the *hamzah* was changed into a *yāʾ* and assimilated into the *yāʾ* that precedes it. On this view it is like the two canonical readings in His words: ﴿The postponement is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37], with *hamzah* and doubling of the *yāʾ*. Other scholars said: according to the reading of the majority, it is from *al-nubuwwah*, meaning elevation, because of the elevated rank and nobility of the Prophet.

The righteous (al-ṣāliḥūn) are those whose beliefs, deeds, words and intentions are sound. Righteousness (al-ṣalāḥ) is the opposite of corruption (al-fasād). Allah the Exalted described Yaḥyā with righteousness together with those of the prophets whom He described with it in Sūrat al-Anʿām, in His words: ﴿And Zakariyyā and Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā and Ilyās, each of them among the righteous﴾ [al-Anʿām: 85].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And mention in the Book Mary, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to mention in the Book, which is the Qur'an, "Mary," when she withdrew from her family to an eastern place. His saying ﴿withdrew﴾ means she moved away from them and separated herself from them, isolated from them. His saying ﴿a place toward the east﴾ means a place on the eastern side of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). As for His saying, the Exalted, in this noble verse, "when" (idh) relating to "Mary," it is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because times include what is in them in the manner that a container includes what it contains. This was stated by al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf, and Abu al-Baqa' and Abu Hayyan objected to him on this point. The apparent view is that their objections fall away, and that the correct position is with him, and Allah knows best.

He does not mention here anything about the lineage of Mary or the story of her birth. He has explained in other places that she is the daughter of Imran, and that her mother vowed what was in her womb to be dedicated (muharraran), meaning for the service of Bayt al-Maqdis, thinking that she would bear a male child, "so she gave birth to her, Mary." In stating that she is the daughter of Imran, He said: ﴿And Mary, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12], and He mentioned the story of her birth in Al 'Imran in His saying: ﴿When the wife of Imran said, "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as dedicated, so accept it from me. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing."﴾ ﴿And when she gave birth to her, she said, "My Lord, I have given birth to a female," and Allah knew best what she had delivered, "and the male is not like the female. And I have named her Mary, and I seek refuge for her with You and for her descendants from Satan, the expelled."﴾ ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good growth and entrusted her to Zakariya. Every time Zakariya entered upon her in the prayer niche, he found with her provision. He said, "O Mary, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35-36]

His saying ﴿makanan﴾ (a place) is in the accusative because it is an adverb of place (zarf).

(p-386) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So she took a screen apart from them, and We sent to her Our Spirit﴾. The most apparent of the opinions is that what is meant by His saying "Our Spirit" is Jibril (Gabriel).

What supports this is His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 26:193], and His saying: ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) brought it down from your Lord in truth﴾ [an-Nahl 16:102]. Its attribution to Allah is an attribution of honour and dignity.

] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then he appeared to her as a man in every respect﴾.

His appearing to her as a man in every respect, as mentioned in the verse, indicates that he was an angel and not a human being. This implication is stated explicitly by Him, may He be exalted, in His saying: ﴿When the angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a Word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:45]. The one who gave her this good tidings is the same one who said to her here: ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure son﴾ [Maryam 19:19]. And His saying: ﴿a man in every respect﴾ are two states (hal) referring to the subject pronoun in His saying "appeared to her" (tamaththala laha).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure son."﴾ In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that this Spirit, who is Jibril (Gabriel), said to her that he is the messenger of her Lord, in order to bestow upon her, i.e., to give her, a boy (ghulaman), i.e., a child (waladan), "zakiyyan," i.e., pure from sins and disobediences, abundant in blessings. In other places He has explained many of the attributes of this boy who was bestowed upon her, who is Isa (Jesus), upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Isa, son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah]﴾ and ﴿He will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and [he will be] among the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45-46], and His saying: ﴿And He will teach him the Book and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel﴾ and ﴿[and make him] a messenger to the Children of Israel: "Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord: that I will create for you from clay like the form of a bird, then I will breathe into it and it will be a bird by permission of Allah. And I will heal the blind and the leper, and I will give life to the dead by permission of Allah. And I will inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 48-49], and other verses containing the attributes of this boy. Abu 'Amr and Warsh from Nafi', and Qalun from him as well (by one of the two transmissions from him), read this word "li-yahaba" with a fatha on the ya' after the lam, i.e., that He (your Lord) may give you a pure boy. The rest read "li-ahaba" with the hamzah of the first person speaker, i.e., I (the messenger) from your Lord will give you a pure boy. Regarding the attribution of the giving to himself according to the reading of the majority, there is a well-known difference among the scholars. The most apparent of the opinions in this matter, in my view, is that what is meant by Jibril's saying to her, ﴿I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy,﴾ i.e., that I may be a cause for the giving of the boy (p-387) by blowing into the garment that reached the private part, whereby her pregnancy with Isa came about. Exalted is He, in Surat at-Tahrim, explained that this blowing was into her private part, in His saying: ﴿And Maryam, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We blew into it of Our Spirit﴾ [At-Tahrim: 12]. The pronoun in His saying "fihi" refers to her private part. This does not contradict His saying in al-Anbiya': ﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We blew into her of Our Spirit﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 91], because the blowing reached the private part and from it came the pregnancy of Isa. On this basis az-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, interpreted the verse.

Some scholars said: Jibril's saying ﴿to give you a boy﴾ is a relating of the saying of Allah, exalted is He, and according to this the meaning is: "I am only the messenger of your Lord, and He has said to me: I have sent you to give a boy." The first is more apparent, and the second is far from the outward meaning of the wording. Some scholars said: He attributed the giving to himself because the announcing of it came from him. With this al-Qurtubi began his tafsir. The most apparent of these is the first, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She said: "How can I have a boy when no man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste?"﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Exalted, mentions that when Jibril (Gabriel) gave Maryam (Mary) the good news of the pure boy, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, she said: ﴿How can I have a boy?﴾ [Maryam: 20], meaning: how can I give birth to a boy when the situation is that no man has touched me, that is, no husband has had intercourse with me in marriage, ﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾, meaning: I have not been an adulteress. Since the touching of men, whether lawful or unlawful, has been negated from her, how then would she conceive? The apparent meaning is that her question is an inquiry and seeking of knowledge about the manner in which the mentioned boy would be conceived, because, with no touching of men, the manner had not become clear to her. It is also possible that her question is an expression of amazement at the perfect power of Allah, Exalted is He. What Allah, Mighty and Exalted, mentioned of her saying here, He also mentioned of her in Surah "Ali 'Imran" in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When the angels said: "O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, 'Isa, son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah]"﴾ ﴿"And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and he will be among the righteous"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45], ﴿She said: "My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 47]. Her limiting herself in the verse of "Ali 'Imran" to her saying, ﴿when no man has touched me﴾, indicates that the touching of man that is negated from her includes touching by marriage and touching by fornication, as is the apparent meaning. Accordingly, her saying in Surah "Maryam": ﴿when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 20], appears to be that her saying ﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾ is a specification after a generalization, since the touching of man includes the lawful and the unlawful. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf, in his interpretation of His saying here: ﴿when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste﴾: he made the touching (al-mass) an expression for lawful marriage, because it is a euphemism for it, as in His saying: ﴿before you have touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], ﴿or you have touched women﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]; and fornication is not like that, rather it is said of it: "he committed fornication with her" (fajara bi-ha), "he defiled himself with her" (khabutha bi-ha) and what resembles that, and it is not fitting that euphemisms and etiquettes be observed in it. End of quote.

The first view is more apparent, and the verse of "Ali 'Imran" indicates it. What supports it is that the word "bashar" (man) is indefinite in the context of negation, so it encompasses every man, and thus the touching of every man is negated, whoever he may be. Al-Baghiyy (the unchaste woman) is one who openly and notoriously commits fornication. Its form is fa'ul according to al-Mubarrad, in which a waw and a ya' came together, the first of which was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed to ya' and assimilated into the ya', and what preceded it was given a kasra for the sake of the ya', as it was given a kasra in 'isiyy and dili(y), plural of 'asa and dalw, as we have mentioned this many times. The one who says that the origin of "al-baghiyy" is fa'ul says: if its origin were fa'il, the feminine ta' would have attached to it, because it is obligatory in fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active). Ibn Jinni said in Kitab al-Tamam: the origin of al-baghiyy is on the pattern of fa'il, and if it were fa'ul, it would be said: baghu', as it is said: fulan nahu' 'an al-munkar. On this view, the non-attachment of the ta' of femininity may be answered by saying that al-baghiyy is a descriptor specific to females, and a man is called ba'in, not baghiyy, as Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr. Descriptors specific to females do not need the ta' of distinction between male and female, like ha'id, as Ibn Malik established in al-Kafiyah with his saying:

"Of the descriptors specific to females, what is independent of the ta' is not restricted, because the wording is explicit."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 21:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He said: "So it will be. Your Lord said: 'It is easy for Me.'"﴾

We have already given the explanation of this verse in full in the story of Zakariyya, so there is no need to repeat it here.

The words of Jibril to Maryam in this verse, ﴿He said: "So it will be. Your Lord said: 'It is easy for Me.'"﴾ [Maryam: 21], mean: you will bear that boy who was promised to you without any human touching you. Allah, the Exalted, has also alluded to the meaning of this verse in Surah "Al 'Imran" in His words: ﴿She said: "My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?" He said: "So it will be. Allah creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 47].

* *

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And that We may make him a sign for the people and a mercy from Us, and it is a matter decreed﴾. In this noble verse, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, mentions that among the wisdoms of His creating 'Isa from a woman without a husband is that He would make this a sign for people, that is, an indication showing the perfection of His power, and that He, the Exalted, creates what He wills in the manner He wills. If He wills, He creates from a female without a male, as He did with 'Isa; and if He wills, He creates from a male without a female, as He did with Hawwa', as He stated in His words: ﴿And He created from it its mate﴾ [An-Nisa': 1], that is, He created from that soul, which is Adam, his mate Hawwa'. If He wills, He creates without either male or female together, as He did with Adam; and if He wills, He creates from a male and a female, as He did with all the children of Adam. Glory be to Allah, the Mighty, the Capable over everything.

What the Exalted mentioned in this noble verse, that He made 'Isa a sign in that his mother bore him without a husband, He also alluded to in "al-Anbiya'" in His words: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91], and in "al-Mu'minun" in His words: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign, and We sheltered them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50].

The words of the Exalted in this noble verse: ﴿And that We may make him a sign for the people﴾ [Maryam: 21] contain an ellipsis that the context indicates. Az-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "﴿And that We may make him a sign for the people﴾ is a statement of purpose (ta'lil) whose object of purpose is omitted, meaning: and that We may make him a sign for the people, We did that; or it is coordinated with an implied purpose, meaning: that We may show by him Our power and that We may make him a sign." A similar example is: ﴿And Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth, and that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 22], and His words: ﴿And thus We established Yusuf in the land, and that We might teach him﴾ [Yusuf: 21]. End of quotation.

His words in this verse: ﴿and a mercy from Us﴾, that is, for whoever believes in him. As for whoever disbelieves in him, he has not sought mercy for himself, as the Exalted said about our Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107].

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and it is a matter decreed﴾ [Maryam: 21], that is, the existence of that boy from you was a matter decreed, meaning predetermined from eternity, written in the Preserved Tablet, which must occur. So it is certain to happen without doubt.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 22:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she conceived him, and withdrew with him to a remote place﴾ ﴿And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said: "Would that I had died before this and had been a thing forgotten and utterly forgotten!"﴾. In this noble verse, He, exalted and majestic, mentions that Maryam conceived Jesus. His saying, ﴿she conceived him﴾, means Jesus. ﴿And withdrew with him﴾ means she secluded herself with him and went far away, isolating herself from her people. ﴿To a remote place﴾ means in a distant place. The majority of scholars hold that the place mentioned is Bethlehem (Bayt Lahm), though there are other opinions besides this.

His saying, ﴿The pains of childbirth drove her﴾, means the labour pains compelled her to the trunk of a palm tree, that is, the trunk of a palm tree in that place. The Arabs say: "Fulan came" (jā'a fulān), and "another made him come" (ajā'ahu ghayruh), when he drove him to come. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"And a neighbour who travelled, relying on us, fear and hope drove him to come."

And the saying of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

"When we charged a true charge, we surprised you, and the labour pains, at the foot of the mountain."

Al-makhāḍ (the labour pains) means al-ṭalq, which is the pain of childbirth. It was called makhāḍ from al-makhḍ, which is the violent movement, due to the intense movement of the foetus in her womb when it wants to come out.

His saying: ﴿She said: "Would that I had died before this and had been a thing forgotten and utterly forgotten!"﴾ [Maryam: 23] means she wished that she had died before that and had not been anything worth mentioning. Now, when you understand the meaning of these two verses, know that here He did not explain the manner of her conception of him, nor did He explain whether this (matter) for which she withdrew from them, and for which she wished she had died before that and been a forgotten thing, was her fear that they would accuse her of fornication, and that she had brought that boy from fornication, whether she had fallen into it or been spared from it. However, He, exalted, has explained all of that in another place. He indicated that the manner of her conception was that He breathed into her, and the breath reached her private part, so conception occurred through that, as He said: ﴿And Maryam, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12], and He said: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾, the verse [al-Anbiya': 91]. The view held by the majority of scholars is that the meant breath is the breath of Jibril into her by the permission of Allah, so she conceived. This is indicated by the reading of the majority in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy﴾ [Maryam: 19], as has preceded. Ascribing that breath to Himself in His saying ﴿so We breathed﴾ does not contradict this, because Jibril only performed it by His permission, command and will. He, exalted, is the One who created the foetus from that breath. Jibril has no power to create the foetus from that breath, and because it was by His permission, will and command, exalted is He, it is impossible that the mentioned breath or the existence of the foetus from it could occur except by His will, exalted and majestic. Therefore He ascribed it to Himself. And Allah knows best.

As for the saying of one who said that the private part into which the angel breathed was the opening of her garment, apparently falling down, but rather the breath that entered the opening of the garment reached the known private part, and so the conception occurred, [this is not accepted].

Allah, exalted, has explained in other places that what she feared, namely their slander of her with lewdness, had indeed befallen her, but Allah cleared her of it. This is like His saying about them: ﴿They said: "O Maryam, you have certainly brought a thing unprecedented"﴾ [Maryam: 27], meaning lewdness;

and His saying about them: ﴿O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 28], meaning: "How then did you commit fornication and bring this child?";

and like His saying, exalted: ﴿And for their disbelief, and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾ [al-Nisa': 156].

His saying: ﴿a remote place﴾. Al-qaṣiyy means the distant. From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"You will surely sit in the seat of the distant one, far from me, you who are filthy and detestable,
Or you will swear by your exalted Lord that I am not the father of that child."

This remote place Allah, exalted, described in another place with His saying: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign, and We gave them refuge on a high ground, one of stability and flowing water﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50].

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿and withdrew with him﴾, meaning she withdrew while he was in her womb. The demonstrative in His saying "this" (hādhā) refers to the pregnancy and the labour pains which befell her for delivery.

As for His saying in this noble verse about her: ﴿and was a thing forgotten﴾, al-nisy and al-nasy, with kasra and with fatha, are that which is supposed to be discarded and forgotten because of its insignificance, such as menstrual rags, and like a peg or a staff, and the like. From the speech of the Arabs, when they departed from a dwelling, is their saying: "Look at your nasā'akum" (your discarded things), the plural of nisy, meaning the insignificant things which are naturally left and forgotten, like a staff and a peg, and the like. So her saying ﴿I was a nisy﴾ means a trivial, insignificant thing which by nature should be left and customarily forgotten. Her saying ﴿mansiyyan﴾ means that this trivial thing, which by its nature is left and forgotten, has indeed been forgotten and discarded in fact, so the forgetting which is its due has occurred. The opinions of the commentators on the verse return to what we have mentioned. From the use of nisy for what we have mentioned is the saying of al-Kumayt:

"Would you make us a bridge for the dog of Quda'a, while we are not an insignificant forgotten thing among Mu'add, nor a cause of entry?"

So his saying "bi-nasy'" means a trivial forgotten thing. And the saying of al-Shanfara:

"As if for her, on the earth, is a nasy she recounts to her mother, and if she speaks to you, she cuts short (her speech from shyness)."

So his saying "nasyan" means a thing she left and forgot. His saying "tabalat" with fatha on the ta', sukun on the ba' with a single dot, and fatha on the lam after it, with the feminine ta', means she cuts off her speech out of modesty. Al-balt in the language means cutting.

Nafi', Hafs from 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yā laytanī mittu﴾ with kasra on the mim, and the rest read "mutu" with damma on the mim. Hafs from 'Asim and Hamzah read "wa kuntu nasyan" with fatha on the nun, and the rest with kasra. Both are eloquent dialects and both are sound readings.

* *

Note (tanbīh)

The reading "mittu" with kasra on the mim is often obscure to students of knowledge as to its basis, because from the verb "mata yamutu" the form "mittu" with kasra on the mim cannot properly arise. The basis of the reading with kasra on the mim is that it comes from "māta yamātu", like "khāfa yakhāfu", not from "māta yamūtu", like "qāla yaqūlu". So the word "māta" in it has two eloquent Arabic dialects. The first of them is "mawita" with fatha on the waw, so the waw became alif according to the morphological rule indicated by his saying in the Khulasa:

"From ya' or waw, with movement, make alif after a connected fatha, when the second is vowelled..." etc.

And the present tense of this fathah-form is "yamūtu" with damma, by analogy. In this and similar cases, if the verb is attributed to the ta' of the subject or its nun, the middle radical drops due to weakness, and the first radical takes a vowel corresponding to the middle radical. The vowel corresponding to waw is damma, so you say "mutu" with damma on the mim, and nothing else is permissible.

The second is that it is "mawita" with kasra on the waw. The waw became alif according to the rule mentioned just above, and the present tense of this is "yamātu" with fatha, because the form "fa'ila" with kasra on the middle radical is conjugated in the present with "fa'ala" with fatha on the middle radical, as Ibn Malik said in the Lamiyya:

"And make the vowel of the kasra in the stem of fa'ala a fatha."

Excepted from this rule are certain well-known words that are transmitted (samā'iyya), which are memorized and not analogised upon. What is established in the science of morphology is that every triliteral hollow verb, meaning one whose middle radical is weak, if it is of the pattern fa'ila with kasra on the middle radical, or fa'ula with damma on it, then when it is attributed to the ta' of the subject or its nun, its middle radical drops due to weakness, and the vowel of the dropped middle radical is transferred to the first radical, so the first radical takes kasra if it is from fa'ila with kasra on the middle, and takes damma if it is from fa'ula with damma. An example of the first is "mittu" from "māta yamātu", because its original form was "mawita" with kasra, and likewise "khāfa yakhāfu" and "nāma yanāmu", for you say of them "mittu" with kasra on the mim, "nimtu" with kasra on the nun, and "khiftu" with kasra on the kha', because the vowel of the middle radical was transferred to the first radical, and it is kasra. An example of it with damma is "ṭāla", whose original form is "ṭawula" with damma on the waw, so you say of it "ṭultu" with damma, due to the transfer of the middle radical's vowel to the first radical. As for when the triliteral is of fa'ala with fatha on the middle radical, like "māta yamūtu" and "qāla yaqūlu", the middle radical drops due to weakness, and the first radical is vowelled with a vowel corresponding to the dropped middle radical. So the first radical takes damma if the dropped middle radical was waw, as in "māta yamūtu" and "qāla yaqūlu", and you say "mutu" and "qultu" with damma. And the first radical takes kasra if the dropped middle radical was ya', as in "bā'a" and "sāra", and you say "bi'tu" and "sirtu" with kasra in both. To this Ibn Malik alluded in the Lamiyya with his saying:

"And transfer to the first radical of the triliteral, in the form of the middle radical when it is weak, and when the subject-pronoun 'nā' is connected or with its nunation (the first radical takes the vowel), and when it is opened, there results from it the vowel homogeneous with that middle radical, transferred."

And know that "māta yamātu", from "fa'ila" with kasra conjugating in the present with fatha, is an eloquent dialect, and of it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"My little daughter, lady of girls, live, and we are not safe that you will die."

As for "māta yamītu", it is a weak dialect. One of the literati of the land of Shinqit (Mauritania) alluded to the three dialects, the two eloquent and the reprehensible, in a rajaz verse, which is his saying:

"Whose wife prevented him from spending the night: he died, he dies, he dies (mātā yamūtu, yamātu, yamītu)."

As for the scholars' opinions about the length of time Maryam carried Jesus before the birth, we have not mentioned them, because there is no evidence for any of them. The most apparent is that it was a pregnancy like the usual pregnancy of women, even though its origin was outside the customary course. And Allah, exalted, knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then he called her from beneath her: "Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a stream."﴾ First, know that this word has two canonical readings (qira'at sab'iyyah, the seven recognized readings). Nafi', Hafs from 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿فَناداها مِن تَحْتِها﴾ [Maryam: 24] with a kasrah on the mim, taking "min" as a preposition (harf jarr), and with the taa' of "tahtaha" in the genitive, because the adverbial noun is governed by "min." Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Shu'bah from 'Asim read "fanadaha man tahtaha," with a fathah on the mim of "man," taking it as a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) that is the subject (fa'il) of "nada," meaning: the one who was beneath her called to her. With the fathah on the taa' of "tahtaha," the first reading makes the subject of the calling a hidden pronoun, while on the second reading the subject is the relative noun "man."

Having understood this, know that the scholars differ over who this caller was, referred to in one reading by a pronoun and in the other by the relative noun "man." Some scholars said he was 'Isa (Jesus). Others said he was Jibril (Gabriel). Among those who said "the one who called Maryam was Jibril" are Ibn 'Abbas, 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one of the two narrations from him. The proponents of this view said: 'Isa did not speak until she brought him to her people.

(p-394) Among those who said the caller was 'Isa at the moment she gave birth to him were Ubayy, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Wahb ibn Munabbih, Sa'id ibn Jubayr in the other narration from him, and Ibn Zayd.

Having learned this, know that whoever holds that it was the angel says: "Jibril called to her from a place beneath her," because she was on a raised mound, and he called to her from a place lower than her. Some proponents of this view say: Jibril was beneath her, receiving the child as a midwife (qabilah) receives it. According to this view the apparent meaning is the first. On the reading "fanadaha man tahtaha" with the fathah of the mim and of the taa' of "tahtaha," the proponents of this view say the meaning is: "he who was beneath her called to her," that is, in a place lower than her place, or he was beneath her receiving the child as a midwife does, though this latter possibility is weak, as we have previously mentioned. That is, he is Jibril. On the first reading, according to this view, "fanadaha" refers to him, that is, Jibril from beneath her; on the second reading, "fanadaha min tahtaha" means: the one beneath her, who is Jibril. As for the view that the caller was 'Isa, the meaning on the first reading is: "fanadaha huwa," that is, the newborn whom she had delivered from beneath her, since he was beneath her at the delivery. On the second reading, "fanadaha man tahtaha" means: the one beneath her, who is the aforementioned newborn present beneath her at the delivery. Among those who chose that the caller was 'Isa is Ibn Jarir al-Tabari in his tafsir, and Abu Hayyan favored it in al-Bahr, while al-Qurtubi favored that it was Jibril.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The more apparent of the two views to me is that the one who called to her was her son 'Isa. Two indications support this. The first is that a pronoun refers to the nearest previously mentioned noun unless there is a decisive evidence diverting it, which obliges returning to that. The nearest mentioned noun in the verse is 'Isa, not Jibril, because Allah said: ﴿فَحَمَلَتْهُ﴾, meaning 'Isa, ﴿فانْتَبَذَتْ بِهِ﴾, that is, with 'Isa.

Then He said after it: ﴿فَناداها﴾. What appears and comes to mind from the context is that it is 'Isa.

The second indication is that when she brought him to her people carrying him, and they said to her what they said, she pointed to 'Isa so that they would speak to him, as Allah said about her: ﴿فَأشارَتْ إلَيْهِ قالُوا كَيْفَ نُكَلِّمُ مَن كانَ في المَهْدِ صَبِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 29], "So she pointed to him. They said: How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?" Her pointing to him so that they would speak to him is evidence that she already knew he would speak by way of a departure from the customary order, because of his calling to her when she gave birth to him. It is with this latter indication that Sa'id ibn Jubayr, in one of his two narrations, argued that it was 'Isa, as many have transmitted from him. The "an" in His saying "alla tahzani" is the explanatory "an" (an mufassirah), meaning "that is." The rule for the explanatory "an" is that it is preceded by a meaning of speech without its letters, as here: the calling in it carries the sense of saying without its letters. The meaning of it being explanatory is that the speech following it is the meaning of what precedes it, so the calling mentioned before it is: ﴿لا تَحْزَنِي قَدْ جَعَلَ رَبُّكَ تَحْتَكِ سَرِيًّا﴾, "Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a stream."

(p-395) The scholars differed about what is meant by "sariyy" here. Some said it is the jadwal, which is a small river, because Allah made a river flow for her beneath her. On this view, His saying ﴿فَكُلِي﴾, "So eat," means of the fresh dates mentioned in His saying ﴿تُساقِطْ عَلَيْكِ رُطَبًا جَنِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 25], "shake toward you fresh ripe dates," and ﴿واشْرَبِي﴾, "and drink" [Maryam: 26], that is, from the river mentioned in His saying ﴿قَدْ جَعَلَ رَبُّكِ تَحْتَكِ سَرِيًّا﴾. The use of "sariyy" for the jadwal is well known in the speech of the Arabs. From it is the saying of Labid in his Mu'allaqah:

"So they both crossed the breadth of the sariyy, and split a current, its bank-edges mutually adjacent."

And Labid's saying also, describing palm trees growing by the water of the river:

"Withered ones, the rock enjoys them, and their sariyy: groves whose soft (branches) have vines among them."

And the saying of another:

"Easy of disposition, generous, possessor of gifts, like the sariyy that the rivers feed."

So His saying "sariyyan," and their saying "al-sariyy," mean the jadwal. Likewise the saying of the rajiz:

"A peaceful one, you see its palm-dates tall, when it gurgles in the sariyy, gushing abundantly."

Some people of knowledge said: "sariyy" means 'Isa, and "sariyy" also means a man who has nobility and manliness. It is said of his act: saruwa with a damma, and sara with a fatha, yasru sarwan in both; and sariya with a kasra, yasri sira', sira'an, and sarwan, when he becomes noble. The plural of this sariyy is asriya' by analogy, and surawa' and sara'ah with a fatha. Sibawayh said that sara'ah with a fatha is a collective noun (ism jam'), not a plural. From it is the saying of al-Afwah al-Awdi:

"People are not made right in chaos, having no nobles; nor are they (right) when their ignorant ones lead."

The plural of sara'ah is saraWat, and from it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Hatim:

"And 'Amrah, of the noble women, their sleeves emit musk."

And from the use of "sariyy" in the sense of noble is the saying of the poet:

"You meet the noblest of men with his own self, and the son of the noble, when he is noble, is the more noble of the two."

His saying "asraha-huma" means "the more noble of them both," as stated in al-Lisan.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The more apparent of the two views to me is that "sariyy" in the verse is the small river (p-396), and the evidence for that is two matters:

The first: the indication from the Qur'an. His saying ﴿فَكُلِي واشْرَبِي﴾ is an indication that the food and drink are the very things previously named as a favor in His saying ﴿قَدْ جَعَلَ رَبُّكِ تَحْتَكِ سَرِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 24] and His saying ﴿تُساقِطْ عَلَيْكِ رُطَبًا جَنِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 25]. Likewise His saying ﴿وَآوَيْناهُما إلى رَبْوَةٍ ذاتِ قَرارٍ ومَعِينٍ﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], "and We gave them refuge on a height with settled ground and running water," since "ma'in" is flowing water, and the apparent meaning is that it is the jadwal called "sariyy" in this verse. And Allah knows best.

The second matter: a hadith that has come about this from the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: A marfu' hadith has come with this. al-Tabarani said: Abu Shu'ayb al-Harrani narrated to us, Yahya ibn 'Abd Allah al-Babili narrated to us, Ayyub ibn Nahik narrated to us, I heard 'Ikrimah, the client of Ibn 'Abbas, say, I heard Ibn 'Umar say: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The sariyy that Allah mentioned to Maryam, 'Your Lord has placed beneath you a sariyy,' is a river that Allah brought forth for her to drink from." This is a very strange (gharib) hadith through this route, and this Ayyub ibn Nahik is al-Hubuli. Abu Hatim al-Razi said of him: weak (da'if). Abu Zur'ah said: munkar al-hadith. Abu al-Fath al-Azdi said: matruk al-hadith (abandoned). End of Ibn Kathir's words.

Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Kafi al-Shaf fi Takhrij Ahadith al-Kashshaf, regarding the aforementioned hadith: It was reported by al-Tabarani in al-Saghir, and by Ibn 'Adi, from the narration of Abu Sinan Sa'id ibn Sinan, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', from the Prophet ﷺ regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿قَدْ جَعَلَ رَبُّكِ تَحْتَكِ سَرِيًّا﴾, that he said: "The sariyy is the river." al-Tabarani said: No one raised it from Abu Ishaq except Abu Sinan, and Yahya ibn Mu'awiyah narrated it from him, and he is weak. 'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted it from al-Thawri, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', as a mawquf (companion's statement), and likewise al-Bukhari mentioned it in suspended form (ta'liq) from Waki', from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Adam, from Isra'il, likewise, and al-Hakim transmitted it through another route from Abu Ishaq as mawquf. And on the subject there is a narration from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The sariyy that He mentioned to Maryam is a river that Allah brought forth for her to drink from," reported by al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, in the biography of 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Umar, and its narrator from 'Ikrimah, Ayyub ibn Nahik, was declared weak by Abu Hatim and Abu Zur'ah. End of quotation.

So this marfu' hadith to the Prophet ﷺ, although none of its routes is free from weakness, is closer to the truth than the claim that the sariyy is 'Isa, without any evidence that must be followed. Among those who chose that the sariyy mentioned in the verse is the river: Ibn Jarir in his tafsir, and al-Bara' ibn 'Azib held this view, as did 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, (p-397) al-Dahhak, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and others. Among those who said it is 'Isa: al-Hasan, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muhammad ibn 'Abbad ibn Ja'far, which is one of the two narrations from Qatadah, and the view of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, as stated by Ibn Kathir and others.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (*Adwa' al-Bayan*) on Surah 19, verse 25:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates﴾ ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted.﴾ In this noble verse, the Exalted and Majestic did not explicitly specify what she was to eat or what she was to drink. However, He indicated that what she was commanded to eat is "the fresh ripe dates" mentioned, and what she was commanded to drink from is the stream mentioned, which is expressed as "the stream" (*al-sariyy*), as has already been explained. This is the apparent meaning.

Some scholars said: the trunk of the palm tree that she was commanded to shake was a dry trunk. When she shook it, Allah made it a palm tree bearing fresh ripe dates. Some scholars said: the trunk was that of a palm tree that was growing but was not bearing fruit. When she shook it, Allah caused fruit to grow on it and made it fresh ripe dates. Some scholars said: the palm tree was bearing fruit, and Allah commanded her to shake it so that the ripe dates that were already present would fall for her. What is understood from the context of the Qur'an is that Allah caused those dates to grow for her by way of breaking the customary order (*kharq al-'adah*, the suspension of ordinary causal patterns), and He caused that stream to flow for her by way of breaking the customary order. The dates and the stream did not exist before that. This holds whether we say the trunk was dry or a palm tree that was not bearing fruit; Allah caused fruit to grow on it and made it fresh ripe dates. The way the context indicates this is that His saying, ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted﴾, shows that her eye would be comforted at that time only by extraordinary matters that break the customary order, because it is she who would demonstrate her innocence of what they had accused her of. Thus, the presence of these extraordinary events, namely the gushing of the stream, the growth of the dates, and the speech of the infant, is what would reassure her soul and remove doubt from her, and thereby become a comfort to her eye. This is because mere eating and drinking, while the accusation by which she had wished she had died beforehand and had been "a thing forgotten" still stood, would not have been a comfort to her eye at that time, as is evident. Allah's breaking of the customary order for her by causing water to gush, dates to grow, and an infant to speak is nothing strange. The Exalted and Majestic has explicitly stated in "Aal 'Imran" His breaking of the customary order for her in His saying: ﴿Every time Zechariah entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found with her provision. He said, "O Mary, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 37]. The scholars said: he would find with her summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer. The flowing of the stream and the growth of the dates are no more remarkable than what is mentioned in Surah "Aal 'Imran."

* *

[p. 398]

**Issue**

Some scholars derived from the words of the Exalted in this noble verse, ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree﴾, and so on, that seeking and taking the means to obtain provision is something commanded by the Sharia, and that it does not contradict reliance upon Allah the Exalted. This is a matter known as necessary from the religion, namely that taking up means to obtain benefits and ward off harms in this world is something commanded by the Sharia, and it does not in any way contradict reliance upon Allah, because the responsible person adopts the means in obedience to the command of his Lord, while knowing with certainty that nothing occurs except what Allah wills to occur. So he is one who relies upon Allah, knowing that nothing will befall him except what Allah has decreed for him of good or evil. Even if Allah willed that the effect of means be separated from their results, it would be separated.

Among the clearest proofs of this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. The nature of burning in fire is one meaning that is not divisible into different meanings, yet despite this, it burned the firewood so that it became ash by its heat, at the very time that it was coolness and safety upon Abraham. This clearly proves that the true effect is only by the will of the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and that He causes whatever results He wills, by whatever means He wills, and that nothing of that has any effect except by His will, the Exalted and Majestic.

Among the most evident proofs of this is that He may make a thing a cause for another thing even though it is contrary to it, such as His making the striking of the dead man of the Children of Israel with a part of a slaughtered cow a cause for his life, while striking him with a dead piece of a dead cow would be contrary to his life. For life is not acquired by striking with something dead. This makes clear that He, the Exalted and Majestic, causes whatever results He wills by whatever means He wills, and that no effect whatsoever occurs except by His will, the Exalted and Majestic.

And among what clarifies that taking up means does not contradict reliance upon Allah is the saying of the Exalted, concerning Jacob: ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates."﴾ [Yusuf: 67]. In these words he commanded them to take up a means, and he took the cause by commanding it, because he feared for them that people would harm them by the evil eye, since they were eleven men, sons of one man, and they were people of beauty, perfection, and largeness of physique. So their entering through one gate was likely to expose them to the evil eye. He therefore commanded them to disperse and enter through different gates, taking the means to safety from the affliction of the evil eye, as many of the scholars of the early generations have said. Yet despite this taking of the cause, Allah said about him: (p. 399) ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates, and I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Judgment is only for Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely put their trust."﴾ [Yusuf: 67]. Observe how he combined taking the cause in His saying, ﴿Do not enter from one gate﴾, with reliance upon Allah in His saying, ﴿Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely put their trust﴾. This is a known matter, hidden only from one whose insight Allah has obliterated.

Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, is able to make the dates fall for her without shaking the trunk, but He commanded her to take the cause of their falling by shaking the trunk. Some have said on this:

Have you not seen that Allah said to Mary, "And shake toward you the trunk, and the ripe dates will fall"?
And had He willed that you pick it without shaking it, you would have picked it, but everything has a cause.

Some scholars have derived from this verse that the best food for a woman after childbirth is fresh ripe dates. They said: if there were anything better for women after childbirth than fresh ripe dates, Allah would have fed it to Mary during her postpartum period after giving birth to Jesus. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and others.

The *ba'* (بِ) in His saying, ﴿And shake toward yourself with the trunk of the palm tree﴾ [Maryam: 25], is extra (*mazidah*) for emphasis, because the verb *hazza* (shake) is transitive by itself. The addition of the particle *ba'* for emphasis before the object of a verb that is transitive by itself is frequent in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. Among its instances in the Qur'an is His saying here, ﴿And shake toward yourself with the trunk of the palm tree﴾, because what comes first to mind from the language is that the original is: "And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree." Also His saying, ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]; His saying, ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]; His saying, ﴿So you will see and they will see, which of you is the afflicted﴾ [al-Qalam: 5–6]; and His saying, "it grows with oil" (*tunbitu bi-al-duhn*), according to the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *ba'*, the present tense of *anbata* (the quadriliteral verb). The quadriliteral verb *anbata yunbitu*, with a *damma* on the initial *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *ba'*, is transitive by itself without a particle. So the *ba'* is extra for emphasis, as you have seen in the aforementioned verses. A parallel from the speech of the Arabs is the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi:

When they used to sift *bi-al-daqiq* (with the flour),
and before that they did not eat unleavened bread.

The original is "they sift the flour" (*yasuffuna al-daqiq*), so the *ba'* was added for emphasis.

And the verse of al-Ra'i:

They are free women, not raisers of ... (?) in the veils,
dark-eyed, who do not read *bi-al-suwar* (with the surahs).

The original is: "who do not read the surahs," so the *ba'* was added for the reason mentioned.

And the verse of Ya'la al-Ahwal al-Yashkuri or another:

In a Yemeni valley whose upper part grows lote-trees,
and whose lower part grows *bi-al-markh* and *al-shabhan*.

The original is: "and its lower part grows the *markh*," meaning, "and its lower part grows the *markh*," so the *ba'* was added for the reason mentioned.

And the verse of al-A'sha:

Our spears have guaranteed *bi-rizq 'iyalina* (the provision of our dependents),
filling the cooking pots and the pure, unblemished (?) ...

The original is: "our spears guaranteed the provision of our dependents."

And the verse of the rajaz poet:

We are the sons of Ja'dah, the people of al-Falaj;
we strike with the sword and hope *bi-al-faraj* (for relief).

That is: "we hope for the relief (*al-faraj*)."

And the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

When we contended in conversation and she inclined,
I bent down a branch with clustered, swaying fruit.

The original is: "I bent a branch (*ghusnan*)," because *hasara* is transitive by itself.

Examples like these are numerous in the speech of the Arabs.

In His saying, the Exalted, in this noble verse, *tassaqata* ("it will drop," in the words *tassaqtu*): there are nine readings, three of which are canonical (*sab'iyyah*) and six of which are irregular (*shadhdhah*). As for the three canonical readings: Hamza alone among the seven read *tasaqatu* with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, a light *sin*, and a *fatha* on the *qaf*. Its original is *tatasaqatu*, and one of the two *ta'*s was deleted. On this reading, *rutaban* (fresh ripe dates) is a *tamyiz* (specification, a noun clarifying the sense of the verb) transferred from the subject. Hafs alone, from 'Asim, read *tusaqitu* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, a *kasra* on the *qaf*, and a light *sin*, the present tense of *saqatat tusqitu*. On this reading, *rutaban* is the direct object of the verb *tusqitu*, meaning: she (the palm tree) causes fresh ripe dates to fall. The rest of the seven read *tassaqatu* with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and the *qaf* and a doubled *sin*. Its original is *tatasaqatu*, and one of the two *ta'*s was assimilated into the *sin*. On the reading of the majority, *rutaban* is a *tamyiz* transferred from the subject, just as it is parsed on the reading of Hamza.

All other readings are irregular.

As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿fresh ripe dates (*rutaban janiyyan*)﴾: *al-janiyy* is what is good and fit to be picked and eaten. It is reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that *al-janiyy* is that which has not dried or withered and has not moved far from the reach of the one who picks it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 26 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if you see any human being, say, "Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being."﴾ The speaker of these words to Maryam is the one who called out to her from beneath her, "Do not grieve." We have already presented the disagreement concerning him: whether he was Jesus or Jibril (Gabriel), and what appears to us to be the stronger view on that.

(p-401) As for his saying in this noble verse, ﴿say, "Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast"﴾ [Maryam: 26], it has been said that she was commanded to say this verbally, and it has been said that she was commanded to say it by gesture. That she was commanded to say it verbally is the view of the majority, as stated by al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, and it is the apparent meaning of the noble verse, because the apparent meaning of "say" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿say, "Indeed, I have vowed"﴾ and so on, is that it is speech by the tongue. Those who held that she was commanded to say it by gesture argued that if she had said it verbally she would have broken the vow she had made, not to speak to any human being today; for when she said to a human being with her tongue, "Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast," she would have spoken to that human being and thus broken her vow. Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, chose this last view because the verse indicates it. He said in his tafsir of this verse: ﴿say, "Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being"﴾, the intended meaning of this speech is pointing to it with a gesture, not that the intended meaning is verbal speech, so that it would not contradict ﴿so I will not speak today to any human being﴾. Those who disagreed answered this by saying that the meaning of ﴿so I will not speak today to any human being﴾ is after my saying: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾. You have seen the words of the scholars on the verse. The first view is indicated by the apparent context, and the second is indicated by His saying: ﴿so I will not speak today to any human being﴾, because it indicates the negation of speech to a human being absolutely. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: As for His saying "human being" (insiyyan), it is because she used to speak with the angels. The sense of his words is that the word "human being" has a implication of contrast (mafhum mukhalafa), i.e., unlike a non-human such as the angels, for I speak to them. What appears to me is that the speech did not intend to remove the implication (mafhum) from the ruling of the explicit statement (mantuq); rather, what is intended is that the negation of speech extends to every human being, whoever he may be.

* *

Issue.

Know that according to this view chosen by Ibn Kathir, that what is meant by His saying ﴿say, "Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast"﴾, i.e., say that by gesture, indicates that gesture takes the place of speech, because in this verse it has been called "saying" on this interpretation. It is frequently attested in the speech of the Arabs to apply the term "speech" to gesture, as in the poet's words:

"When the languid eyes speak to me, I return to them with flowing tears."

Here, God willing, we will mention the texts that indicate that a meaningful gesture takes the place of speech, and the texts that indicate that it is not like speech, along with the views of the scholars on that.

Know that there are evidences indicating that a meaningful gesture takes the place of speech, and other evidences come from which the opposite is understood. Among the evidences indicating that gesture takes the place of speech is the story of the black slave woman, to whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Where is Allah?" She pointed to the sky, and he ﷺ said: "Free her, for she is a believer." So he made her gesture equivalent to her speech in faith, which is the foundation of religions, by which blood and property are protected, by which Paradise is deserved, and by which one is saved from the Fire. The story is well known and transmitted from a group of the Companions, among them Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Abbas, Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami, and al-Sharid ibn Suwayd al-Thaqafi, may Allah be pleased with them. In some of their narrations she pointed to the sky. Abu Dawud said in his Sunan: Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub al-Jawzajani narrated to us, Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, he said: al-Mas'udi informed me, from Awn ibn Abdullah, from Abdullah ibn Utbah, from Abu Hurayrah: "A man came to the Prophet ﷺ with a black slave girl and said: O Messenger of Allah, I am obligated to free a believing slave. He said to her: 'Where is Allah?' She pointed to the sky with her finger. He said to her: 'Who am I?' She pointed to the Prophet ﷺ and to the sky, meaning: you are the Messenger of Allah. He said: 'Free her, for she is a believer.'" The apparent meaning of the narrations in which, when he said to her, "Where is Allah?", she said "in the sky" without mention of gesture, is to be understood as her having said it by gesture, because the story is one and the narrations explain one another. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir, in surah Ali Imran, in his commentary on the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture"﴾ [Ali Imran: 41], the following text: In this verse is evidence that gesture takes the place of speech, and this exists in much of the Sunnah, and the most emphatic of the gestures is that which the Prophet ﷺ ruled concerning the matter of the black woman, when he said to her: "Where is Allah?" She pointed with her head to the sky, and he said: "Free her, for she is a believer." So he permitted Islam by gesture, which is the foundation of the religion by which blood and property are secured, by which Paradise is deserved and by which one is saved from the Fire, and he judged her to be a believer just as he judges by the speech of one who says that. Therefore gesture must be effective in the rest of the religion, and this is the view of the majority of jurists.

Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that if a mute man gestures with divorce, it binds him. al-Shafi'i said concerning a man who falls ill and his tongue becomes impaired: he is like the mute in return (to marriage) and divorce. Abu Hanifah said: that is permissible if his gesture is understood, and if there is doubt about it then it is invalid; this is not by analogy (qiyas) but by juristic preference (istihsan), and by analogy in all of this it is invalid, because he cannot speak and his gesture is not understood. End of the relevant part of al-Qurtubi's words, may Allah have mercy on him.

Many authentic hadiths have come indicating that gesture takes the place of speech in several matters. Among them is what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned Ramadan, struck with his hands and said: "The month is like this and like this and like this," and then he folded his thumb at the third. "So fast when you see it, and break your fast when you see it, and if it is obscured for you, then estimate it as thirty." This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih, and it is explicit that he ﷺ gave his gesture with his fingers the status of his speech that the month may be twenty-nine days and may be thirty. An-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim, in discussing this hadith: In this hadith is the permissibility of relying on a meaningful gesture in such a matter. The hadith of Ibn Umar was cited by al-Bukhari in the chapter on li'an (mutual imprecation), using it as evidence that gesture is like the spoken word. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his Sahih many hadiths indicating that gesture is treated like speech. He said, may Allah be exalted: Chapter: Gesture in divorce and matters. Ibn Umar said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah does not punish for tears of the eye, but He punishes for this," and he pointed to his tongue. Ka'b ibn Malik said: The Prophet ﷺ gestured to me, meaning: take half. Asma' said: The Prophet ﷺ prayed during the eclipse, and I said to Aisha: What is the matter with the people? And she was praying, so she gestured with her head to the sun, and I said: A sign? And she gestured with her head: Yes. Anas said: The Prophet ﷺ gestured with his hand to Abu Bakr to advance. Ibn Abbas said: The Prophet ﷺ gestured with his hand: no blame. Abu Qatadah said: The Prophet ﷺ said concerning game for the one in ihram: "Did any of you order him to attack it, or gesture toward it?" They said: No. He said: "Then eat." Abdullah ibn Muhammad narrated to us, Abu Amir Abdul-Malik ibn Amr narrated to us, Ibrahim narrated to us, from Khalid, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ circumambulated on a camel, and whenever he came to the corner he gestured toward it and said Allahu akbar." Zaynab said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There has been opened from the barrier of Gog and Magog the like of this and this," and he made the sign of ninety.

Musaddad narrated to us, Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, Salamah ibn Alqamah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah who said: Abu al-Qasim ﷺ said: "On Friday there is an hour in which no Muslim who is standing and praying and asking Allah for good will fail to be given it." And he gestured with his hand and placed the tip of his finger on the middle finger and the little finger. We said: he makes it small (yuzahhiduha). Al-Uwaysi said: Ibrahim ibn Sa'd narrated to us, from Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj, from Hisham ibn Yazid, from Anas ibn Malik who said: "A Jew attacked a girl during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and took the ornaments she was wearing, and crushed her head. Her people brought him to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while she was at her last breath and had been rendered mute. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to her: 'Did so-and-so kill you?' naming someone other than her killer. She gestured with her head: No. He said: 'Did so-and-so?' naming another man, and she gestured: No. He said: 'Did so-and-so?' naming her killer, and she gestured: Yes. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered him, and his head was crushed between two stones." Qabisah narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Dinar, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Strife comes from here," and he gestured toward the east. Ali ibn Abdullah narrated to us, Jarir ibn Abd al-Hamid narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq al-Shaybani, from Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa who said: "We were on a journey with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When the sun set he said to a man: 'Get down and mix the drink for me.' He said: O Messenger of Allah, if only you would wait until evening. Then he said: 'Get down and mix it.' He said: O Messenger of Allah, if only you would wait until evening, for there is still daylight upon you. Then he said: 'Get down and mix it.' So he got down and mixed it for him the third time, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ drank. Then he gestured with his hand toward the east and said: 'When you see the night has come from here, the faster has broken his fast.'" Abdullah ibn Maslamah narrated to us, Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Abu Uthman, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Let not the call of Bilal, or his adhan, prevent any of you from his suhur, for he calls, or adhans, so that your one who is standing (praying at night) may return, and it is not that..." He meant the dawn or the daybreak. Yazid showed his two hands, then he stretched one from the other. Al-Layth said: Ja'far ibn Rabi'ah narrated to me, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Hurmuz, I heard Abu Hurayrah say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The likeness of the miser and the spender is like the likeness of two men wearing coats of iron from their breasts to their collarbones. As for the spender, he does not spend anything except that it expands over his skin until it covers his fingertips and erases his traces. As for the miser, he does not intend to spend except that each ring clings to its place, and he tries to widen it but it does not widen." And he pointed with his finger to his throat. End of what is from the Sahih of al-Bukhari.

These are hadiths indicating that gesture takes the place of speech in several matters. Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath in this chapter: He mentioned in it a number of hadiths, suspended and connected, the first of which is his saying: "Ibn Umar said." It is a fragment of a hadith previously cited with a connected chain in the Funerals, in which there is a story about Sa'd ibn Ubadah, and in it: "But Allah punishes for this," and he pointed to his tongue.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 26 (part 2 of 3):

Second: Ka'b ibn Malik said. This is also a fragment of a hadith that was previously narrated with its full chain in the chapter on "al-Mulazama" (sticking close to the one owed a debt). In it: "And he gestured to me, meaning: take half."

Third: Asma', the daughter of Abu Bakr, said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed during the eclipse..." The hadith was previously narrated with its full chain in the Book of Faith, with the wording: "She pointed to the sky," and in it: "She pointed with her head, meaning: yes." It also appears in the prayer of eclipse with a similar meaning, and in the prayer of forgetfulness in abridged form, to the end of his statement. In sum, all the hadiths that al-Bukhari mentioned in the mentioned chapter are established in the Sahih with full chains. As for those that came with full chains in the mentioned chapter, their status is clear; and as for those that came as mu'allaq (suspended) in the mentioned chapter, they have come with full chains in another place in al-Bukhari. (p-405)

The first hadith shows that the Prophet (ﷺ) treated his gesture toward the tongue as a statement that God punishes by it, just as his speech would be.

The second hadith: in it the Prophet (ﷺ) made his gesture toward Ka'b ibn Malik, that he should waive half of the blood-money owed by Ibn Abi Hadrad and take the remaining half from him, just as his speech would be.

The third hadith: in it 'A'isha made her gesture to her sister that the eclipse is one of the signs of God, which was the cause of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer, just as her speech would be.

The fourth hadith: in it the Prophet (ﷺ) made his gesture to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) that he should lead forward, just as his speech to him would be. The clarification of this is what al-Bukhari narrated from Anas in the chapter (of) "The people of knowledge and virtue are most entitled to lead the prayer." Anas said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not come out for three [days], then the prayer was established, and Abu Bakr went forward to lead, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said, by the curtain, and he lifted it. When the face of the Prophet (ﷺ) became clear, we had never seen a sight more pleasing to us than the face of the Prophet (ﷺ) when it became clear to us. The Prophet (ﷺ) gestured with his hand to Abu Bakr that he should go forward, and the Prophet (ﷺ) let down the curtain, and he was not able to [see] it until he died." End of quotation. This is the wording of al-Bukhari.

In this hadith, during the Prophet's (ﷺ) final illness and shortly before his death (ﷺ), he made his gesture to Abu Bakr that he should go forward to lead the people in prayer, just as his speech to him would be; because when Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) saw the Prophet (ﷺ) uncover the curtain, he withdrew backward to join the row, and thought that the Prophet (ﷺ) was going out to the prayer, as established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari in the chapter mentioned just above, from the hadith of Anas. So he gestured to him to go forward, and the gesture took the place of speech.

The fifth hadith: in it the Prophet (ﷺ) made a fatwa by a hand gesture equal to a fatwa by speech. Its clarification is what al-Bukhari narrated in the Book of Knowledge, in the chapter "Whoever answers a fatwa by a gesture of the hand and head": "Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, he said: Wuhayb narrated to us, he said: Ayyub narrated to us, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked during his Hajj, and he said: 'I slaughtered before I threw [the pebbles].' He gestured with his hand, and said: 'There is no blame.' He said: 'I shaved before I slaughtered,' and he gestured with his hand, 'There is no blame.'" Among the examples of fatwa by gesture of the hand is what al-Bukhari narrated in this mentioned chapter from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "'Knowledge will be taken away, ignorance and trials will appear, and al-Harj will increase.' It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Harj?' He said, 'Like this,' with his hand, and he turned it as if he meant killing." End of quotation.

So he (ﷺ) made his gesture with his hand equal to his speech, in that al-Harj (p-406) means killing.

The sixth hadith: in it the Prophet (ﷺ) made the gesture of the muhrim toward the game in order to alert the non-muhrim to it, just as his command to him to hunt it by speech. We have already presented this hadith in the commentary on Surat al-Ma'ida.

The seventh hadith: in it the Prophet (ﷺ) made a gesture toward the Corner (al-Rukn) in his circumambulation, like touching it and kissing it by action.

The eighth hadith: in it the Prophet (ﷺ) made his gesture with his fingers, like the counting of ninety, to clarify the amount of the breach opened in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, just as speech would.

The ninth hadith: in it he placed his fingertip on the middle finger and the little finger, indicating by that the shortness of the time of the Hour in which the supplication for good is answered on Friday; or indicating by that its time according to those who said that placing the fingertip in the middle of the palm is meant to indicate that the hour of Friday is in the middle of the day of Friday, and placing it on the little finger is meant to indicate that it is at the end of the day, because the little finger is the last of the fingers of the palm, just as speech would be. Ibn Hajar mentioned from some scholars that this gesture with the hand for the hour of Friday is from the action of Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal, the narrator of the hadith from Salamah ibn 'Alqamah, as was mentioned in the chain of the hadith. Accordingly, there is an interpolation (idraj) in the context of this hadith in al-Bukhari.

The tenth hadith: in it the Prophet (ﷺ) made the gesture of the slave girl whom the Jew killed, just as her speech, that the Jew killed her, and that the one named to her other than him was not the one who killed her. We have already presented this hadith in the commentary on Surat Bani Isra'il, and we explained there that the Prophet (ﷺ), although he treated the girl's gesture as her speech, did not execute the Jew on the basis of the gesture of the girl standing in place of her speech naming her killer; rather, he (the Jew) confessed that he had killed her, so the killing was established against him by his confession, and retaliation was exacted for her from him on that basis.

The eleventh hadith: in it the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fitnah is from here," and he gestured toward the east. So he treated his gesture toward the east as his speech with that.

The twelfth hadith: in it "he (ﷺ) gestured with his hand toward the east and said: 'When you see the night coming from here, the fasting person has broken his fast.'" So he treated his gesture with his hand toward the east as his speech with the word "east."

The thirteenth hadith: in it he made the gesture with the hand to distinguish between the false dawn and the true dawn by that.

The fourteenth hadith: he (ﷺ) said in it: "He widens it, but it does not widen," and he points with his finger to (p-407) his throat. So he treated his gesture to indicate that the iron coat of mail, of which the proverb is made for the miser, stays fixed at his throat, not descending from it, nor covering his private parts or his body, just as speech would.

These are fourteen hadiths that al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, cited in the mentioned chapter, and we have brought them here, and explained the mode of indication in each one that the gesture is like speech, along with what we previously presented of hadiths indicating that, in addition to what al-Bukhari mentioned here.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, also mentioned at the beginning of the chapter on "li'an" (mutual imprecation) five hadiths, each of which contains the indication that gesture is like speech, but we have not mentioned them here, because what we have mentioned is sufficient.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath, at the end of his discussion of the hadiths of the mentioned chapter: Ibn Battal said: The majority went to the view that a comprehensible gesture takes the place of speech, and the Hanafis disagreed with him in some of that; and perhaps al-Bukhari answered them with these hadiths in which the Prophet (ﷺ) made the gesture stand in place of speech. And if gesture is permitted in rulings that differ in religious matters, then for one who cannot speak it is more permissible.

Ibn al-Munayyir said: Al-Bukhari meant that gesture in divorce and other matters from the mute and others, by which the principle and the number are understood, is effective like the word. End of quotation.

It appears to me that al-Bukhari cited this chapter and its hadiths as a preface to what he mentions of discussion in the chapter that follows, with those who distinguish between the li'an of the mute and his divorce. And God knows best.

These hadiths and their like are the proof of those who say that comprehensible gesture stands in place of the word. Those who said that gesture is not like the word argued that the Great Qur'an indicates this, in His Exalted saying in the verse under discussion: ﴿So say: Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being﴾ [Maryam: 26]. In this verse there is an explicit statement of her vow to abstain from speaking to any human being, while He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So she pointed to him﴾ [Maryam: 29], meaning: she pointed to them toward him, that they should speak to him and he would inform them of the truth of the matter. So this is a comprehensible gesture, and her people understood it and answered her with a reply matching their understanding of what she pointed to: ﴿They said: How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾ [Maryam: 29]. And if this comprehensible gesture were like speech, it would have invalidated Maryam's vow not to speak to a human being. So the verse is explicit that speaking with the word breaks her vow, while gesture is not so. Thus the distinction between word and gesture has come explicitly in the Qur'an.
