فالنِّداءُ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ هو المَذْكُورُ في ”مَرْيَمَ“، و”طه“، و”النَّمْلِ“، وقَدْ بَيَّنَ هُنا أنَّهُ نُودِيَ مِن شاطِئِ الوادِي الأيْمَنِ في البُقْعَةِ المُبارَكَةِ مِنَ الشَّجَرَةِ، فَدَلَّتِ الآياتُ عَلى أنَّ الشَّجَرَةَ الَّتِي رَأى فِيها النّارَ عَنْ يَمِينِ الجَبَلِ الَّذِي هو الطُّورُ، وفي يَمِينِ الوادِي المُقَدَّسِ الَّذِي هو طُوًى عَلى القَوْلِ بِأنَّ طُوًى اسْمٌ لَهُ. وقَدْ قَدَّمْنا قَوْلَ ابْنِ جَرِيرٍ: أنَّ المُرادَ يَمِينُ مُوسى؛ لِأنَّ الجَبَلَ ومِثْلَهُ الوادِيَ لا يَمِينَ لَهُ ولا شِمالَ. وقالَ ابْنُ كَثِيرٍ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿نُودِيَ مِن شاطِئِ الوادِي الأيْمَنِ﴾ [القصص: ٣٠]: أيْ: مِن جانِبِ الوادِي مِمّا يَلِي الجَبَلَ عَنْ يَمِينِهِ مِن ناحِيَةِ الغَرْبِ، كَما قالَ تَعالى: ﴿وَما كُنْتَ بِجانِبِ الغَرْبِيِّ إذْ قَضَيْنا إلى مُوسى الأمْرَ﴾ [القصص: ٤٤]، فَهَذا مِمّا يُرْشِدُ إلى أنَّ مُوسى قَصَدَ النّارَ إلى جِهَةِ القِبْلَةِ والجَبَلُ الغَرْبِيُّ عَنْ يَمِينِهِ. انْتَهى مِنهُ، وهو مَعْنى قَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَنادَيْناهُ مِن جانِبِ الطُّورِ الأيْمَنِ﴾ الآيَةَ [مريم: ٥٢]، وقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَما كُنْتَ بِجانِبِ الطُّورِ إذْ نادَيْنا﴾ الآيَةَ [القصص: ٤٦].

والنِّداءُ المَذْكُورُ في جَمِيعِ الآياتِ المَذْكُورَةِ نِداءُ اللَّهِ لَهُ، فَهو كَلامُ اللَّهِ أسْمَعَهُ نَبِيَّهُ مُوسى، ولا يُعْقَلُ أنَّهُ كَلامٌ مَخْلُوقٌ، ولا كَلامٌ خَلَقَهُ اللَّهُ في مَخْلُوقٍ كَما يَزْعُمُ ذَلِكَ بَعْضُ الجَهَلَةِ المَلاحِدَةِ، إذْ لا يُمْكِنُ أنْ يَقُولَ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ: ﴿إنَّهُ أنا اللَّهُ العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾ [النمل: ٩]، ولا أنْ يَقُولَ: ﴿إنَّنِي أنا اللَّهُ لا إلَهَ إلّا أنا فاعْبُدْنِي﴾ [طه: ١٤]. ولَوْ فُرِضَ أنَّ الكَلامَ المَذْكُورَ قالَهُ مَخْلُوقٌ افْتِراءً عَلى اللَّهِ، كَقَوْلِ فِرْعَوْنَ: ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ [النازعات: ٢٤]، عَلى سَبِيلِ فَرْضِ المُحالِ، فَلا يُمْكِنُ أنْ يَذْكُرَهُ اللَّهُ في مَعْرِضِ أنَّهُ حَقٌّ وصَوابٌ.

فَقَوْلُهُ: ﴿إنَّنِي أنا اللَّهُ لا إلَهَ إلّا أنا فاعْبُدْنِي﴾ [طه: ١٤]، وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿إنَّهُ أنا اللَّهُ العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾ [النمل: ٩]، صَرِيحٌ في أنَّ اللَّهَ هو المُتَكَلِّمُ بِذَلِكَ صَراحَةً لا تَحْتَمِلُ غَيْرَ ذَلِكَ، كَما هو مَعْلُومٌ عِنْدَ مَن لَهُ أدْنى مَعْرِفَةٍ بِدِينِ الإسْلامِ.

(p-٤٣٣) وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿مِن شاطِئِ الوادِي الأيْمَنِ في البُقْعَةِ المُبارَكَةِ مِنَ الشَّجَرَةِ﴾ [القصص: ٣٠]، قالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ في ”الكَشّافِ“: ”مِن“ الأُولى والثّانِيَةُ لِابْتِداءِ الغايَةِ، أيْ: أتاهُ النِّداءُ مِن شاطِئِ الوادِي مِن قِبَلِ الشَّجَرَةِ، و﴿مِنَ الشَّجَرَةِ﴾ بَدَلٌ مِن قَوْلِهِ: ﴿مِن شاطِئِ الوادِي﴾ بَدَلُ اشْتِمالٍ (أيْ بَدَلٌ يَدُلُّ عَلى مُتَعَلَّقٍ بِالمُبْدَلِ مِنهُ)؛ لِأنَّ الشَّجَرَةَ كانَتْ نابِتَةً عَلى الشّاطِئِ، كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿لَجَعَلْنا لِمَن يَكْفُرُ بِالرَّحْمَنِ لِبُيُوتِهِمْ﴾ [الزخرف: ٣٣].

وَقالَ القُرْطُبِيُّ رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ في تَفْسِيرِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿نُودِيَ مِن شاطِئِ الوادِي الأيْمَنِ﴾ الآيَةَ: قالَ المَهْدَوِيُّ: وكَلَّمَ اللَّهُ تَعالى مُوسى عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ مِن فَوْقِ عَرْشِهِ، وأسْمَعَهُ كَلامَهُ مِنَ الشَّجَرَةِ عَلى ما شاءَ. انْتَهى مِنهُ. وشاطِئُ الوادِي جانِبُهُ. وقالَ بَعْضُ أهْلِ العِلْمِ: مَعْنى ”الأيْمَنِ“ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿مِن شاطِئِ الوادِي الأيْمَنِ﴾، وقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَنادَيْناهُ مِن جانِبِ الطُّورِ الأيْمَنِ﴾ [مريم: ٥٢]، مِنَ اليُمْنِ وهو البَرَكَةُ؛ لِأنَّ تِلْكَ البِلادَ بارَكَ اللَّهُ فِيها. وأكْثَرُ أهْلِ العِلْمِ عَلى أنَّ النّارَ الَّتِي رَآها مُوسى ”نُورٌ“ وهو يَظُنُّها نارًا، وفي قِصَّتِهِ أنَّهُ رَأى النّارَ تَشْتَعِلُ فِيها وهي لا تَزْدادُ إلّا خُضْرَةً وحُسْنًا، قِيلَ: هي شَجَرَةُ عَوْسَجٍ، وقِيلَ: شَجَرَةُ عَلِيقٍ، وقِيلَ: شَجَرَةُ عُنّابٍ، وقِيلَ: سَمُرَةٌ، واللَّهُ تَعالى أعْلَمُ.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى في سُورَةِ ”النَّمْلِ“: ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَها نُودِيَ أنْ بُورِكَ مَن في النّارِ ومَن حَوْلَها﴾ [النمل: ٨]، اخْتَلَفَتْ عِباراتُ المُفَسِّرِينَ في المُرادِ بِـ﴿مَن في النّارِ﴾ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ في سُورَةِ ”النَّمْلِ“، فَقالَ بَعْضُهم: هو اللَّهُ جَلَّ وعَلا، ومِمَّنْ رُوِيَ عَنْهُ هَذا القَوْلُ: ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ، والحَسَنُ، وسَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ، ومُحَمَّدُ بْنُ كَعْبٍ، قالُوا: ﴿بُورِكَ مَن في النّارِ﴾ أيْ: تَقَدَّسَ اللَّهُ وتَعالى، وقالُوا: كانَ نُورُ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ في الشَّجَرَةِ، واسْتَدَلَّ مَن قالَ بِهَذا القَوْلِ بِحَدِيثِ أبِي مُوسى الثّابِتِ في الصَّحِيحِ: أنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ قالَ: «إنَّ اللَّهَ عَزَّ وجَلَّ لا يَنامُ ولا يَنْبَغِي لَهُ أنْ يَنامَ، يَخْفِضُ القِسْطَ ويَرْفَعُهُ، يُرْفَعُ إلَيْهِ عَمَلُ اللَّيْلِ قَبْلَ عَمَلِ النَّهارِ، وعَمَلُ النَّهارِ قَبْلَ عَمَلِ اللَّيْلِ، حِجابُهُ النُّورُ - أوِ النّارُ - لَوْ كَشَفَهُ لَأحْرَقَتْ سُبُحاتُ وجْهِهِ ما انْتَهى إلَيْهِ بَصَرُهُ مِن خَلْقِهِ».

قالَ مُقَيِّدُهُ عَفا اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: وهَذا القَوْلُ بَعِيدٌ مِن ظاهِرِ القُرْآنِ، ولا يَنْبَغِي أنْ يُطْلَقَ عَلى اللَّهِ أنَّهُ في النّارِ الَّتِي في الشَّجَرَةِ، سَواءٌ قُلْنا: إنَّها نارٌ أوْ نُورٌ، سُبْحانَهُ جَلَّ وعَلا عَنْ كُلِّ ما لا يَلِيقُ بِكَمالِهِ وجَلالِهِ. وتَأْوِيلُ ذَلِكَ بِـ﴿مَن في النّارِ﴾ سُلْطانُهُ وقُدْرَتُهُ، لا يَصِحُّ؛ لِأنَّ صَرْفَ كِتابِ اللَّهِ عَنْ ظاهِرِهِ المُتَبادِرِ مِنهُ لا يَجُوزُ إلّا بِدَلِيلٍ يَجِبُ الرُّجُوعُ (p-٤٣٤) إلَيْهِ مِن كِتابِ اللَّهِ أوْ سُنَّةِ نَبِيِّهِ ﷺ. وبِهِ تَعْلَمُ أنَّ قَوْلَ أبِي حَيّانَ في ”البَحْرِ المُحِيطِ“: قالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ، وابْنُ جُبَيْرٍ، والحَسَنُ وغَيْرُهم: أرادَ بِمَن في النّارِ: ذاتَهُ، وعَبَّرَ بَعْضُهم بِعِباراتٍ شَنِيعَةٍ مَرْدُودَةٍ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلى اللَّهِ تَعالى.

وَإذا ثَبَتَ ذَلِكَ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ ومَن ذُكِرَ أُوِّلَ عَلى حَذْفٍ، أيْ: بُورِكَ مَن قُدْرَتُهُ وسُلْطانُهُ في النّارِ. انْتَهى، أنَّهُ أصابَ في تَنْزِيهِهِ لِلَّهِ عَنْ تِلْكَ العِباراتِ، ولَمْ يُصِبْ فِيما ذَكَرَ مِنَ التَّأْوِيلِ، واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

وَقالَ بَعْضُهم: إنَّ مَعْنى ﴿بُورِكَ مَن في النّارِ﴾، أيْ: بُورِكَتِ النّارُ لِأنَّها نُورٌ، وبُعْدُهُ عَنْ ظاهِرِ القُرْآنِ واضِحٌ كَما تَرى. وقالَ بَعْضُهم: ﴿أنْ بُورِكَ مَن في النّارِ﴾ أيْ: بُورِكَتِ الشَّجَرَةُ الَّتِي تَتَّقِدُ فِيها النّارُ، وبُعْدُهُ عَنْ ظاهِرِ القُرْآنِ أيْضًا واضِحٌ كَما تَرى، وإطْلاقُ لَفْظَةِ ”مَن“ عَلى الشَّجَرَةِ وعَلى ما في النّارِ مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ غَيْرُ مُسْتَقِيمٍ في لُغَةِ العَرَبِ الَّتِي نَزَلَ بِها القُرْآنُ العَظِيمُ كَما تَرى.

١ تَتِمَّةُ القُرْطُبِيِّ ١٣ \ ٢٨٢: ولا يَجُوزُ أنْ يُوصَفَ اللَّهُ تَعالى بِالِانْتِقالِ والزَّوالِ، وما يُشْبِهُ ذَلِكَ مِن صِفَةِ المَخْلُوقِينَ.

وَأقْرَبُ الأقْوالِ في مَعْنى الآيَةِ إلى ظاهِرِ القُرْآنِ العَظِيمِ قَوْلُ مَن قالَ: إنَّ في النّارِ الَّتِي هي نُورٌ مَلائِكَةً، وحَوْلَها مَلائِكَةٌ ومُوسى، وأنَّ مَعْنى: ﴿أنْ بُورِكَ مَن في النّارِ﴾ أيْ: المَلائِكَةُ الَّذِينَ هُمْ في ذَلِكَ النُّورِ، ﴿ومَن حَوْلَها﴾ أيْ: وبُورِكَ المَلائِكَةُ الَّذِينَ هُمْ حَوْلَها، وبُورِكَ مُوسى لِأنَّهُ حَوْلَها مَعَهُمْ، ومِمَّنْ يُرْوى عَنْهُ هَذا: السُّدِّيُّ.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 52 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: The meaning of ﴿That blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾ is: blessed is whoever is in the place of the fire and whoever is around the place of it. Its place is the spot in which it occurred, and it is the blessed spot mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot﴾ [al-Qasas: 30]. And the reading of Ubayy supports this: "that the fire has been blessed and whoever is around it," and it is also transmitted from him: "the fire has been blessed."

Al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding His saying ﴿That blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: This is a greeting from Allah to Musa and an honouring of him, just as He greeted Ibrahim through the tongues of the angels when they entered upon him and said: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house﴾. His saying ﴿whoever is in the fire﴾ is the deputy subject (na'ib fa'il) of "buriku" (was blessed). The Arabs say: barakaka Allah (Allah blessed you), wa baraka fika (blessed you), wa baraka 'alayka (blessed upon you), and wa baraka laka (blessed for you), so these are four dialects. The poet said:

"So you were blessed as a newborn, and you were blessed as a youth, and you were blessed at the time of grey hair when you are grey-haired."

Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib said, lamenting Musafir ibn Abi Amr ibn Umayya: (p. 435)

"Would that I knew, Musafir ibn Abi Amr, and would that the grieving one would say it:
Blessed is the stranger dead, as
the fresh basil and the olive were blessed."

Another said:

"So may there be blessing upon your children and upon theirs, whenever they are mentioned, and we are your ransom."

The verses in this narrative indicate that He showed him the sign of the hand and the staff so that he would be trained in it before his presence before Pharaoh and his people, and that he fled turning back in fear of it the first time when it became a serpent. It came in several places, such as His saying, exalted is He, in Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿He said: Throw it, O Musa.﴾ ﴿So he threw it, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly.﴾ ﴿He said: Take it and do not fear; We will return it to its original form.﴾ ﴿And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white without harm, as another sign.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 19–22]. So His saying ﴿and do not fear﴾ indicates that he was frightened by it when it became a clearly visible serpent, as was made clear in "an-Naml" and "al-Qasas".

His saying in this verse of Ta-Ha ﴿without harm﴾ [Ta-Ha: 22] means: without leprosy. In it is what the rhetoricians call ihtiras (precautionary qualification). Similarly His saying, exalted is He, in Surat an-Naml: ﴿O Musa, indeed it is I, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿And throw your staff.﴾ So when he saw it moving as if it were a jann, he turned back fleeing and did not return. ﴿O Musa, do not fear; indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence.﴾ ﴿Except one who wrongs, then replaces evil with good after bad; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without harm.﴾ [an-Naml: 9–12]. And His saying in "al-Qasas": ﴿And throw your staff.﴾ So when he saw it moving as if it were a jann, he turned back fleeing and did not return. ﴿O Musa, come forward and do not fear; indeed, you are among the secure.﴾ ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without harm. And draw your arm to your side against fear. These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs; indeed, they have been a defiant people.﴾ [al-Qasas: 31–32]. The two proofs referred to by His saying ﴿these are two proofs﴾ are the hand and the staff. When Musa was trained in the two mentioned proofs, and he and his brother conveyed the message to Pharaoh and his chiefs, they demanded from him a sign indicating his truthfulness, so he brought them the two mentioned proofs, and he did not fear the serpent into which the staff had turned, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said: Even if I bring you something clear?﴾ ﴿He said: Bring it, if you are among the truthful.﴾ ﴿So he threw his staff, and suddenly it was a clear serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and suddenly it was white to the onlookers.﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 30–33], and similar verses.

His saying in "an-Naml" and "al-Qasas": ﴿and did not return﴾ means: he did not come back from fleeing from it. It is said: 'aqqaba al-faris (the horseman "returned") when he charged again after fleeing. And from this is the saying of the poet: (p. 436)

"So they did not return when it was said: Is there anyone who returns? Nor did they dismount at the day of the hardship in any place."

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam: 52] means: Allah brought Musa near while he was a confidant, i.e., one who speaks privately with his Lord. The form fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active) is common, as in qa'id (sitter) and jalis (companion). Ibn Kathir, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said in explaining this verse: Ibn Jarir narrated: Ibn Bashshar told us, Yahya (that is, al-Qattan) told us, Sufyan told us, from Ata' ibn Yasar, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾, he said: He was brought close until he heard the scratching of the pen.

Likewise Mujahid, Abu al-Aliyah and others said, meaning the scratching of the pen writing the Torah. As-Suddi said regarding ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾: He was taken up into the heaven and spoken to. A similar report is from Mujahid. Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾, he said: a confidant by his truthfulness. End of the relevant part of Ibn Kathir's words, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him.

His saying, exalted is He, in Ta-Ha: ﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 31] means: strengthen me through him. Al-azr means strength, and "azarahu" means he strengthened him. His saying in al-Qasas: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35] means: We will strengthen you through him. This is because the arm (adud) is the support of the hand, and through its strength the hand becomes strong. Tarafa said:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand except a hand that has no arm."

His saying: ridan, means: a helper, because ridr is a name for everything by which one is aided. It is said: radatahu, meaning: I aided him.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 19, verse 53:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun as a prophet﴾. The meaning of this noble verse is that Allah granted Musa the prophethood of Harun. The meaning is that Musa asked Him for this, and He gave him what he asked for. Allah clarified this meaning in other verses,

• such as His saying about him in Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿And appoint for me a helper from my family, Harun, my brother. Increase my strength through him, and make him a partner in my task﴾, up to His saying: ﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Musa"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 29–36],

• and His saying in al-Qasas: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I killed a person among them, so I fear that they will kill me. And my brother Harun is more eloquent than me in speech, so send him with me as a supporter to confirm me. Indeed, I fear that they will deny me."﴾ ﴿He said, "We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will give you both authority, so they will not reach you. By Our signs, you and those who follow you will be the victorious."﴾ [al-Qasas: 33–35],

• and His saying in Surat ash-Shu'ara': (p-437) ﴿And when your Lord called Musa, "Go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Fir'awn. Will they not fear Allah?" ﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me, and my chest will be constricted, and my tongue will not be freed, so send for Harun. And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ ﴿He said, "No! Go, both of you, with Our signs. We are with you, listening."﴾ ﴿So come to Fir'awn and say, "We are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 10–16].

These verses show that he asked his Lord to send his brother with him, and his Lord, may He be majestic and exalted, answered his request in this matter. This shows that the gift in His saying "and We gave" refers in reality to his messengership, not to the person of Harun itself; because Harun was older than Musa, as the historians have stated.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 54 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet.﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, may He be exalted, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to mention in the Book, which is this Mighty Qur'an, his (the Prophet's) forefather Isma'il, and He praised him, meaning Isma'il, by saying that he was true to his promise and that he was a messenger and a prophet. Among what the Qur'an makes clear regarding the intensity of his truthfulness in his promise is that he promised his father that he would patiently endure being slaughtered, and then he fulfilled that promise. Whoever fulfils his promise by surrendering himself to be slaughtered, that is among the greatest proofs of the great truthfulness of his promise. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I sacrifice you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast."﴾ This is his promise.

Allah has clarified his fulfilment of it in His saying: ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103], and the verified position is that the one who was sacrificed was Isma'il. Two verses of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, have indicated this with a clear indication that admits no ambiguity. We shall, if Allah wills, clarify this to the utmost clarity in surah "al-Saffat". His praise, may He be exalted, of His Prophet Isma'il in this noble verse for truthfulness of promise is understood from the implication of His speech, meaning the implication of its opposite, that breaking a promise is blameworthy. This implication has come clearly stated in other places in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, such as His saying: ﴿So He caused them to be followed by hypocrisy in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they promised Him and because they had been lying﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77], and His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 2–3], in addition to other verses. And in the hadith: "The sign of the hypocrite is three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays."

His saying, may He be exalted, in this verse: ﴿And he used to enjoin on his people prayer and zakah﴾ [Maryam: 55]. It has been clarified in other places that our Prophet (ﷺ) used to do that which Allah praised his forefather Isma'il for, as in His saying: ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132], and it is known that he (ﷺ) carried out this command [p. 438], and as in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. Included in that is their (the believers') commanding their families to pray and to pay zakah, in addition to other verses.

* *

Issue

The scholars differed regarding the obligation of fulfilling a promise. Some said: fulfilling it is obligatory absolutely. Some said: it is not obligatory absolutely. Some said: if the promiser, by his promise, has placed the promisee in a predicament, then fulfilling it is obligatory; otherwise it is not. An example of this is if one says to someone, "Marry," and he says, "I do not have what I can give as dowry to the wife," and the other says, "Marry, and take on the obligation of the dowry for her, and I will pay it on your behalf." So he marries on this basis. Indeed, by his promise, he has placed him in the predicament of being obligated to pay the dowry.

Those who said it is obligatory argued with evidences, among them verses from the Book of Allah which indicate, through the apparent generality of their wording, this ruling, and hadiths. As for the verses:
• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fulfil the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned about﴾ [al-Isra': 34],
• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], to the end of the verse,
• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have taken it, and do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾ [al-Nahl: 91], to the end of the verse,
• His saying here: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], to the end of the verse,
and similar verses.

As for the hadiths, such as the hadith "A promise is a debt," the making of it a debt is evidence of its obligation. The author of Kashf al-Khafa' wa Muzil al-Ilbas 'amma ushtahara min al-ahadith 'ala alsinat al-nas (Clarification of what is Hidden and Removal of Confusion regarding what is Famous among the Hadiths on the Tongues of People) said: "The promise is a debt." It was narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Qudha'i and others, from Ibn Mas'ud, with the wording: He said: None of you should promise his child and then not fulfil it for him, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The promise is a debt." Abu Nu'aym narrated it from him with the wording: "When one of you promises his child, let him fulfil it for him, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and he mentioned it with the wording "a gift." Al-Bukhari narrated it in al-Adab al-Mufrad as a mawquf (a report ending with a Companion). Al-Tabarani and al-Daylami narrated it from Ali as a marfu' (a report traced to the Prophet) with the wording: "The promise is a debt. Woe to one who promises and then breaks it, woe to him," three times. Al-Qudha'i narrated it with the wording of the title only, and al-Daylami also with the wording: "The one who promises with a promise is like the debt or worse," meaning the promise of the promiser. In another wording of his: "The promise of the believer is a debt, and the promise of the believer is like taking by the hand." Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Qubath ibn Ashyam al-Laythi as a marfu': "The promise is a gift."

Al-Khara'iti in al-Makarim narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri as a mursal (a report whose chain omits the Companion): "A woman asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for something and he did not have it with him. She said, 'Promise me.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Indeed, the promise is a gift.'" It is in the Marasil of Abu Dawud. Likewise in al-Samt of Ibn Abi al-Dunya from al-Hasan: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "The promise is a gift." In another narration of both of them from al-Hasan that he said: "A man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for something and he said, 'I do not have what I can give you.'" He (the author of al-Maqasid) said after mentioning the hadith and its routes: "I have devoted a separate part to it along with what is suitable to it." End of quotation from him. He (al-Suyuti) marked this hadith in al-Jami' al-Saghir, from the narration of Ali in the Musnad al-Firdaws of al-Daylami, as weak.

Its commentator al-Manawi said: "In it is Darim ibn Qabisah. Al-Dhahabi said: he is not known." End of quotation. But it has already passed for you that its routes are numerous, and it has been narrated from Companions other than Ali, as we have already cited its narration from Ibn Mas'ud and from Qubath ibn Ashyam al-Kinani al-Laythi, may Allah be pleased with them both. And there will come in this section, if Allah wills, authentic hadiths indicating the fulfilment of promises.

Those who said that a promise does not oblige fulfilment argued by consensus that if someone promises a man money and then the promiser becomes bankrupt, the promisee is not counted with the creditors, and he does not have a share like the debts that are binding without a promise. Ibn Abd al-Barr related the consensus on this, as al-Qurtubi quoted from him in his tafsir of this noble verse, and there is discussion in it. The argument of those who distinguished between the case where he has placed him in a predicament by the promise, so it is obligatory, and the case where he has not placed him in it, so it is not obligatory, is that if he places him in a predicament by a promise and then retracts the promise and leaves him in the predicament into which he placed him, he has harmed him. It is not permissible for a Muslim to harm his brother, due to the hadith "There is no harm and no reciprocating harm."

Abu Abd Allah al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: Malik said: "If a man asks another to grant him a gift, and he says 'yes,' then it becomes apparent to him not to do it, I do not see that it is binding on him." Malik said: "And if that was regarding the settlement of a debt, so he asked him to settle it on his behalf, and he said 'yes,' and there were men witnessing against him, then it is more fitting that it binds him if two witnessed against him."

Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and the rest of the jurists said: "A promise does not oblige anything, because they are benefits which he has not taken possession of in a loan, since it is a temporary matter. In other than a loan, they are specific items and objects which were given as a gift but have not been taken possession of, so the owner may retract them." In al-Bukhari: "And mention in the Book Isma'il. Indeed, he was true to his promise" [Maryam: 54]. "Ibn Ash'a judged by the promise," and he mentioned this from Samurah ibn Jundub. Al-Bukhari said: "And I saw Ishaq ibn Ibrahim arguing with the hadith of Ibn Ash'a." End of al-Qurtubi's words. The words of al-Bukhari of which al-Qurtubi quoted part are his statement at the end of the Book of "Testimonies": Chapter: One who commands the fulfilment of a promise and does it, al-Hasan did so. "And mention in the Book Isma'il, indeed he was true to his promise." "Ibn Ash'a judged by the promise," and he mentioned that from Sumrah. al-Miswar ibn Makhramah said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ)," and he mentioned a son-in-law of his, saying: "He promised me and fulfilled it for me." Abu Abd Allah said: "And I saw Ishaq ibn Ibrahim arguing with the hadith of Ibn Ash'a: Ibrahim ibn Hamzah narrated to us, Ibrahim ibn Sa'd narrated to us [p. 440] from Salih, from Ibn Shihab, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah, that Abd Allah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, informed him, saying: Abu Sufyan informed me that Heraclius said to him: 'I asked you what he commands you, and you claimed that he commands you to prayer, truthfulness, chastity, fulfilment of covenant and the rendering of trusts.' He said: 'And this is the attribute of a prophet.'"

Qutaybah ibn Sa'id narrated to us, Isma'il ibn Ja'far narrated to us, from Abu Suhayl Nafi' ibn Malik ibn Abi Amir, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The sign of the hypocrite is three: when he speaks he lies, when he is entrusted he betrays, and when he promises he breaks it." Ibrahim ibn Musa narrated to us, Hisham informed us, from Ibn Jurayj who said: Amr ibn Dinar informed me, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) died, wealth came to Abu Bakr from al-Ala' ibn al-Hadrami. Abu Bakr said: 'Whoever has a debt upon the Prophet (ﷺ), or had a promise from him, let him come to us.' Jabir said: 'So I said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) promised me that he would give me like this and like this and like this,' and he spread his hands three times. Jabir said: 'So he counted into my hand five hundred, then five hundred, then five hundred.'"

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahim narrated to us, Sa'id ibn Sulayman informed us, Marwan ibn Shuja' narrated to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "A Jew from the people of al-Hirah asked me: 'Which of the two terms did Musa fulfil?' I said: 'I do not know until I come to the scholar of the Arabs and ask him.' So I came and asked Ibn Abbas. He said: 'He fulfilled the more complete and the better of them both. Indeed, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said he would do something, he did it.'" End of quotation from the Sahih of al-Bukhari. His saying in the chapter title, "and al-Hasan did it," means the command to carry out the promise. The way he argues with the verse "Indeed, he was true to his promise" is that praise for him for truthfulness of promise implies that breaking it is blameworthy for its doer, so it is not permissible.

Ibn al-Ash'a mentioned is Sa'id ibn Amr ibn Ash'a al-Hamdani al-Kufi, who was the judge of Kufah during the governorship of Khalid al-Qasri over Iraq. The narration mentioned from Samurah ibn Jundub has been recorded in the tafsir of Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and he is Ishaq ibn Ibrahim whom al-Bukhari mentioned he saw arguing with the hadith of Ibn Ash'a, as Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath. The meaning is that he used to argue with it regarding the position that fulfilling a promise is obligatory. The son-in-law of the Prophet (ﷺ) whom he praised for fulfilling his promise to him is Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi', husband of Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Muslims took him captive on the day of Badr while he was a disbeliever, and the Prophet promised to return his daughter Zaynab to him, and he returned her to him. This is contrary to those who claimed that the son-in-law mentioned was Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Bukhari, in the chapter mentioned, cited four hadiths, each of which contains evidence for the fulfilment of promises.

The first: the hadith of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb in the story of Heraclius, which is a part of a famous authentic hadith [p. 441]. The point of evidence in it is his saying: "You claimed that he commands you to prayer, truthfulness, chastity, fulfilment of covenant and the rendering of trusts." All the things mentioned in this hadith, together with fulfilling the covenant, are obligatory: prayer, truthfulness, chastity, and rendering trusts. He also said after that that these matters are the attribute of a prophet, and following the prophets is obligatory.

The second: the hadith of Abu Hurayrah on the sign of the hypocrite. The point of evidence from it is his saying "and when he promises he breaks it." That breaking a promise is among the signs of the hypocrite indicates that a Muslim is not permitted to adopt the characteristics of the hypocrites.

The third: the hadith of Jabir in his story with Abu Bakr. The point of evidence from it is that Abu Bakr said: "Whoever has a debt upon the Prophet (ﷺ), or had a promise from him..." (the hadith), so he made the promise like a debt, and he fulfilled for Jabir what the Prophet (ﷺ) had promised him of wealth. This indicates obligation.

The fourth is the hadith of Ibn Abbas about which of the two terms Moses fulfilled. The basis for using it as evidence is that he fulfilled the better and more complete of the two. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: when he says something, he does it. So it is incumbent on the believers to follow the Messengers, doing what they say they will do. There are objections from those who disagree with the use of these hadiths as evidence.

Among the strongest proofs for fulfilling a promise is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 3]. This is because the great hatred of Allah toward failing to fulfil one's word indicates a severe prohibition of failing to fulfil it.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath, in discussing the chapter heading mentioned: al-Muhallab said: fulfilling a promise is commanded and recommended according to all scholars, but it is not obligatory, because they agree that a person who has been promised something cannot be counted among creditors in a claim against the estate together with the creditors. (End of quotation.)

The reporting of a consensus on this is rejected, for the disagreement is well known, though those who hold it are few. Ibn Abd al-Barr and Ibn al-Arabi said: the most prominent of those who held it was Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. This ends the point of relevance from the words of the Hafiz in al-Fath. He also said: some of them traced the disagreement on this question to the disagreement over gifts, namely whether ownership is acquired by taking possession or before it.

Now, once you know the statements of the people of knowledge on this question, and the evidence each group relied upon, know that what appears to me on this question, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that breaking a promise is not permissible, because it is one of the signs of hypocrites, and because Allah says: ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾. The apparent generality of this includes breaking a promise. However, if the one who promised refrains from fulfilling the promise, he is not judged to be bound by it and is not compelled to it by force. Rather, he is commanded to do it but is not forced to do it, because most of the scholars of the Ummah hold that he is not compelled to fulfil it, since it is a promise of pure goodness. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

(p-442) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom Allah bestowed favour from among the prophets, of the descendants of Adam, and of those We carried with Noah, and of the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping.﴾ The demonstrative in His saying "those" (ulaika) refers back to the prophets mentioned in this noble surah. Allah has here made clear that He bestowed favour upon them, chose them, and guided them. In Surat an-Nisa' He added to this by explaining all who received His favour apart from the prophets, in His saying: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among the prophets, the truthful ones (as-siddiqin), the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾ [An-Nisa: 69]. In Surat al-Fatiha He made clear that the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour is other than the path of those who earned anger and of those who are astray, in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray.﴾ [Al-Fatiha: 6-7].

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this noble verse: al-Suddi and Ibn Jarir, may Allah have mercy on them both, said: "The one meant from the descendants of Adam is Idris; the one meant from the descendants of those carried with Noah is Abraham; the one meant from the descendants of Abraham is Isaac, Jacob and Ishmael; and the one meant from the descendants of Israel is Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John and Jesus son of Mary." Ibn Jarir said: "That is why He separated their lineages, although Adam encompasses all of them, because among them is one who is not a son of those who were with Noah in the ark, namely Idris, for he is the grandfather of Noah."

I say: This is the more apparent view, that Idris is in the direct lineage of Noah, peace be upon them and upon our Prophet. It has been said, however, that he is one of the prophets of the Children of Israel, based on the hadith of the Night Journey (isra'), where he said in greeting to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Welcome to the righteous prophet and the righteous brother," and did not say "the righteous son," as Adam and Abraham said, peace be upon them and upon our Prophet. End of the purpose of Ibn Kathir's words, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him.

Ibn Kathir also said in his tafsir of this noble verse: He, may He be exalted, says: "These are the prophets," and the intended meaning is not only those mentioned in this surah, but the category of prophets, peace be upon them, digressing from naming individuals to the category, until he said at the end of his words: What supports that the meaning of this verse is the category of prophets is that it is like His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people; We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed, your Lord is Wise and Knowing.﴾ ﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob, all of whom We guided; and Noah We guided before; and among his descendants David, Solomon...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance.﴾ [Al-An'am: 83-90]. Ends. (p-443) He, may He be exalted, has said of these mentioned in al-An'am: ﴿and We chose them and guided them to a straight path.﴾ [Al-An'am: 87], just as He said of those mentioned in Surat Maryam: ﴿and of those whom We guided and chose.﴾ [Maryam: 58].

As for His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping﴾, in it He made clear that these prophets mentioned, when the verses of their Lord were recited to them, wept and prostrated. He alluded to this meaning in other places concerning the believers in general, not only the prophets:

• As in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down prostrating on their faces, and they say, 'Exalted is our Lord; indeed, the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled.' And they fall down on their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility."﴾ [Al-Isra': 107-109],

• and His saying: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 83],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾ [Al-Anfal: 2],

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeating; the skins shiver therefrom of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 23].

All these verses indicate that when they hear the verses of their Lord recited, they are greatly affected, which results in weeping and prostration for some of them, and for others a shivering of the skin and softening of hearts and skins, and the like.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿wa-bukiyyan﴾, is the plural of bakin (weeping ones). It is reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited this verse from Surat Maryam and prostrated, and said: "This is the prostration, so where is the weeping?" meaning crying. This place is among the prostrations of obligation (azaim al-sujud), without any disagreement among the scholars concerning that.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 59 (part 1 of 6):**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet ghayy (error, or its consequence)﴾ ﴿except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged in the least﴾.

The pronoun in His saying "from after them" refers to the prophets mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom God bestowed favor from among the prophets, of the descendants of Adam and of those We carried with Noah﴾ [Maryam: 58], that is: there succeeded, after those prophets, a khalf (successor), meaning evil offspring. Al-Qurtubi, may God have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of the surah "al-A'raf": Abu Hatim said: *al-khalf* with a sukun on the lam (*khalf*) means offspring; its singular and plural are the same. *Al-khalaf* with a fatha on the lam (*khalaf*) means a substitute, whether a son or a stranger. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-khalaf* with a fatha is the righteous, and with a sukun is the wicked. Labid said:

*Gone are those in whose shelter one used to live, and I remain among a khalf like the mangy skin of a camel.*

From this is said of poor speech: *khalf*. And from it comes the well-known proverb: "He kept silent for a thousand and spoke a *khalf*." So *khalf* with a sukun is used in dispraise, and *khalaf* with a fatha in praise. This is the common and well-known usage. The Prophet ﷺ said: "This knowledge will be carried by the just (*'udul*) of every *khalaf*." Each of the two may be used in place of the other. Hassan ibn Thabit, may God be pleased with him, said:

*For us is the first step toward You, and our khalf follows our first in obedience to God.*

Another said:

*Indeed we found a khalaf, an evil successor, who shut his door on us and then swore an oath.*

*The gatekeeper admits none except one who is known, a servant who, when he staggers under the load, halts.*

It is also narrated as *khadaf*, meaning he blocked up (the door). Here ends what is from him. *Al-Rudam* means flatulence.

The meaning of the noble verse is that this evil succession that came after those noble prophets had among its ugly traits that they neglected the prayer and followed their desires. The people of knowledge differed over what is meant by their neglecting the prayer. Some said: what is meant by neglecting it is delaying it beyond its time. Among those from whom this view is narrated are Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira, Mujahid, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and others. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this verse that this view is the correct one. Others said: neglecting it is failing to observe its conditions; among those who chose this view was al-Zajjaj. Others said: what is meant by neglecting it is denying its obligation; this view and the preceding one are narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. It was also said: neglecting it is performing it outside of congregation. It was said: neglecting it is leaving the mosques idle and occupying oneself with crafts and worldly means.

The one who ties down this work, may God pardon him and forgive him, said: All of these views fall within the verse, because delaying the prayer beyond its time, not performing it in congregation, failing to observe its conditions, denying its obligation, and leaving the mosques idle from it are all neglect of it, although the kinds of neglect differ in degree.

The scholars also differed over who the *khalf* mentioned are. It was said: they are the Jews. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. It was said: they are the Jews and Christians, narrated from al-Suddi. It was said: they are a people of the nation of Muhammad ﷺ who come after the righteous of it have passed away; some of them ride one another in the alleys in fornication. This is narrated from Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatada, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. It was said: they are the people of the West. There are other views on this as well.

The one who ties down this work, may God pardon him, said: That they are from the nation of Muhammad ﷺ is not, in my view, a sound opinion, because His saying, "from after them" [Maryam: 59], is a form indicating occurrence in the past tense, and it cannot be turned to the future except by an evidence that must be relied upon, as you see. The apparent meaning is that they are the Jews, the Christians, and other disbelievers who succeeded their prophets and righteous ones before the revelation of this verse; they neglected the prayer and followed their desires. In any case, what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion of revelation. So every succession that neglects the prayer and follows its desires falls under the blame and the warning mentioned in this verse. And the following of desires mentioned in the verse is general: it covers following every desire that distracts from the remembrance of God and from the prayer. It is narrated from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him: "Whoever builds lofty buildings, rides the showy mounts, and wears the famous garments, is among those who followed desires."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so they will meet ghayy﴾. Know first that the Arabs use *al-ghayy* for every evil, and *al-rashad* for every good. Al-Muraqqish al-Asghar said:

*Whoever meets good, people will praise his affair; and whoever goes astray (yaghwi) will not lack a blamer for his error.*

So his saying "whoever goes astray (yaghwi)" means whoever falls into evil. The well-known usage is that *al-ghayy* is misguidance. Regarding what is meant by "ghayy" in the verse, there are closely related views. Among them: the speech is elliptical, meaning "they will meet the recompense of ghayy." There is no doubt that they will meet the recompense of their misguidance. Among those who said this is al-Zajjaj. A parallel to this interpretation is His saying: ﴿he will meet sin (athaman)﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], according to those who say it means he will meet the recompense of his sins in this world. Similar to this meaning is His saying: ﴿They only consume fire in their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], and His saying: ﴿Those are they who consume nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾ [al-Baqara: 174]. Here fire is used for what they consumed in their bellies in this world of unlawful wealth, because it is its recompense; just as ghayy and athaman are used for punishment because it is their recompense.

Among the views also: *ghayy* in the verse means loss and falling into ruin. Among those narrated as saying this are Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd. It is also narrated from Ibn Zayd that *ghayyan* means evil, or misguidance, or failure. Some said: what is meant by His saying "ghayyan" in the verse is a valley in Hell filled with pus, because the pus and matter of the people of the Fire flow into it; it is deep in its bottom and foul in taste. Among those who said this are Ibn Mas'ud, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and it is narrated from 'A'isha and Shafi ibn Ma'tic.

A raised (marfu') hadith in accordance with this view has come from the hadith of Abu Umama and Ibn 'Abbas, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Ghayy is a valley in their Hell," as in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. And in the hadith of Abu Umama: "Ghayy and Athaman are two rivers at the bottom of Hell, into which flows the pus of the people of the Fire." The apparent view is that nothing authentic has been established from the Prophet ﷺ on this. Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir of this verse the hadith of Abu Umama Sudayy ibn 'Ajlan al-Bahili, which we have referred to just now, then said: "This is a gharib hadith, and its raising to the Prophet is munkar." It was also said that the meaning is: ﴿so they will meet ghayy﴾, that is, misguidance in the Hereafter away from the path to Paradise. This was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. There are other views as well, but all the views rest on one thing, which is that those successors who neglected the prayer and followed their desires will meet on the Day of Resurrection a great punishment.

Now that you know the scholars' words on this noble verse, and that God threatened in it those who neglected the prayer and followed desires with ghayy, which is great evil and painful punishment, know that He has indicated this meaning in other places:

• As in His saying, condemning those who waste the prayer and do not guard it, and threatening them: ﴿So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, who make show (of their deeds), and withhold common kindnesses﴾ [al-Ma'un: 4–7];

• And His saying, condemning the hypocrites: ﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to the people, and remember God only a little﴾ [al-Nisa': 142];

• And His saying about them also: ﴿Nothing prevented their contributions from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in God and His Messenger, and they do not come to prayer except lazily, and they do not spend except unwillingly﴾ [al-Tawba: 54]. He has also indicated in many places the condemnation and threat against those who follow desires:

• As in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their abode﴾ [Muhammad: 12];

• And His saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will come to know﴾ [al-Hijr: 3];

• And His saying: ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals. Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 46–47], and other verses.

It is understood from the implicit contrary meaning of the noble verse that the good successors do not neglect the prayer and do not follow desires. God has indicated this in several places in His Book:

• As in His saying: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their prayer﴾, up to His saying: ﴿And those who guard their prayers. Those are the inheritors, who will inherit Paradise (al-Firdaws); they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1–11], and other verses;

• And as in His saying: ﴿But as for one who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire, indeed Paradise will be his refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 40–41], and other verses.

* *

**Issues related to this noble verse**

**The first issue:** The scholars agreed that one who abandons the prayer while denying its obligation is a disbeliever, and that he is to be killed as a disbeliever unless he repents. The apparent view is that abandoning what the prayer is not valid without, such as ablution and the ghusl of major impurity, is like abandoning the prayer itself, and denying its obligation is like denying the obligation of the prayer.

* *

**Second issue: the ruling on one who deliberately abandons the prayer out of negligence and laziness while acknowledging that it is obligatory.** The scholars differed over whether such a person is a disbeliever (kafir) or a Muslim, and whether he is to be killed as an unbeliever, killed as a prescribed penalty (hadd), or not killed at all. Some scholars held that he is an apostate disbeliever who must be asked to repent. If he repents, that is well; if he does not, he is killed as a disbeliever. Among those who held this view is Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) in the more sound of his two reported positions. It is also narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him). Ibn al-Mubarak and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh held it, as did Mansur al-Faqih among the Shafi'is. It is also narrated from Abu al-Tayyib ibn Salamah among the Shafi'is, and it is a weak narration from Malik.

Those who held this view cited evidence, including the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿But if they repent, establish the prayer and give the zakat, then they are your brothers in religion﴾ [al-Tawbah: 11]. By the implication of this verse, if they do not establish the prayer, they are not brothers of the believers. And whoever is denied the brotherhood of the believers is among the disbelievers, because Allah says: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10].

Another piece of evidence is the hadith of Jabir, which is established in Sahih Muslim from him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), through two chains. The wording of the text in the first of them is: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'Between a man and shirk and kufr is the abandoning of the prayer.'" The wording in the second is: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Between a man and shirk and kufr is the abandoning of the prayer.'" End of quotation. It is clear that the one who abandons the prayer is a disbeliever, because coupling shirk with kufr is a strong emphasis that he is a disbeliever.

Another is the hadith of Umm Salamah and the hadith of 'Awf ibn Malik, which will come, indicating the fighting of rulers when they do not pray. Both are in Sahih Muslim, together with the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, which is agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim). He said: "We pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to hear and obey, in ease and in hardship, in what we like and dislike, and in the preference given to others over us, and that we would not dispute the command with its people." He said: "Except that you see clear disbelief (kufran bawahan) with you, concerning which you have a proof from Allah."

So the combined force of the aforementioned hadiths shows that abandoning the prayer is clear disbelief, concerning which there is a proof from Allah. We have already presented these hadiths in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah. This is among the strongest evidences of those who hold this view.

Another is the hadith of Buraydah ibn al-Husayb al-Aslami (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The covenant that is between us and them is the prayer. Whoever abandons it has disbelieved." It was recorded by Imam Ahmad, the authors of the Sunan, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim. Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar regarding this hadith: al-Nasa'i and al-'Iraqi authenticated it. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on al-Muhadhdhab: al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated it. Al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a hasan sahih hadith." Al-Hakim said in al-Mustadrak after he cited this hadith with its chain: "This is a hadith whose chain is sahih, and no defect is known in it in any respect. Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) relied on 'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah from his father, and Muslim relied on al-Husayn ibn Waqid, though they did not record it with this wording. This hadith has a sahih corroboration that meets the conditions of both of them together: Ahmad ibn Sahl al-Faqih informed us in Bukhara, Qays ibn Unayf narrated to us, Qutaybah ibn Sa'id narrated to us, Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, from al-Jurayri, from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, from Abu Hurayrah who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not regard any of the deeds as kufr when abandoned, except the prayer." Al-Dhahabi affirmed al-Hakim's authentication of the hadith of Buraydah mentioned above. Regarding the report of Ibn Shaqiq from Abu Hurayrah mentioned above, al-Dhahabi said: "It has not been discussed, and its chain is acceptable."

The annotator of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: It appears that the statement of the memorizer al-Dhahabi (may Allah have mercy on him), "it has not been discussed," is an oversight on his part, because he did discuss it in his remarks on the hadith of Buraydah mentioned just above, where he said: "This hadith has a sahih corroboration that meets the conditions of both of them together," meaning the report of Ibn Shaqiq mentioned, as you see. Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on al-Muhadhdhab: "And from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq al-'Uqayli, the Tabi'i whose eminence is agreed upon: The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not regard any of the deeds as kufr when abandoned, except the prayer." It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi in the Book of Iman with a sahih chain. End of quotation. Al-Nawawi (may Allah have mercy on him) in this statement mentioned the agreement on the eminence of the aforementioned Ibn Shaqiq, although there is an element of nasb in him. Al-Majd said in al-Muntaqa: "And from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq al-'Uqayli: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) . . . to the end of it." Then he said: "al-Tirmidhi narrated it." Ended.

It is not hidden from you that the narration of al-Hakim includes Abu Hurayrah, whereas the narration of al-Tirmidhi does not include Abu Hurayrah. The hadith of Buraydah ibn al-Husayb and the report of Ibn Shaqiq, both mentioned, contain clear indication that abandoning the prayer deliberately out of negligence is kufr, even if the one who abandons it acknowledges its obligation. This is reinforced by the hadith of Jabir mentioned above in Sahih Muslim.

Among the evidences indicating that abandoning the prayer is kufr is what Imam Ahmad and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir and al-Awsat narrated from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned the prayer one day and said: "Whoever preserves it, it will be a light, a proof, and a salvation for him on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever does not preserve it, there will be no light, proof, or salvation for him, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be with Qarun, Pharaoh, Haman, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf." End of quotation. This hadith is the clearest indication of the disbelief of one who abandons the prayer, because the negation of light, proof, and salvation, and being with Pharaoh, Haman, Qarun, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf on the Day of Resurrection, is, as you see, the clearest evidence of disbelief. al-Haythami said in Majma' al-Zawa'id regarding this hadith: "It was narrated by Ahmad and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir and al-Awsat, and the narrators of Ahmad are trustworthy." End of quotation.

There are other hadiths on this subject besides what we have mentioned. Some of them are weak and some are fit to be used as evidence. al-Haythami mentioned a portion of them in Majma' al-Zawa'id. What we have mentioned is sufficient.

A group of scholars held that one who deliberately abandons the prayer out of negligence and laziness, while acknowledging its obligation, is not a disbeliever, and that he is to be killed as a prescribed penalty (hadd), like the married adulterer, not as an unbeliever. This is the position of Malik and his companions, and it is the position of al-Shafi'i and the majority of his companions. Al-Nawawi in his commentary on al-Muhadhdhab attributed it to the majority of the earlier and later scholars. In his commentary on Sahih Muslim he said: Malik, al-Shafi'i (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on both of them), and the majority of the earlier and later scholars held that he is not declared a disbeliever but is judged a sinner (fasiq), and is asked to repent. If he repents, well; otherwise we kill him as a prescribed penalty, like the married adulterer, but he is killed by the sword. End of quotation.

Know that this position requires evidence on two counts: that he is not a disbeliever, and that he is to be killed. These are the proofs of its holders for both matters together. As for their proofs that he is to be killed:

Among them is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿But if they repent, establish the prayer, and give the zakat, then let them go on their way﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. In this verse Allah the Exalted made the release of their way conditional upon their establishing the prayer. By the implication of the condition, if they do not establish it, their way is not released, and this is so.

Among them is what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and establish the prayer and give the zakat. When they do that, they protect their blood and their property from me, except by its right." End of quotation.

This sahih hadith indicates that their blood and property are not protected except by establishing the prayer, as you see.

Among them is what al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), while in Yemen, sent to the Prophet (ﷺ) a piece of gold in its ore, and he divided it among four people. A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, fear Allah!' He (ﷺ) said: 'Woe to you! Am I not the most deserving of the people of the earth to fear Allah?' Then the man turned away. Khalid ibn al-Walid said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I not strike his neck?' He said: 'No, perhaps he prays.' Khalid said: 'And how many a worshipper says with his tongue what is not in his heart?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I have not been commanded to probe the hearts of people or to split open their bellies.'" This is an abridgment of an agreed-upon hadith. His (ﷺ) saying in this sahih hadith, "No," means: do not kill him. His giving as the reason, "perhaps he prays," contains clear indication of the prohibition of killing those who pray. It is understood from it that if he does not pray, he is to be killed, and this is so.

Among them is what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Rulers will be placed over you. You will recognize some of their actions and reject others. Whoever dislikes them is free of blame, and whoever rejects them is safe, but whoever is content and follows..." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we not fight them?" He said: "No, as long as they pray." This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih. The "ma" in his saying "ma sallaw" is a temporal verbal particle, meaning: do not fight them for as long as they are praying. It is understood from it that if they do not pray, they are to be fought, and this is so. Yet the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the agreed-upon hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit: "Except that you see clear disbelief with you, concerning which there is a proof from Allah." So the hadith of Umm Salamah and the like of the hadith of 'Awf ibn Malik, which will come, indicates the killing of one who does not pray. When the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit is combined with it, the evidence for disbelief by abandoning the prayer becomes apparent, because he said in the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit: "Except that you see clear disbelief..." and so on. In the hadith of Umm Salamah and 'Awf ibn Malik he indicated that if they abandon the prayer they are to be fought. This indicates that abandoning it is among the clear disbelief. This is among the strongest evidences of the first position's holders.

The hadith of 'Awf ibn Malik mentioned is what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with the wording: He said: "The best of your rulers are those whom you love and who love you, who pray for you and you pray for them. The worst of your rulers are those whom you hate and who hate you, whom you curse and who curse you." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we not confront them with the sword?" He said: "No, as long as they establish the prayer among you." And so on. In it is clear indication of fighting them if they do not establish the prayer, as you see.

Among the evidences of this position for killing the one who abandons the prayer is what the three Imams narrated: Malik in his Muwatta', al-Shafi'i and Ahmad in their Musnads, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Adi ibn al-Khiyar: "That a man from the Ansar narrated to him that he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in a gathering, and asked him privately for permission to kill a man among the hypocrites. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke aloud and said: 'Does he not testify that there is no god but Allah?' The Ansari said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, but there is no testimony for him.' He said: 'Does he not testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Yes, but there is no testimony for him.' He said: 'Does he not pray?' He said: 'Yes, but there is no prayer for him.' He said: 'Those are the ones whom Allah has forbidden me to kill.'" End of quotation. In another narration: "from them."

This is the summary of the evidences of the holders of this position for killing one who abandons the prayer. Know that most of those who held that he is to be killed say that he is killed by the sword. Some of them said that he is beaten with a stick until he dies. Ibn Surayj said: He is prodded with an iron implement or struck with a stick, and it is said to him: "Pray, or we will kill you." This is repeated to him until he prays or dies.

They differed over whether he should be asked to repent. Some said: he is asked to repent for three days, and if he repents, well and good; otherwise he is put to death. Others said: he is not asked to repent, because he is put to death as a *hadd* (a fixed penalty prescribed by God), and the *hadd*s are not dropped by repentance. Others said: if no more than the time for one *rak'ah* (a unit of prayer) remains of the necessary time (*al-waqt al-ḍarūrī*) and he has not prayed, he is put to death. Others said: he is not put to death until its time has passed. The majority hold that he is put to death for abandoning a single prayer, and this is the apparent meaning of the evidences. It was also said: he is not put to death until he abandons more than one prayer. From Imam Ahmad there are two reports: one, that he is not put to death until the time of the second abandoned prayer, together with the first, becomes narrow; and the other, that he is not put to death until the time of the fourth prayer becomes narrow.

The one who restricts this ruling, may God pardon and forgive him, says: the view that appears most correct to me is that he is put to death by the sword, and that he is asked to repent, because there is *ijma'* (scholarly consensus) on accepting his repentance if he repents. The more apparent position is that he is asked to repent immediately and is not given three days, while he refuses to pray, in keeping with the apparent meaning of the texts mentioned, and that he is not put to death until no more of the necessary time remains than what suffices for one *rak'ah* with its two prostrations. And God knows best.

As for the evidence of those who hold that he is not an unbeliever (*kāfir*), among it is the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 116]. Among it is the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, may God be pleased with him, which Malik related in the *Muwatta'* from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban, from Ibn Muhayriz, that a man from the Banu Kinanah called al-Mukhaddaji heard a man in Syria, known by the *kunya* Abu Muhammad, saying: "The witr (a prayer performed at night) is obligatory." Al-Mukhaddaji said: "So I went to 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, intercepted him as he was heading to the mosque, and informed him of what Abu Muhammad had said." 'Ubadah said: "Abu Muhammad has lied. I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Five prayers God, Mighty and Majestic, has prescribed for the servants. Whoever comes with them, without neglecting any of them out of disregard for their right, has with God a covenant that He will admit him to Paradise. And whoever does not come with them, has no covenant with God: if He wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will admit him to Paradise.'" End of his words, verbatim.

In the *Sunan* of Abu Dawud: "Al-Qa'nabi related to us from Malik, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Hibban," up to the end of the chain, and the text is like the wording of the *Muwatta'* that we mentioned. In the *Sunan* of al-Nasa'i: "Qutaybah informed us from Malik, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban," up to the end of the chain, and the text is like the wording mentioned. In the *Sunan* of Ibn Majah: "Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us: Ibn Abi 'Adi related to us from (p-452) Shu'bah, from 'Abd Rabbihi ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban, from Ibn Muhayriz, from al-Mukhaddaji, from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: '*Five prayers God has enjoined upon His servants*'..." up to the end of the hadith mentioned, with its meaning, nearly in its wording.

It is well known that the men in these chains are trustworthy (*thiqat*) and well known, except al-Mukhaddaji mentioned; yet Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy, and by his being declared trustworthy you know the soundness of the hadith mentioned. It also has corroborating reports (*shawahid*) by which it is further strengthened. Abu Dawud said in his *Sunan*: "Muhammad ibn Harb al-Wasiti related to us: Yazid, that is Ibn Harun, related to us: Muhammad ibn Mutarrif related to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, from 'Abd Allah al-Sunabihi, who said: Abu Muhammad claimed that the witr is obligatory. 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit said: Abu Muhammad has lied. I bear witness that I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: '*Five prayers God has enjoined*'..." up to the end of the hadith, with its meaning. 'Abd Allah al-Sunabihi, mentioned here, is said to have been a Companion from Medina; and it is said he is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Usaylah al-Muradi, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Sunabihi, a trustworthy senior Successor (*tabi'i*), who came to Medina five days after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), and died during the caliphate of 'Abd al-Malik. On either assessment, the narration of al-Sunabihi mentioned is either the narration of a Companion or of a trustworthy Successor, and by it the narration of al-Mukhaddaji mentioned is strengthened. The men in the chain of Abu Dawud's report, other than 'Abd Allah al-Sunabihi, are trustworthy, well known, with no blemish upon them; and by this you know the soundness of the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit mentioned.

Al-Zurqani said, in his commentary on the *Muwatta'*: "In it, that is, the hadith of 'Ubadah mentioned, is that the one who abandons prayer does not become an unbeliever, and his punishment is not certain; rather he is under the Will of God, by the explicit text of the hadith. It has been related by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, through the route of Malik, and Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr declared it sound. It came by another route from 'Ubadah with similar wording in Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Bayhaqi, and it has a witness with Muhammad ibn Nasr from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As." End of his words.

Al-'Allamah al-Shawkani, may God have mercy on him, said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: "This hadith has a witness from the hadith of Abu Qatadah in Ibn Majah, and from the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah in Ahmad, and Abu Dawud related it from al-Sunabihi." End of the point of relevance from him.

Al-Nawawi said in the *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, after citing the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit mentioned: "This is a sound hadith. Abu Dawud and others related it with sound chains." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "It is a sound and established hadith, on which there is no disagreement from Malik." If it is asked: how did Ibn 'Abd al-Barr declare it sound while he also said that al-Mukhaddaji in its chain is unknown (*majhul*)? The answer to this is from two angles. The first: its soundness is by way of the corroborating reports we have mentioned, for they make it sound. The second is what we have already stated of Ibn Hibban's declaring al-Mukhaddaji trustworthy. The hadith of 'Ubadah mentioned contains clear indication that abandoning prayer is not disbelief, because his being under the Will mentioned in it is evidence of the absence of disbelief, by the saying of God: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 116].

Among the evidences of those who hold that the one who abandons prayer while acknowledging its obligation is not a disbeliever is what Imam Ahmad and the authors of the *Sunan* related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The first thing a servant will be reckoned for on the Day of Resurrection is the obligatory prayer. If he has completed it, well and good; otherwise it will be said: Look, does he have any voluntary prayer? If he has voluntary prayer, the obligatory prayer will be completed from his voluntary prayer. Then the rest of the obligatory deeds will be dealt with in the same way." End.

Al-Shawkani, may God have mercy on him, said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: The hadith was related by Abu Dawud by three routes: two routes connected to Abu Hurayrah, and a third route connected to Tamim al-Dari. All of them are free of any blemish, and neither he nor al-Mundhiri commented on it in a way that would render it weak. al-Nasa'i related it through a route whose chain is good and whose men are the men of the Sahih, as al-'Iraqi said, and Ibn al-Qattan declared it sound. al-Hakim related the hadith in *al-Mustadrak* and said: "This is sound in its chain, but they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not record it." In the same chapter, from Tamim al-Dari, there is in Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah a hadith similar to that of Abu Hurayrah. Al-'Iraqi said: its chain is sound. al-Hakim related it in *al-Mustadrak* and said: "Its chain is sound according to the condition of Muslim." End of the point of relevance from him.

The way of deriving evidence from the hadith mentioned, that abandoning prayer is not disbelief, is that the deficiency of the obligatory prayers and their completion from the supererogatory prayers encompasses, by its generality, abandoning some of them deliberately, as the apparent generality of the wording requires, as you see.

Al-Majd (Ibn Taymiyyah's grandfather) said in *al-Muntaqa*, after citing the evidences we have mentioned for the non-disbelief of the one who abandons prayer while acknowledging its obligation, the following text: "This position is supported by general statements, among them what is related from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: '*Whoever bears witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and that 'Isa is the servant of God and His word which He cast to Maryam and a spirit from Him, and that Paradise and Hellfire are true, God will admit him to Paradise, according to what deeds he had*.' Agreed upon. And from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) said while Mu'adh was riding behind him on the saddle: '*O Mu'adh!*' He said: 'At your service, O Messenger of God, and I am at your command,' three times. Then he said: '*There is no servant who bears witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger (p-454), except that God forbids him to the Fire.*' He said: 'O Messenger of God, shall I not inform the people of it so that they will rejoice?' He said: '*Then they will rely on it.*' So Mu'adh informed of it at his death, out of fear of sin (*ta'ththum*)," that is, fear of sin for withholding the report of it; agreed upon. And from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: '*Every prophet has an answered supplication, and each prophet hastened his supplication, but I have kept my supplication as an intercession for my nation on the Day of Resurrection, and it will reach whoever of my nation dies without associating anything with God*,' related by Muslim. And from him also: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: '*The happiest of people with my intercession is whoever says there is no god but God, sincerely from his heart*,' related by al-Bukhari." End of the point of relevance from him.

A group of scholars, among them Imam Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, and his companions, a group of the people of Kufa, Sufyan al-Thawri, and al-Muzani, the companion of al-Shafi'i, said: the one who deliberately abandons prayer out of laziness and negligence, while acknowledging its obligation, is not put to death nor declared a disbeliever; rather he is disciplined (*yu'azzaru*) and imprisoned until he prays. They argued for his not being a disbeliever with the evidences we mentioned just above for the second position. They argued for his not being put to death with evidences, among them the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud agreed upon, which we presented in Surat al-Ma'idah and elsewhere: "The blood of a Muslim man who bears witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God is not lawful, except in one of three cases: the married adulterer, a life for a life, and one who abandons his religion and separates from the community." They said: this is an agreed-upon hadith, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly stated that the blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in one of three cases, and did not mention abandoning prayer among them; this indicates that it does not necessitate execution. They said: the evidences you cite for his execution indicate it only by their implicit meanings (*mafahim*), namely the meanings of contradiction (*mafhum al-mukhalafah*), as was previously explained. The hadith of Ibn Mas'ud indicates what we have mentioned by its explicit meaning (*manṭuq*), and the explicit meaning takes precedence over the implicit meaning. Moreover, what is established in the principles of Imam Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, is that he does not treat as valid the well-known implicit meaning known as the implication of the address (*dalil al-khitab*), which is the meaning of contradiction. Accordingly, he does not accept the indication of the hadiths mentioned for his execution, because they indicate it only by the implicit meaning of their contradiction, whereas the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud indicates that by its explicit meaning. Another of their arguments is their analogy of abandoning prayer to abandoning fasting and pilgrimage, for example: each of these is one of the pillars of Islam, and the one who abandons them is not executed; so likewise prayer.

As for those who said that he is a disbeliever and that he is to be executed, they answered the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud by saying it is general and is specified (*yukhassas*) by the hadiths that indicate the execution of the one who abandons prayer. As for their analogy to abandoning pilgrimage and fasting, they said it is invalid as an argument, because it contradicts the hadiths mentioned that indicate his execution. As for the hadiths that indicate non-disbelief, they said that some of them are general and are specified by the hadiths that indicate his disbelief, and some of them are not like that, such as the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, which indicates that he is under the Will. So the hadiths indicating his disbelief take precedence over it, because they are more authentic than it; for some of them are in the Sahih of Muslim, and in it there is explicit statement of his disbelief and polytheism. And among them is the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit agreed upon, together with the hadith of Umm Salamah and 'Awf ibn Malik in the Sahih of Muslim, as was previously explained.

The scholars who held that he is not a disbeliever answered the proofs of their opponents by saying that the word *kufr* in the hadiths cited means a lesser kufr, not the kufr that takes a person out of the religion of Islam. For this they cited many hadiths in which the Prophet ﷺ explicitly uses the word *kufr* without meaning that a person leaves the religion of Islam. Al-Majd (in *al-Muntaqa*) said: "Those who hold this view have interpreted the hadiths describing someone as a disbeliever as referring to ingratitude (*kufr al-ni'mah*), or to a meaning that comes close to disbelief. There are also hadiths outside the context of prayer that are meant in this way. Ibn Mas'ud narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Abusing a Muslim is wickedness (*fusuq*), and fighting him is disbelief (*kufr*).' (Agreed upon.) And Abu Dharr narrated that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'No man claims to be the son of someone other than his father while knowing it, except that he has disbelieved. And whoever claims what is not his, is not one of us, and let him take his seat in the Fire.' (Agreed upon.) And Abu Hurairah said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Two things among people are disbelief (*kufr*) in them: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead.' (Narrated by Ahmad and Muslim.) And Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: 'Umar used to swear, "By my father!" The Prophet ﷺ forbade him and said: "Whoever swears by other than Allah has committed shirk."' (Narrated by Ahmad.) And Ibn Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'The habitual drinker of wine, if he dies, will meet Allah like an idol-worshipper.' End of quotation in its wording. Similar statements in the Sunnah are very numerous. Of this kind is calling showing-off (*riya'*) shirk. Among them is the authentic hadith in al-Bukhari and others that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'I saw the Fire, and I have never seen a sight more dreadful than today, and I saw that most of its people are women.' They said: 'Why, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Because of their kufr.' It was said: 'Do they disbelieve in Allah?' He said: 'They disbelieve in their husbands (*al-'ashir*), and they disbelieve in kindness. If you were to be kind to one of them all her life, and then she saw something from you, she would say: I have never seen any good from you at all.'" This is the wording of al-Bukhari in one of the places where he narrated the said hadith. The Prophet ﷺ applied the name *kufr* to them, but when they asked him about it, it became clear that he meant other than the kufr that takes a person out of the religion of Islam.

This is the essence of the words and evidences of the scholars on the question of deliberately abandoning prayer while acknowledging its obligation.
