The most evidence-supported view in my opinion is the view of those who said he is a disbeliever. But if the views are assessed according to the discipline of *usul al-fiqh* (principles of jurisprudence) and the sciences of hadith, then the view of the majority is that it is a kufr that does not remove a person from the religion, because it is obligatory to reconcile the evidences when possible. When the kufr and shirk mentioned in the hadiths are understood as the kufr that does not remove one from the religion, reconciliation between the evidences is achieved, and reconciliation is obligatory when possible, because implementing both evidences is better than disregarding one of them, as is known in the principles and the science of hadith. Al-Nawawi, in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, after citing the evidences of those who said he is not a disbeliever, said the following: "The Muslims have never ceased to inherit from the one who abandons prayer, and he inherits from them. Had he been a disbeliever, he would not have been forgiven, would not have inherited, and would not have been inherited from."

As for the answer to what those who declared him a disbeliever cited from the hadith of Jabir and Buraydah, and the narration of Ibn Shaqiq: all of that is understood as meaning that he shares with the disbeliever some of his rulings, namely execution. This interpretation is necessary to reconcile the texts of the Shari'ah and its rules that we have mentioned. End of the relevant part of his words.

* *

**The third issue**

The scholars agreed that whoever forgets the prayer, or sleeps through it until its time has passed, must make it up (*qada'*). Authentic evidences establish this:

From these is what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated in their two *Sahih*s from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it; there is no expiation for it except that."

From these is what Muslim narrated, also from Anas, as a marfu' hadith (traced directly to the Prophet ﷺ): "When one of you sleeps through the prayer or neglects it, let him pray it when he remembers it, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]."

And from these is what Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, for Allah says: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]."

And from these is what al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih) narrated from Abu Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: They mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ their sleeping through the prayer, and he said: "There is no negligence in sleep; negligence is only in wakefulness. When one of you forgets a prayer or sleeps through it, let him pray it when he remembers it."

And from these is what Muslim and Ahmad narrated from Abu Qatadah in the story of their sleeping through the Fajr prayer, who said: "Then Bilal called the adhan for the prayer, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed two rak'ahs, then prayed the morning prayer, doing as he used to do every day."

And from these is what Ahmad, Ibn Khuzaymah, and Ibn Hibban in their *Sahih*s, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tabarani, and others narrated from Imran ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We travelled with the Prophet ﷺ, and when it was the end of the night we stopped to rest, and we did not wake until the heat of the sun woke us. Each of us man began to get up, startled, to his water for ablution. Then he ordered Bilal, and he gave the adhan, then he prayed the two rak'ahs before Fajr, then he gave the iqamah and we prayed." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, should we not repeat it at its time tomorrow?" He said: "Does your Lord forbid you from usury while accepting it from you?" End of quotation. The original of this hadith of Imran is in the two *Sahih*s, but the mention of the adhan and iqamah is not in them, nor is his saying: "They said, O Messenger of Allah, should we not repeat it," to the end.

The conclusion is that there is no disagreement among the scholars about making up the prayer for the one who slept or forgot, and the hadiths we have mentioned, and others like them that we have not mentioned, establish it.

* *

**The fourth issue**

Know that the verified position is that the missed prayers (*fawa'it*) must be given precedence over the present prayer. The evidence for this is what is established in the two *Sahih*s from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him: "Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, came on the day of the Trench after the sun had set, and began to revile the disbelievers of Quraysh. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I was almost unable to pray the 'Asr until the sun was nearly setting.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'By Allah, I have not prayed it.' We went to Buthan, and he performed ablution for the prayer, and we performed ablution for it. Then he prayed the 'Asr after the sun had set, and then he prayed the Maghrib after it."

This hadith, agreed upon, explicitly states that the Prophet ﷺ prayed 'Asr as a make-up prayer after the sunset and gave it precedence over Maghrib. It is an authentic and clear text on giving precedence to the missed prayer over the present one. In the principles it is established that the Prophet's ﷺ actions which are not accompanied by an indication of obligation or otherwise are to be understood as obligatory, because of the general texts commanding us to follow him ﷺ in his sayings and actions, and for caution in fulfilling the duty.

Among the clearest evidences for this is that when he ﷺ removed his sandal during the prayer, his companions removed their sandals, following him ﷺ, before they knew that Jibril had informed him that there was filth on its underside. He ﷺ asked them why they had removed their sandals, and they answered that they saw him remove his sandal, which is a bare action without indicators of obligation or otherwise. He approved of that and did not reject it, and this shows that following him in his bare actions is binding. Although some have criticized the hadith as mursal (missing a companion in its chain), some have preferred to connect it.

The many evidences showing the obligation to follow him ﷺ in the Qur'an and Sunnah testify to this. On the point that his bare actions are to be understood as obligatory, the author of *Maraqi al-Su'ud* in the chapter on the Sunnah stated:

"Every action whose manner is unknown, is taken, according to the sounder view, as obligatory."

There are well-known objections to the view that it implies obligation, which can be found in the principles, see *Nashr al-Bunud* and others.

This supports what we have mentioned, that his bare action, which is giving precedence to the missed 'Asr over the present Maghrib, implies obligation, by his ﷺ saying: "Pray as you have seen me pray." Al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) said in *Fath al-Bari*, on al-Bukhari's use of the Prophet's action to show that the earlier missed prayers should be prayed first, the following: "The argument does not stand for one who holds that missed prayers must be performed in sequence, unless we say that the Prophet's bare actions indicate obligation. The exception is if it can be supported by the general wording of his saying: 'Pray as you have seen me pray.' The Shafi'is have taken this into account in other matters besides this." End of quotation.

We say: The more evident view is that bare actions imply obligation, as the author of *Maraqi* asserted in the verse mentioned, and likewise the general wording of the hadith "Pray as you have seen me pray" implies that as well. And Allah knows best.

Know that if a person remembers a missed prayer during the narrow time of a present prayer, the scholars differ on whether he should give precedence to the missed prayer even if the time of the present prayer runs out, or not, into three positions:

The first: he gives precedence to the missed prayer even if the time of the present prayer runs out. This is the position of Malik and most of his companions.

The second: he begins with the present prayer, to preserve its time. This is the position of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions, and most of the people of hadith.

The third: he is given the choice to give precedence to whichever of the two he wishes. This is the view of Ashhab, one of Malik's companions. 'Iyad said: The point of disagreement applies when the missed prayers are not numerous. But if they are numerous, there is no disagreement that he begins with the present prayer. They differed on the limit of what counts as few in this matter: it was said a day's prayers, and it was said four prayers.

* *

**The fifth issue**

As for the sequence of the missed prayers among themselves, most scholars hold that it is obligatory when one remembers them, not when one forgets them, and this is the more evident view. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The sequence among them is not obligatory but recommended. This is also reported from Tawus, al-Hasan al-Basri, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, Abu Thawr and Dawud.

Some scholars said: The sequence is obligatory absolutely, whether the missed prayers are few or many. This is the view of Ahmad and Zufar. It is reported from Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, that if one forgot the missed prayers, the prayers he prayed after them are valid. Ahmad and Ishaq said: If one remembers a missed prayer while he is in a present prayer, he completes the one he is in, then makes up the missed prayer, and then it is obligatory to repeat the present prayer. They argued for their view with a hadith from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever forgets a prayer and does not remember it except while he is with the imam, when he finishes his prayer, let him repeat the prayer he forgot, then let him repeat the prayer he prayed with the imam." Al-Nawawi in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* said: This hadith is weak; Musa ibn Harun al-Hammal (spelled with a ḥā’) al-Hafiz graded it weak, and Abu Zur'ah al-Razi, then al-Bayhaqi, said: The sound version is that it is a mawquf (stopping at a companion) report.

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: The more evident view in my opinion is that the sequence of the missed prayers among themselves is obligatory, first-to-first. The evidence for this is the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Nasa'i in his *Sunan* said: Amr ibn Ali related to us, saying: Yahya related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Dhi'b related to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id related to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Sa'id, from his father, who said: "The polytheists kept us busy on the day of the Trench from the Dhuhr prayer until the sun set, and that was before fighting was legislated as it later was. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in battle﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered Bilal, and he gave the iqamah for the Dhuhr prayer, and he prayed it as he used to pray it at its time. Then he gave the iqamah for 'Asr, and he prayed it as he used to pray it at its time. Then he gave the adhan for Maghrib and prayed it as he used to pray it at its time." End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 59 (part 5 of 6):

Thus this chain of narration is sound, as you see, and its narrators are reliable and well known. ʿAmr ibn ʿAli is Abu Hafs al-Fallas (al-Fallas, "the seller of salt"), who was trustworthy and a memorizer of hadith. Yahya is al-Qattan, whose eminence is well known. Likewise Ibn Abi Dhi'b, whose eminence is well known. Saʿid ibn Saʿid is al-Maqburi, who is trustworthy. And ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Saʿid al-Khudri is trustworthy. So this chain is sound, as you see, and in it there is an explicit statement that the Prophet ﷺ arranged the missed prayers in their making up: the earliest first, then the next.

We have already mentioned that his actions (ﷺ) which are free of contextual indicators demand obligation according to the most correct view, and that this is reinforced by the hadith of Malik ibn al-Huwayrith, which is established in the Sahih: "Pray as you have seen me pray." This hadith of Abu Saʿid was also related by the Imam Ahmad. Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih. Al-Shawkani also said, quoting Ibn Sayyid al-Nas al-Yaʿmuri: the hadith of Abu Saʿid was related by al-Tahawi from al-Muzani from al-Shafiʿi: Ibn Abi Fudayk related to us, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Maqburi, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Saʿid, from his father, who said... And this is a sound and eminent chain. End quote.

Al-Nasa'i said in his Sunan: Hannad informed us, from Hushaym, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Nafi' ibn Jubayr, from Abu ʿUbayda, who said: ʿAbd Allah said: "The polytheists distracted the Prophet ﷺ from four prayers on the day of the Trench, so he commanded Bilal, who called the adhan, then gave the iqama and prayed the Zuhr, then gave the iqama and prayed the ʿAsr, then gave the iqama and prayed the Maghrib, then gave the iqama and prayed the ʿIsha'." End quote.

Al-Qasim ibn Zakariyya ibn Dinar informed us, saying: Husayn ibn ʿAli related to us, from Za'ida, who said: Saʿid ibn Abi ʿArubah related to us, who said: Hisham related to us that Abu al-Zubayr al-Makki narrated to them, from Nafi' ibn Jubayr, that Abu ʿUbayda ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud narrated to them that ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud said: "We were on a military campaign when the polytheists kept us from the prayers of Zuhr, ʿAsr, Maghrib and ʿIsha'. When the polytheists withdrew, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered a caller, who gave the iqama for the Zuhr prayer and we prayed; he gave the iqama for the ʿAsr prayer and we prayed; he gave the iqama for the Maghrib prayer and we prayed; he gave the iqama for the ʿIsha' prayer and we prayed. Then he came around to us and said: 'There is no group on earth remembering Allah, Mighty and Majestic, other than you.'" End quote. This hadith of Ibn Masʿud was also related by al-Tirmidhi. Al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: its chain is not objectionable.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: It appears that the chain of this hadith of Ibn Masʿud contains some weakness, because its transmitter from him is his son Abu ʿUbayda, and his narration from him is mursal (disconnected), since he did not hear from him. However, this mursal narration is reinforced by the hadith of Abu Saʿid which we mentioned just above and which is sound, and those scholars who accept the mursal as evidence accept it even if it is not reinforced by anything else.

Know that the two hadiths of Abu Saʿid and Ibn Masʿud mentioned are not contradicted by what is in the two Sahihs, that the distraction was from ʿAsr alone; because what is in them is an addition, and the addition of trustworthy narrators is accepted. "Whoever memorized is a proof over whoever did not memorize." By this you know that what Ibn al-ʿArabi mentioned, giving precedence to what is in the two Sahihs over the addition found in the hadiths of Abu Saʿid and Ibn Masʿud, is contrary to scholarly verification.

* *

A NOTE

Know that the Four Imams and their companions and the majority of jurists of the regions hold that whoever forgets a prayer or sleeps through it makes it up alone, and is not obliged to add another prayer. Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Chapter: Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, and he should not repeat anything except that prayer." Ibrahim said: "Whoever left one prayer for twenty years need only repeat that one prayer." Abu Nuʿaym and Musa ibn Isma'il related to us, both saying: Hammam related to us, from Qatada, from Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it; there is no expiation for it except that," and [the Qur'an verse]: "And establish prayer for My remembrance" [Ta-Ha: 14]. Musa said: Hammam said: I heard him say after "And establish prayer for My remembrance" [Ta-Ha: 14]. Hammam also said: Qatada related to us, (p-461) Anas related to us from the Prophet ﷺ similarly. End quote.

In *Fath al-Bari*, in discussing this hadith and its chapter heading, he said: Ali ibn al-Munayyir said: al-Bukhari affirmed this ruling explicitly, although it is one on which opinions differ, because of the strength of its evidence. But it is in accordance with analogy, since the obligation is five prayers and no more; so whoever makes up the missed prayer completes the number commanded. It also accords with the apparent meaning of the address, by the Lawgiver's words "let him pray it," without mentioning any addition. He also said: "There is no expiation for it except that," and from this restriction it is understood that nothing is obligatory except repeating it. Malik held that whoever remembers, after having prayed a prayer, that he had not prayed the one before it, should pray the one he remembered and then pray the one he had prayed, out of regard for the order. End quote. If it is said: there occurs in Sahih Muslim, in some routes of the hadith of Abu Qatada concerning the story of the Prophet ﷺ and his companions sleeping through the Subh prayer until the sun struck them, the wording: Then he said, meaning the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed there is no negligence in sleep; negligence is only upon one who does not pray the prayer until the time of the next prayer comes. Whoever does that, let him pray it when he wakes for it, and when tomorrow comes, let him pray it at its time." End quote.

His saying in this hadith "when tomorrow comes..." etc. indicates that he makes up the missed prayer twice: the first at its remembrance, and the second at the entry of its time the next day? The answer is what al-Nawawi mentioned in his commentary on the said hadith. He said: As for his saying ﷺ: "When tomorrow comes, let him pray it at its time," its meaning is that if a prayer is missed and he makes it up, its time is not changed and shifted in the future; rather it remains as it was. When tomorrow comes, he prays the prayer of tomorrow at its usual time and it does not shift. Its meaning is not that he makes up the missed prayer twice: once immediately and once tomorrow. Rather its meaning is what we have mentioned. This is the correct understanding of this hadith, and the views of scholars concerning it have varied, and the verifiers have chosen what I have mentioned, and Allah knows best. End quote. And this interpretation he gave of this report is the one whose correctness appears to us, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

However, there occurs in Sunan Abi Dawud, in some routes of the hadith of Abu Qatada concerning the story of the sleepers from the aforementioned prayer, the wording: "Whoever among you reaches the prayer of tomorrow in a sound state, let him make up with it its like." End quote. This wording is explicit that he makes up the missed prayer twice, and it does not admit the meaning which al-Nawawi and others gave to the wording of Muslim's report.

Scholars have given several answers regarding this report. Ibn Hajar, in *Fath al-Bari*, after pointing to the aforementioned report of Abu Dawud, said: Al-Khattabi said: I know of no one who held it obligatory according to its apparent meaning. He said: It may be that the command in it is for recommendation, so as to obtain the excellence of the time in making up. End quote. No one of the early generations said that this is recommended either; rather they counted the hadith an error by its narrator, as al-Tirmidhi and others related from al-Bukhari. This is supported by what al-Nasa'i related (p-462) from the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn, that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we not make it up at its time on the next day?" He ﷺ said: "Allah does not forbid you from usury while taking it from you." End quote of the author of *al-Fath*. The hadith of Imran mentioned has already been cited by us, and we mentioned who related it, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

THE SIXTH ISSUE

Know that scholars differ regarding one who deliberately abandons the prayer out of laziness until its time has passed, while acknowledging its obligation: is it obligatory upon him to make it up or not? We have already mentioned the scholarly disagreement over his disbelief. So, according to the view that he is a disbelieving apostate, the matter follows the disagreement concerning the apostate: is it obligatory upon him to make up what he missed during the period of his apostasy or not?

Know first that the disbeliever is sometimes an original disbeliever who never previously had Islam, and sometimes a disbeliever by apostasy from the religion of Islam after having been a Muslim.

As for the original disbeliever, he is not obliged to make up the acts of worship he left during his disbelief. There is no disagreement about this among the scholars of the Muslims, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. Many people accepted Islam in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and he did not command any of them to make up anything missed in their disbelief.

As for the apostate, there is a well-known disagreement among the scholars. Some scholars said: he is not obliged to make up what he left during his apostasy, nor during his time of Islam before apostasy; because apostasy nullifies all his deeds and makes him like an original disbeliever, God forbid. If he had performed the pilgrimage of obligation, his apostasy nullifies it according to this view, so he must repeat it when he returns to Islam. Those who hold this rely on the apparent sense of Allah's words: ﴿If you associate partners, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ the verse [al-Zumar: 65], and His words: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void, and he is in the Hereafter among the losers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5]. Other scholars said: he is obliged to make up the acts of worship he left during his apostasy and during his time of Islam before apostasy, and he is not obliged to repeat the pilgrimage of obligation, because apostasy did not nullify it. Those who hold this rely on Allah's words: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter﴾ the verse [al-Baqarah: 217], where He made dying in disbelief a condition for the nullification of the deed. The first view is that of Malik and those who agree with him, and the second is that of al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him; and these are two reports from Imam Ahmad. We have mentioned elsewhere that the view of al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him on this issue is more in line with the principles, because of the obligation to (p-463) apply the unrestricted to the restricted, especially when the ruling and the cause are the same, as here.

As for the view of the majority that he is not a disbeliever, they also differed on whether making up is obligatory upon him.

Know first that the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) differed concerning a command to an act of worship restricted to a specific time: does it entail a command to make it up after its time has passed without needing a new command for making up, or does it not entail making up after the time has passed, so that a new command is necessary for making up? Abu Bakr al-Razi of the Hanafis, in agreement with the majority of the Hanafis, held that the command to a time-bound act of worship entails a command to make it up after the time has passed, without needing a new command. They argued for this with a principle: the command to a compound is a command to each of its parts; so when some parts become impossible, performing the part that is not impossible becomes obligatory. Thus the command to a time-bound act of worship, like the five prayers, is a command to a compound of two things: the first is performing the act of worship; the second is its being joined to its specified time. When the time passes, one of them becomes impossible, namely being joined to the specified time, and the other remains possible, namely performing the act of worship; so from the first command there follows the performance of the part that is within one's power, since a command to a compound is a command to its parts.

This view was introduced by Ibn Qudamah in *Rawdat al-Nazir*, and he and al-Ghazali in *al-Mustasfa* attributed it to some jurists.

The majority of the scholars of usul (usul al-fiqh) held that a command to perform a time-bound act of worship (ibadah mu'aqqatah) does not necessarily entail a command to make it up (qada') after its time has passed. They based this on a principle: that restricting an act of worship to a specific time, rather than other times, is only for a benefit that pertains to that specific time and not to others. For if the benefit lay in other times, there would be no point in restricting it to this time instead. They said: so restricting the prayers to their appointed times, fasting to Ramadan, is similar to restricting the Hajj to 'Arafat, zakat to the poor, the prayer to the qiblah, the killing to the unbeliever, and the like.

Know that those who said that a command does not entail qada', and they are the majority, differed concerning repeating a prayer that was deliberately abandoned, given their view that the one who abandons it is not a disbeliever. The majority of them held that it is obligatory to repeat it. They said: We say that qada' necessarily requires a new command, but the deliberately abandoned prayer has evidences for its qada', among them: analogy (qiyas) of the one who deliberately abandons it upon the forgetful person (al-nasi) and the sleeper (al-na'im), for whom the obligation of qada' is explicitly stated. They said: If qada' is obligatory upon the sleeper and the forgetful person, then it is obligatory upon the deliberate abandoner a fortiori (min bab awla). Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: Among what indicates the obligation of qada' is the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the one who had intercourse during the day in Ramadan to fast one day together with the expiation (kaffarah)," meaning in place of the day which he had invalidated by deliberate intercourse. It was narrated by al-Bayhaqi with a good chain, and Abu Dawud narrated something similar. End of al-Nawawi's words.

Among the strongest evidences for the obligation of qada' upon the one who deliberately abandons it is the general wording of the authentic hadith that we mentioned earlier in surah al-Isra', in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The debt owed to Allah has more right to be paid." His saying "debt of Allah" is a generic noun (ism jins) made genitive to a definite noun, so it is general to every debt, like His saying: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], which is general to every favour. There is no doubt that the deliberately abandoned prayer is a debt of Allah upon the one who abandons it, so the generality of the hadith indicates that it is a matter truly deserving to be paid. And there is no contradicting evidence against this generality.

Some scholars said: There is no qada' for one who deliberately abandons the prayer, because qada' requires a new command, and no new command has come for the qada' of the one who deliberately abandons it. Among those who held this is Ibn Hazm, and Abu al-Abbas Ibn Taymiyah (may Allah have mercy on him) preferred it. To this question al-Shinqiti alluded in Maraqi al-Su'ud with his saying:

The command does not entail qada',
rather it comes with a new command.
For it is in a specific time that it arrives,
for the benefit upon which it was built.
Al-Razi disagreed, since the compound
has for each part its ruling that extends to it.

* *

Note (tanbih)

The reason for the scholars' disagreement on this question is that it was pulled between two differing principles, and each group looked to one of the two differing principles:

The first: a command to a compound act is a command to its parts. This is the view of the Hanafiyyah and those who agree with them.

The second: a command to an act of worship at a specific time is only for a benefit that pertains to the stated time. This is the view of the majority. Such things are a cause of disagreement in the question, as Shaykh Mayyara indicated in al-Takmil, with his saying:

If in the branch there are two formulations, by prohibition and permission, then there are two opinions.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever coming to pass.﴾ In this noble verse, may He be exalted and high, He made clear that He promised His servants, the believing and obedient, gardens of Eden. Then He made clear that His promise is "coming" (ma'tiyy), meaning that they will come to it and attain what they were promised, because He, may He be exalted and high, does not break the appointment (al-mi'ad) (p-465). He alluded to this meaning in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Allah's promise; Allah does not fail His promise﴾ [al-Rum: 6],

• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail the appointment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31],

• and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, You do not fail the appointment.﴾ ﴿So their Lord responded to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 193-194],

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down upon their faces in prostration﴾ ﴿and say, "Glory to our Lord! Indeed, the promise of our Lord is ever fulfilled."﴾ [al-Isra': 107-108],

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How, then, will you guard yourselves if you disbelieve on a Day that will make the children grey-haired?﴾ ﴿The sky will be split by it; His promise is ever fulfilled.﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 17-18],

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which the righteous have been promised? It is for them a reward and a destination.﴾ ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding eternally; it is upon your Lord a promise that is sought.﴾ [al-Furqan: 15-16],

along with other verses.

As for His saying "ma'tiyyan" (مَأْتِيًّا), it is the passive participle of "ata-hu" (أتاه), meaning when it reaches him. The meaning is that they must surely come to what they were promised. This is contrary to those who claimed that "ma'tiyyan" is in the form of the passive participle but is intended to mean the active, i.e., "his promise was coming," since there is no need for this with the clear apparent meaning of the verse.

* *

Note

Some scholars of rhetoric (balagha) cited this verse as an example of one type of apposition (badal), namely badal al-kull min al-ba'd (the whole substituted for a part). They said: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ [Maryam: 61] is an apposition to "al-Jannah" in His saying: ﴿So those will enter Paradise (al-jannah)﴾ [Maryam: 60], an apposition of the whole for a part.

They said: Among examples of badal al-kull min al-ba'd is his saying:

*May Allah have mercy on bones they buried in Sijistan, Talhat al-Talahat*

So "Talhah" is an apposition to "a'zaman" (bones), being badal al-kull min al-ba'd. Accordingly, the types of apposition are six: badal al-shay' min al-shay' (apposition of a thing to a thing), badal al-ba'd min al-kull (apposition of a part to a whole), badal al-kull min al-ba'd, badal al-ishtimal (apposition of inclusion), badal al-bada' (apposition of change of mind), and badal al-ghalat (apposition by error).

The one who restricts this (its author), may Allah pardon him, says: In my view, it is not necessary in the verse and the line of poetry that the apposition be badal al-kull min al-ba'd. Rather, it may be badal al-shay' min al-shay', because the alif and lam in His saying "fa-ula'ika yadkhulun al-jannah" are for the genus (lil-jins). When it is for the genus, it may be intended to include all the gardens, so His saying "Gardens of Eden" is an apposition to "al-Jannah" as badal al-shay' min al-shay', because what is meant by the first is the plural (p-466), as many examples of this were mentioned earlier. And "al-a'zam" in the line of poetry is a metonymy for the person, and "Talhah" is an apposition to it, badal al-shay' min al-shay', because they did not bury the bones alone, but buried the whole person mentioned, his bones and the rest of his body, and he expressed it by the word "bones."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 62 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They shall hear therein no idle talk, but only "Peace." And they shall have their provision therein morning and evening.﴾

In this noble verse, the Majestic and Exalted mentions that when their Lord admits the believers into the Gardens of Eden which He has promised them, ﴿they shall hear therein﴾ [Maryam: 62], that is, in the aforementioned Gardens, ''laghw'' (idle talk), that is, worthless, base speech such as is heard in this world. ''Laghw'' is the excess of speech and that which has no benefit in it, and it includes obscene and false speech. From it is the saying of Ru'bah, or it is said of al-Ajjaj:

"And by the Lord of the troops of pilgrims, restrained from idle talk and obscene speech."

As has preceded in surah "al-Ma'idah."

Apparently, His words "except 'Peace'" are an exceptive construction of the disconnected type (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "but they shall hear therein 'Peace,'" because they greet one another, and the angels greet them, as His words indicate: ﴿Their greeting therein will be "Peace"﴾ [Ibrahim: 23], and His words: ﴿The angels will enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23-24], as has preceded in full.

This meaning which he indicated here has also come in other places, such as His words in "al-Waqi'ah": ﴿They shall not hear therein any idle talk or sinful speech, but only the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25-26]. The disconnected exception has come in other verses of the Book of Allah, such as:

- His words: ﴿They have no knowledge of it, except the following of assumption﴾ [al-Nisa': 157].
- His words: ﴿And for no one has he any favor to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Layl: 19-20].
- His words: ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56].
- And His words: ﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except [in] trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 29].

And other verses besides these. So all the exceptions mentioned in these verses are disconnected. A parallel to this in the speech of the Arabs regarding the disconnected exception is the saying of Nabighah Dhubyani:

"I stood there at dusk, asking it, but it could not answer, and there was no one in the abode [but]
except the stakes of the horses, which I cannot clearly describe, and the stone-ring like a basin in the hard, firm ground."

So "al-Awari" (the tethering posts for horses) are not of the kind of "anyone" (ahad).

And the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"And the daughter of a noble man, whom we married, though no suitor had sought her except the spear and its handler."

And the saying of Jiran al-'Awd:

"And a land in which there is no companion, except the wild cattle and the camels."

"The spear" is not of the kind of "the suitor," and "the wild cattle and the camels" are neither of them of the kind of "the companion."

And the saying of Dirar ibn al-Azwar:

"I strive, when striving is a spoil, and Allah knows best about the striving servant.
On an evening when spears do not avail in its place, nor do arrows, except the Mashriqi (sword) that is well-tempered."

By what we have mentioned you will know the validity of the occurrence of the disconnected exception, as is the view of the majority of the scholars of legal theory (usul), unlike Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and some of the Shafi'is, who say that the disconnected exception is not valid, because exception is the exclusion of what entered the wording, and what is not of the kind of the excepted-from did not enter the wording at all, so that it could be excluded by the exception.

* *

Notes (tanbihat)

The first: Know that the clarification of the difference between the connected and disconnected exception is achieved by two matters; when both are present, the exception is connected, and if either one of them is missing, it is disconnected. The first: that the excepted item be of the same kind as the excepted-from, as in: "The people came except Zayd." If it is not of its kind, it is disconnected, as in: "The people came except a donkey." The second: that the judgment about the excepted item be the opposite (naqid) of the judgment about the excepted-from. It is known that the opposite of affirmation is negation, and vice versa. Hence the exception from a negative is an affirmation, and from an affirmation a negation. If the judgment about the excepted item is not the opposite of the judgment about the excepted-from, it is disconnected, even if the excepted item is of the same kind as the excepted-from. So His words: ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56], is definitely a disconnected exception, although the excepted item is of the same kind as the excepted-from. Likewise His words: ﴿Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except [in] trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. It is disconnected in both verses because the judgment on the excepted item is not the opposite of the judgment on the excepted-from. The opposite of "They will not taste death therein, except" is "They will taste death therein," and this opposite, which is tasting death in the Hereafter, is not what is judged of the excepted item; rather the tasting in this world is judged. And the opposite of "Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly" is "Consume it unjustly," which is not judged of the excepted item.

It results that the disconnection of the exception is of two types: one by a judgment about something not of the kind of the excepted-from, like your saying: "I saw your two brothers, except a garment." The second: by a judgment not in the opposite, like: "I saw your two brothers, except Zayd, who did not travel."

* *

The second notice

Know that some of the juristic (fiqh) branches are built upon the disagreement about the validity of the disconnected exception. If a man acknowledged a debt to another and said to him: "I owe you a thousand dinars except a garment," then according to the view that the disconnected exception is invalid, his words "except a garment" are void, and he is bound to the full thousand. According to the view that the disconnected exception is valid, his words "except a garment" are not voided, and the value of the garment is deducted from the thousand. Those who said the value is deducted differed about its interpretation into two views. One: that it is a metaphor (majaz), and that he used the term "garment" and meant its value. The second: that there is an implication (idmar), that is, an omitted modifier (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "except the value of a garment." Whoever said that metaphor takes precedence over implication said that "except a garment" is a metaphor, using "garment" and meaning its value, like the use of "blood" for the blood-money. Whoever said that implication takes precedence over metaphor said "except a garment," meaning "except the value of a garment." The author of Maraqi al-Su'ud relied on giving metaphor precedence over implication in his words:

"After specification comes metaphor, then implication, and transfer (naql) is the most reliable."

The meaning of the verse is that the order of precedence among them is: specification (takhsis), then metaphor, then implication, then transfer (naql). An example of giving specification precedence over metaphor is when the wording admits both of them, as in His words: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. It admits specification, because some polytheists, such as the protected non-Muslims (dhimmis) and those under treaty, are excluded by a specifying indicator from the generality of "the polytheists." It also admits, according to those who hold the view of metaphor, that it is a metonymic metaphor (majaz mursal), in which the whole is used and the part is meant. Specification takes precedence for two reasons. The first: the wording remains literal (haqiqah) in what the specifier did not exclude, and the literal takes precedence over the metaphorical. The second: the wording remains in force (mustasḥab) over the remaining individuals after specification without needing an indicator. An example of giving metaphor precedence over implication, when the wording admits both, is a master's saying to his servant who is older than him: "You are my father." It admits that it is a metonymic metaphor, from using the necessary cause for the consequence, meaning "You are free," because fatherhood entails manumission. It also admits implication, meaning "You are like my father in compassion and respect." On the first, he is freed; on the second, he is not freed. Among its examples is the case we are concerned with. An example of giving implication precedence over transfer, when the wording admits both, is His words: ﴿And He has forbidden riba﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]. It admits implication, meaning the taking of riba, which is an increase in selling one dirham for two dirhams, for example. On this view, if the extra dirham were removed, the sale of a dirham for a dirham would be valid. It also admits the transfer of riba to the meaning of the contract, so the contract of selling a dirham for two dirhams is prohibited; and if the extra were removed, a new contract would be required in every case.

The one who annotated it, may Allah pardon him, said: On these two views which they mentioned regarding "He owes me a thousand dinars except a garment," namely implication and transfer, the exception returns to being connected, because the value of the garment is of the same kind as the thousand which he acknowledged, whether we say that the value is implied or we say that it is expressed by the word "garment."

* *

The third notice

Know that the disagreement about the validity of the disconnected exception is in reality a verbal disagreement, because those who prohibited it did not prohibit it entirely. They only said that it is not of the true exception, because the exception particle in it has the meaning of "but" (lakin), so it is closer to the adversative (istidrak) than to the exception. Some of those who hold the disconnected exception say that the garment in the earlier example is superfluous, and it is counted as a regret of the one who acknowledged the thousand. The relation between the connected and disconnected exception, according to those who hold it, has been said to be a relation of correspondence (tawatu'), and it has been said that it is of the category of shared meaning (ishtirak). The author of Maraqi al-Su'ud pointed to the question of the disconnected exception and the difference between it and the connected in his words:

"The judgment by the opposite of the judgment on what preceded it is connected to it;
and other than that is disconnected, and they preferred its validity, and it is a metaphor, as he made clear.
So sleep, after a thousand dirhams, a sum, for deletion and metaphor, or for regret.
It was said: by deletion at the acknowledgment, and the contract, the meaning of 'and' is in it, by partnership.
And by correspondence some said, and he required connection in it."

What we have mentioned, that the exception in His words: ﴿They shall hear therein no idle talk, but only "Peace"﴾ [Maryam: 62], is disconnected, is the apparent view. It has been said that it is of the category of emphasizing praise with what resembles blame, like the saying of Nabighah Dhubyani:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

And the saying of another:

"So if there is any fault in me, I am a coward of the dog and of lean young camel."

On this view, the verse is like His words: ﴿And you do not blame us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 126], and His words: ﴿And they resented only that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74], and similar verses, as has preceded in full in surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah).

And His words in this noble verse: ﴿And they shall have their provision therein morning and evening﴾, there is a well-known question about it, which is to be asked: what is the reason for mentioning morning and evening, given that Paradise is perpetual light and there is no night in it? The scholars have several answers to this question:

The first: that what is meant by "morning and evening" is the amount of time equal to that, as in His words: ﴿Its morning journey is a month, and its evening journey is a month﴾ [Saba': 12], meaning the duration of a month. This meaning has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Juraij, and others.

The second answer: that the Arabs in their time considered whoever had lunch and dinner to be among the prosperous, so the verse came encouraging them, even though there is more than that in Paradise. This is reported from Qatadah, al-Hasan, and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir.

The third answer: that the Arabs express perpetuity by "morning and evening," and "dawn and dusk," as a man says: "I am with so-and-so in the morning and evening, and morning and evening," meaning constancy, and not intending the two specific times.

The fourth answer: that "morning" is the time before they are occupied with their pleasures, and "evening" is the time after they finish with their pleasures, because between them intervals of transition from one state to another occur. This meaning returns to the first answer.

Fifth answer: it is what al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim narrated in Nawadir al-Usul (Rare Principles of Jurisprudence), from the hadith of Aban, from al-Hasan and Abu Qilaba, who said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is there night in Paradise?' He said: 'What prompts you to this?' He said: 'I heard Allah, the Exalted, mention: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾, and I said: night lies between morning and evening.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no night there. Rather, it is only light and radiance. The morning comes after the evening and the evening after the morning. There come to them gifts from Allah, the Exalted, at the times of the prayers which they used to pray in the world, and the angels greet them.'" End of quotation (p-471), transmitted through the citation of the author of ad-Durr al-Manthur and al-Qurtubi in his tafsir. Al-Qurtubi, after quoting this, said: "This is in the utmost clarity regarding the meaning of the verse, and we have mentioned it in the book al-Tadhkira." Then he said: "The scholars have said: there is no night or day in Paradise; rather, they are in light always. They know the measure of night from day by the lowering of the veils and the closing of the doors, and they know the measure of day by the raising of the veils and the opening of the doors." This was mentioned by Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi, al-Mahdawi and others. End of his words. This last answer, which al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related from al-Hasan and Abu Qilaba from the Prophet (ﷺ), goes back to the first answer. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 66:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And man says, "When I have died, will I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ ﴿Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾

Some of the people of knowledge (ahl al-'ilm) said: This verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who found decayed bones, crumbled them with his hand, and said, "Does Muhammad claim that we will be resurrected after death?" This was related by al-Kalbi, and mentioned by al-Wahidi and al-Tha'labi. Al-Mahdawi said: It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and his companions, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: It was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il, and it was said: concerning Abu Jahl. In every one of these reports, Allah attributed this statement to the whole category of man, while it was uttered by some individuals of that category. This is because among the methods of Arabic speech is attributing an action to a group, even though its doer is only some of them and not all of them. Among the clearest Qur'anic proofs for this is the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i: ﴿So if they fight you, then kill them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], with "qatala" (to kill) in both verbs, meaning: if some of them kill some of you, then let some of you kill them, as was mentioned many times before. Among the clearest Arabic evidences for this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"So the sword of the Banu 'Abs, when they struck with it, cut off the hand of Waraqa from the head of Khalid."

He attributed the striking to the Banu 'Abs, even though he explicitly stated that the one striking with the sword in his hand was Waraqa, who is the son of Zuhayr ibn Jadhima al-'Absi, and Khalid is the son of Ja'far al-Kilabi. The story of his killing of the aforementioned Zuhayr is well known.

In this verse, Allah has clarified that this disbelieving man says, denying resurrection: ﴿When I have died, will I really be brought forth alive?﴾, supposing that once he dies it is impossible for him to live again after death. Allah refuted this statement of his with His saying: ﴿Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾, meaning: Does man say this statement of his in denial of resurrection, without remembering that We brought him into existence with the first creation when he was nothing, but was non-existence and We brought him into being? Our creating him the first time is a decisive proof of Our power to bring him into being again through resurrection.

The argument that He indicates here has been preceded by verses that demonstrate it in Surah al-Baqarah, al-Nahl and others, such as:

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he presents to Us an example and forgets his own creation. He says, "Who will give life to bones while they are decomposed?" Say, "He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knowing of all creation."﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78-79],

• His saying: ﴿Were We incapable of the first creation? Rather, they are in confusion about a new creation.﴾ [Qaf: 15],

• His saying: ﴿And you have already known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62],

• His saying: ﴿And it is He who begins creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27], to the end of the verse,

• His saying: ﴿They will say, "Who will restore us?" Say, "He who created you the first time."﴾ [al-Isra: 51],

• His saying: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], to the end of the verse,

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it; it is a promise upon Us. Indeed, We will do it.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 104],

and other verses besides these, as has been explained before.

In the authentic hadith which he (ﷺ) narrates from his Lord: "Allah, exalted is He, says: The son of Adam has denied Me, and it was not for him to deny Me; and the son of Adam has harmed Me, and it was not for him to harm Me. As for his denying Me, it is his saying: 'He will not restore me as He originated me'; and the first creation is not easier for Me than the last. As for his harming Me, it is his saying: 'Allah has a son,' while I am the One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is begotten, and to whom no one is equal."

If it is asked: What is the governing element (al-'amil) of the adverb "idha" (when)? The answer: it is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by the conditional response; its estimated form is: "Shall I be brought forth alive when I have died?" meaning: at the time when death and destruction take hold of me, shall I be brought forth alive? That is, this is impossible. If it is asked: Why do you not say that it is governed by "ukhraju" (be brought forth) mentioned in His saying ﴿will I really be brought forth alive﴾, according to the well-known custom that the governing element of "idha" is its response? The answer: the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') in His saying ﴿will I really be brought forth alive﴾ prevents what follows it from governing what precedes it, as is known in the science of Arabic grammar. So it is not permissible to say: "Today Zayd is standing," meaning "Zayd is standing today." As for what some of them claim, that the particle of futurity (harf al-tanfis), which is "sawfa," also prevents what follows it from governing what precedes it, to the extent that according to the reading of Talha ibn Musarrif, "a-idha ma mittu sa-ukhraju hayyan" without the lam, the accusative of "idha" by the mentioned "ukhraju" is impossible, this is contrary to what is verified.

The verified view is that the particle of futurity does not prevent what follows it from governing what precedes it. The evidence for this is its occurrence in Arabic speech, such as the saying of the poet:

"When our mother saw him, her grief subsided, and she said, 'Our father, this is how he will do.'"

His saying "hakadha" (this way) is in the accusative by his saying "yaf'alu" (he will do), as Abu Hayyan clarified in al-Bahr. Accordingly, on the reading of Talha ibn Musarrif, his saying "idha" is in the accusative by his saying "ukhraju," because the lam is absent from it and the particle of futurity does not prevent what follows it from governing what precedes it.

* *

Note

If you say: The lam of initiation that enters upon the present tense gives the meaning of the present, so how does it combine with the particle of futurity, which indicates the future? The answer: the lam here has been stripped of the meaning of the present and is restricted only to the meaning of emphasis, and for this reason it combines with the particle of futurity, as al-Zamakhshari explained in al-Kashshaf. Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr al-Muhit, objected to this, saying that some scholars of Arabic deny that the said lam gives the meaning of the present; and according to his view the difficulty falls away entirely. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils, then We will surely bring them forth around Hell on their knees.﴾ When Allah, exalted and high, established the proof for the Resurrection by His saying: ﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ [Maryam: 67], He swore by His noble Self that He would gather them—that is, the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection—and others among mankind, and that He would gather with them the devils who used to lead them astray in this world, and that He would bring them forth around Hell on their knees. These two matters mentioned in this noble verse, He has alluded to elsewhere. As for His gathering them together with their devils, He has alluded to it in His saying: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their wives, and what they used to worship ﴿besides Allah, and lead them to the path of Hellfire.﴾ [As-Saffat: 22–23], according to one of the interpretations, (p-475) and in His saying: ﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 38].

As for bringing them forth around Hell on their knees, He has alluded to it in His saying: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling; every nation will be called to its record. Today you will be recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ [Al-Jathiyah: 28]. And His saying in this noble verse: "jithiyyan" (on their knees) is the plural of "jathin," and "al-jathi" is an active participle of "jatha yajthu juthuwwan," and "jatha yajthi jithiyyan," meaning: he sat on his knees or stood on the tips of his toes. The custom among the Arabs was that when they were in a situation of distress and severe matter, they would kneel on their knees. From this is the saying of one of them:

So who will protect the defenders, and who will protect the warriors, when the warriors kneel upon their knees?
When it is said: "Abu Malik has died, the youth of noble deeds, the foremost of the Arabs."

That the meaning of His saying "jithiyyan" in this verse, and His saying: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling﴾ [Al-Jathiyah: 28], is that they kneel upon their knees, is the apparent meaning; it is the view of the majority, and it is the well-known usage in the language. From this is the saying of al-Kumayt:

They left their nobles kneeling, while they were below the nobles, bound together.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying in this noble verse "jithiyyan," that its meaning is "groups." And it is related from Muqatil that "jithiyyan" means "gathered in groups, group by group." According to this view, it is the plural of "juthwah" (with the jim having three vowelizations), which is a heap of stones or a gathered heap of earth. So the people of wine gather around Hell separately, the people of fornication separately, the people of theft separately, and so on. From this meaning is the saying of Tarafah ibn al-ʿAbd in his Mu'allaqah:

You see two heaps of earth upon them, with solid slabs of well-arranged stone.

Thus said some of the scholars. But it is objected that the pattern "fuʿlah," like "juthwah," is not known to have its plural in "fuʿul," like "juthiyy." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read this letter "jithiyyan" with a kasra on the jim, assimilating it to the kasra following it; and the rest read "juthiyyan" with a damma on the jim, according to the original form.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 69:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We will surely drag out from every sect (shi'ah) whichever of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿Then We are most knowing of those most deserving of burning therein﴾.

His saying in this noble verse, "la-nanzi'anna" (We will surely drag out) [Maryam: 69], means: "la-nastakhrijanna" (We will surely extract), (p-476) ﴿from every sect﴾, i.e., from every community of people of one religion. The root of "shi'ah" is the form "fi'lah," like "firqah" (group), and it is the group that follows (shaa'a) others, meaning that it follows them in guidance or in misguidance. The Arabs say: "shaa'ahu shiyaran" when he followed him.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿whichever of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful﴾, it means: "la-nastakhrijanna wa-lunmayyizanna" (We will surely extract and distinguish) from every group among the groups of error and corruption, the most disobedient of them first, then the most disobedient after them, and the most rebellious first, then the most rebellious after them. So they are begun with in punishment and in being made to enter the Fire, according to their ranks in disbelief, misguidance and leading others astray. This is the apparent meaning of the noble verse: that the leaders and chiefs in disbelief are punished before others, and their punishment is intensified because of their misguidance and their misguiding of others.

Verses from the Book of Allah, may He be exalted, have come indicating this:

• Like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah, We will increase them in punishment upon punishment because of what they used to spread corruption﴾ [al-Nahl: 88].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens, and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to fabricate﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

• And His saying: ﴿That they may bear their full burdens on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]. For this reason there are "first" (uula) and "last" (ukhra) communities in the Fire. The "first" are those whose punishment and entry into the Fire is begun with, and the "last" are those who enter after them according to their differing kinds of disbelief and error, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿He will say: Enter among nations that have passed away before you of jinn and mankind into the Fire. Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister until, when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them: Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire. He will say: For each is double, but you do not know.﴾ ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them: So you had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn﴾ [al-A'raf: 38-39].

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿Then We are most knowing of those most deserving of burning therein﴾ [Maryam: 70], it means that He, may He be exalted, is most knowing of who among them deserves to burn in the Fire and who is most deserving of it. He has made clear that the leaders and the followers are all among those who deserve it, in His saying: ﴿He will say: For each is double﴾, and so on. "Al-saliyy" is the verbal noun of "saliya al-nar" (like "radiya"), "yaslaha saliyyan" (with dammah and kasrah), when one endures its pain and is in direct contact with its heat.

The scholars differed about the case of "ayyu" (which) despite it being in the accusative, since it is the object of "la-nanzi'anna." Sibawayh and those who followed him held that the word "ayyu" is a relative (mawsulah), and that it is built on dammah when it is annexed and its relative clause has an omitted pronoun, as here. Ibn Malik set this down in al-Khulasah with his saying:

"Ayyu, like 'kama,' is inflected when not annexed, and the pronoun of its relative clause is omitted."

"And some of them inflected it in all cases..." etc.

What indicates the soundness of Sibawayh's view, may Allah have mercy on him, is the saying of Ghassan ibn Wa'lah:

"When you meet the Banu Malik, then greet whichever of them is best."

The narration has "ayyuhum" with dammah.

Al-Khalil, Yunus and others disagreed with Sibawayh about this "ayyu." Al-Khalil said: in the verse it is an interrogative, reported by an implied saying, and the implied meaning is: "Then We will surely drag out from every sect those about whom it is said: which of them is most insolent." Al-Khalil cited for this meaning the poet's saying:

"I spent the night with the girl in a place, and I spent it neither embarrassed nor deprived."

That is: "I spent it in the position of one who is told: you are neither embarrassed nor deprived."

As for Yunus, he held that it is also interrogative, but he ruled that the verb before it is suspended by the interrogative, because suspension (ta'liq) for him is not restricted to verbs of the heart. He argued against al-Khalil, Yunus and their followers, in favour of Sibawayh, with the verse of Ghassan ibn Wa'lah mentioned above, since the narration there has "ayyuhum" with dammah, although prepositions do not have an implied saying or suspension placed between them and their governed noun, according to the more correct view, though some of them disagreed on this with some interpretations. From what we have mentioned you know that what some of them said, that all the grammarians erred against Sibawayh in his saying about "ayyu" in this noble verse, is contrary to the verification, and Allah knows best.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "'itiyyan" with a kasrah on the 'ayn, and "saliyyan" with a kasrah on the sad, for assimilation (al-itba'). The rest read both with dammah, according to the original form.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 71 (part 1 of 2):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it (the Fire). That is a decree of your Lord, inevitable.﴾ ﴿Then We shall save those who were righteous, and leave the wrongdoers therein, kneeling.﴾

The scholars differed about the meaning of the "coming to" (wurud) of the Fire in this noble verse, and they stated several opinions:

The first: the meaning of wurud is entering (ad-dukhul), but Allah averts its harm from His righteous servants at the moment of entering.

The second: the meaning of the mentioned coming to the Fire is crossing over the Sirat (the bridge), because it is a bridge set up over the back of Hell.

(p-478) The third: the mentioned coming to is standing over it and drawing near to it.

The fourth: the share of the believers from that coming to is the heat of fever in the life of this world. We have already mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that among the types of explanation (bayan) it contains is deriving evidence for one of the meanings that fall within the meaning of the verse from that meaning being the predominant one in the Qur'an. Its predominance there is an inductive proof that it is not outside the meaning of the verse. We have already given examples of this. Know, then, that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) derived evidence for the meaning of the coming to the Fire in the verse by the same kind of proof which we mentioned as one of the types of explanation in this blessed book.

Its clarification: the coming to the Fire occurs in the Qur'an in several verses, and in each of them the meaning is entering. So Ibn 'Abbas used this to conclude that "the wurud in the verse under dispute is entering," because the other verses indicate this, such as His saying: ﴿He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them to the Fire. And wretched is the place they are led to.﴾ (Hud: 98). He said: this is wurud of entering. And His saying: ﴿If these were gods, they would not have come to it; and all will abide therein.﴾ (al-Anbiya': 99), which is also wurud of entering. And His saying: ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell in a herd.﴾ (Maryam: 86). And His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will be coming to it.﴾ (al-Anbiya': 98). With this Ibn 'Abbas argued against Nafi' ibn al-Azraq that "wurud is entering."

Those who said that wurud means standing over and drawing near argued from His saying: ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan...﴾ (al-Qasas: 23), and said: this is wurud of drawing near and standing over it. Similarly His saying: ﴿So they sent their water-carrier.﴾ (Yusuf: 19). A parallel from the speech of the Arabs is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma in his Mu'allaqa:

*"When they came to the water, its surface blue-tinted, they laid down the staves of the settled camp."*

They said: the Arabs say, "the caravan came to the city" even if it did not enter it, but only drew near to it. Those who said that the wurud in the verse under discussion is not the entering itself argued from His saying: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward from Us has preceded, they will be kept far from it. They will not hear its faintest sound, and they will abide in what their souls desire.﴾ (al-Anbiya': 101–102). They said: their being kept far from it, mentioned in this verse, indicates that they do not enter it; therefore wurud is other than entering.

Those who said that the coming to the Fire in the verse, with respect to the believers, is the heat of fever in the life of this world argued from the hadith: "Fever is from the intense heat (fayh) of Hell, so cool it with water." This hadith is agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh) from the narrations of 'A'isha and Asma', the two daughters of Abu Bakr, and of Ibn 'Umar and Rafi' ibn Khadij (may Allah be pleased with them all). Al-Bukhari also narrated it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report from Ibn 'Abbas.

The one who clarifies it (muqayyiduh), may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: There are evidences that the meaning of the wurud in the verse is entering. The first: what Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) mentioned, that all the coming to the Fire in the Qur'an means entering it, other than the place of dispute. This indicates that the place of dispute is likewise. And the best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

The second evidence: there is in the verse itself a clear indicator of this. When He addressed all people, that they will all come to the Fire, righteous and wicked alike, by His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it. That is a decree of your Lord, inevitable.﴾ (Maryam: 70–71), He explained their fate and final outcome after that mentioned coming by His saying: ﴿Then We shall save those who were righteous, and leave the wrongdoers therein﴾ (Maryam: 72), meaning: We leave the wrongdoers therein. This is evidence that their coming to it is their entering into it. For if they did not enter it, He would not have said: ﴿and leave the wrongdoers therein,﴾ but rather He would say: "and We shall cause the wrongdoers to enter." This is clear, as you see. Likewise His saying: ﴿Then We shall save those who were righteous﴾ is evidence that they fell into what is by nature a destruction. That is why He joined to His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ His saying: ﴿Then We shall save those who were righteous.﴾

The third evidence: what has been related of this from the Prophet (ﷺ). The author of ad-Durr al-Manthur, in speaking on this noble verse, said: Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim at-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Sumayya, who said: We differed about the wurud. Some of us said: no believer enters it. Others said: they will all enter it, then Allah saves those who were righteous. So I met Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with them both) and mentioned that to him. He said, and pointed with his two index fingers to his ears: "May my ears be deaf if I did not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Neither righteous nor wicked will remain but that he will enter it. It will be coolness and safety for the believers, as it was for Ibrahim, to the extent that the Fire will cry out from their coolness. Then Allah saves those who were righteous, and leaves the wrongdoers therein, kneeling.'" End of quotation.

Ibn Hajar said, in *al-Kafi ash-Shafi fi Takhrij Ahadith al-Kashshaf*, concerning this hadith: It was narrated by Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shayba, and 'Abd ibn Humayd, who said: "Sulayman ibn Harb narrated to us." Abu Ya'la, an-Nasa'i in *al-Kuna*, al-Bayhaqi in *ash-Shu'ab* in the chapter on the Fire, and al-Hakim in *an-Nawadir* also narrated it, all of them through Sulayman, who said: "Abu Salih Ghalib ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Kathir ibn Ziyad, from Abu Sumayya, who said: We differed about the wurud, so we asked Jabir, and he mentioned the hadith more completely than the wording which az-Zamakhshari mentioned (p-480). But al-Hakim contradicted all of them: he narrated it through Sulayman with this isnad, and said: 'from Sumayya al-Azdiyya, from 'Abd ar-Rahman ibn Shayba,' in place of 'Abu Sumayya, from Jabir.' End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his tafsir of this verse: Imam Ahmad said: Sulayman ibn Harb narrated to us, Ghalib ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Kathir ibn Ziyad al-Bursani, from Abu Sumayya, who said: We differed about the wurud. Some of us said: no believer enters it. Others said: they will all enter it, then Allah saves those who were righteous. So I met Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and said: "We differed about the wurud," and he said: "They will all enter it," then he mentioned the hadith previously cited. Then Ibn Kathir said: It is gharib (a narration with a single line of transmission at some level), and they did not narrate it.

The one who clarifies it, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The apparent position is that the mentioned isnad (chain of narration) is not below the level of hasan (good), because its first tier is Sulayman ibn Harb, who is a trustworthy, eminent, memorized and well-known imam. Its second tier is Abu Salih or Abu Salama Ghalib ibn Sulayman al-'Ataki al-Jahdami al-Khurasani, originally from Basra, who is trustworthy. Its third tier is Kathir ibn Ziyad Abu Sahl al-Bursani, a Basran who settled in Balkh, who is trustworthy. Its fourth tier is Abu Sumayya, whom Ibn Hibban mentioned in *ath-Thiqat* (the trustworthy), as Ibn Hajar stated in *Tahdhib at-Tahdhib*. With the authentication of the aforementioned Abu Sumayya, the soundness of the hadith becomes clear, because the others in this isnad are well-known trustworthy narrators. Moreover, the hadith of Jabir is reinforced by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, by the other verses from which Ibn 'Abbas derived evidence, and by reports that came from the scholars of the early generations (may Allah be pleased with them), as Ibn Kathir mentioned from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, and from 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha (may Allah be pleased with him). He and Ibn Jarir mentioned it from Abu Maysara, and Ibn Kathir mentioned it from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, from al-Hasan al-Basri. All of them say that it is the wurud of entering.

Those who said that the wurud in the verse means entering answered the argument from His saying: ﴿They will be kept far from it﴾ (al-Anbiya': 101), by saying that they are kept far from its punishment and its pain. So this does not contradict their coming to it without feeling any pain or heat from it, as we have explained in our book *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* in the discussion of this noble verse.

They also answered the argument from the hadith "Fever is from the intense heat of Hell" by accepting its implication. They said: the hadith is true and sound, but there is no evidence in it for the point of dispute, because the context is explicit that the speech is about the Fire in the Hereafter, not about its heat in this world. For the beginning of the passage is His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils; then We will surely bring them around Hell, kneeling.﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ (Maryam: 68–70). This shows that all of that is in the Hereafter, not in this world, as you see.

As for the qira'a (recitation) of the word *jithiyyan* (kneeling) in His saying, as we mentioned earlier in His saying: (p-481) ﴿then We will surely bring them around Hell, kneeling﴾.

As for His saying *thumma nunajjee* (then We shall save), it is the qira'a of al-Kisa'i, with the second nun sukun (unvowelled) and the jim lightened. The rest read it with the second nun fatha (vowelled) and the jim doubled. We have mentioned in our book *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* that a group narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that the mentioned wurud of the Fire in the verse is passing over it, because people pass over the Sirat, which is a bridge set up over the back of Hell. They also said that al-Hasan and Qatada were narrated to have said something similar. It was also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, as a marfu' report: "They will all come to it and will depart from it according to their deeds." And from him is also the explanation of wurud as standing over it. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying in the noble verse: ﴿was a decree of your Lord, inevitable﴾, it means that their coming to the Fire mentioned was a decree, inevitable upon your Lord, that is, a matter obligatory and necessarily carried out. *Al-Hatm* is what is obligatory and cannot be avoided. From it is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi as-Salt ath-Thaqafi:

*"Your servants sin, and You are Lord, with Your two palms are the deaths and the decisive matters."*

So his saying "al-Hutum" is the plural of *hatm*, meaning the obligatory matters that must occur. As for what a group of the people of knowledge mentioned, that the meaning of ﴿a decree inevitable﴾ is an obligatory oath, as was narrated from 'Ikrima, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, Qatada and others, it is not wholly evident.

Those who said that there is an oath in the verse argued from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, established in the two Sahihs. Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: Ali narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, who said: I heard az-Zuhri from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No Muslim loses three children and then enters the Fire, except for the fulfilment of the oath (tahillat al-qasam)." Abu 'Abd Allah (al-Bukhari) said: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it.﴾ End of quotation. Muslim said in his Sahih: Yahya ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: I read to Malik, from Ibn Shihab, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No one among the Muslims loses three children and then the Fire touches him, except for the fulfilment of the oath." Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba, 'Amr an-Naqid, and Zuhayr ibn Harb narrated to us, saying: Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna narrated to us (transition: ḥ). And 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Rafi' narrated to us, from 'Abd ar-Razzaq, Ma'mar informed us, both of them from az-Zuhri with the isnad of Malik, and with the meaning of his hadith, except that in the hadith of Sufyan it is: "then he enters the Fire, except for the fulfilment of the oath." End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 71 (part 2 of 2):

They said: The oath mentioned in this authentic hadith refers to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it. That is ever, with your Lord, a decreed matter [that must come to pass]﴾. This is the meaning of what we mentioned from al-Bukhari, in his saying: Abu 'Abdullah said, ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾. (p-482) Those who used the mentioned hadith as evidence that the noble verse is an oath disagreed about where the oath lies in the verse. Some of them said: it is an implied oath, indicated by the mentioned hadith, meaning: "By Allah, there is none of you but will pass over it." Some of them said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the oath before it, and what is conjoined to an oath is itself an oath. The meaning is: "By your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils, and by your Lord, there is none of you but will pass over it." Some of them said: the mentioned oath is derived from His saying: ﴿That is ever, with your Lord, a decreed matter﴾, meaning: a binding oath, as we previously cited from Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. Some of them said: it is possible that what is meant by the oath is what the context indicates of certainty and categorical affirmation, for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿That is ever, with your Lord, a decreed matter﴾ is a concluding affirmation (tadhyil) and confirmation of His saying ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾. This stands in the place of an oath in emphasising the report, indeed it is more emphatic in restricting the verse through negation and affirmation.
