The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that the verse does not necessarily contain an oath, because it is not accompanied by any of the particles of oath, nor by any clear indication showing an oath, and its being conjoined to an oath is not determined. Ruling that an oath is implied in the Book of Allah without any clear indicator in it is an addition to the meaning of the speech of Allah without any evidence that must be returned to. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah, which is agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh), does not establish that the verse contains an oath, because among the methods of the Arabic language is the expression "tahillat al-qasam" (the minimal amount needed to fulfil an oath) to denote extreme scarcity, even when there is no oath at all. They say: "I did not do such-and-such except tahillat al-qasam," meaning, "except a very small action, just enough for the swearer to fulfil his oath (yuhallilu bihi al-halif qasamahu)." This is a well-known idiom in the speech of the Arabs, and among it is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr describing his she-camel:

"She strides upon swift [legs], while they are close-set, slender, quick; their touching the ground is only tahlil."

He means: the hooves of his she-camel barely touch the ground, because of her extreme lightness, except to the extent of fulfilling an oath. It is known that there is no oath from his she-camel that she touches the ground, so that this touching would be a fulfilment of it, as you see. On this well-known meaning, the meaning of his saying ﷺ "except tahillah" is: he will not enter the Fire except by a very brief entry, without pain or heat, as we previously mentioned in the marfu' hadith of Jabir. The closest of the views of those who said that the verse contains an oath is the view of the one who said that it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾, because the sentences mentioned after it are conjoined to it, like His saying: ﴿Then We will surely bring them forth﴾, and His saying: ﴿Then We will surely draw out﴾, and His saying: ﴿Then We know best﴾, by the indication of the context of the oath-lam (lam al-qasam) in the mentioned sentences. As for His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾, it admits of conjunction as well, and it admits of being a new sentence (isti'naf). And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-333) In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah Maryam.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾.

This noble verse indicates that all people must pass over the Fire. This is emphasised by His saying: ﴿That is ever, with your Lord, a decreed matter﴾ [Maryam: 71]. In another verse there is what indicates that some people are kept far from it and do not hear its sound, namely His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those, for them, are kept far from it. They will not hear its faintest sound﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101-102].

The answer is what al-Alusi and others mentioned: the meaning of His saying "kept far" (mub'adun) is far from the punishment of the Fire and its pain. It was also said: what is meant is that they are removed from it after they had been near it. The first interpretation is supported by what Imam Ahmad, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and a group related from Abu Sumayyah, who said: We disagreed here about the passing over (al-wurud). Some of us said: no believer will enter it. Others said: they will all enter it, then Allah will deliver those who were mindful of Him. So I met Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, and mentioned that to him. He said, and he gestured with his two fingers towards his ears: "Deaf, if I did not hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'The wurud is entering. No righteous nor wicked person will remain but will enter it. It will be cool and safe for the believers, just as it was for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, so much so that the Fire will cry out from their coolness. Then Allah will deliver those who were mindful of Him, and leave the wrongdoers in it, kneeling.'"

A group related from Ibn Mas'ud that the passing over of the Fire is passing by it, because people pass over the Sirat (the bridge), which is a bridge set up over the back of Hell (jahannam).

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Anbari and al-Bayhaqi related from al-Hasan: the wurud is passing by it without entering. This was also related from Qatadah. This was mentioned by al-Alusi.

Those who held that wurud is itself entering, such as Ibn 'Abbas, used as evidence His saying: ﴿So He will lead them to the Fire﴾ [Hud: 98], (p-334) and His saying: ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have passed over it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 99], and His saying: ﴿You and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell; you are to it passing over﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]. So wurud in all of these means entering.

Those who held that wurud is nearness to it without entering used His saying: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], and the saying of Zuhayr:

"When they reached the water, its pools blue, they set down the staves of the settled, encamped [traveller]."

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 73:**

(p-483) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieved say to those who believed, "Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in assembly?"﴾.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿better in position﴾ [Maryam: 73]. Ibn Kathir recited it with a *dammah* on the *meem*, and the rest recited it with a *fathah*. His saying "wari'an" (ﷺ)... Qalun and Ibn Dhakwan recited "wariyyan" with a doubled *yaa* and without a *hamzah*, and the rest recited it with a silent *hamzah* after the *raa'* followed by a light *yaa*.

The meaning of the noble verse: the disbelievers of Quraysh, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions recited to them the verses of this Qur'an, which were "clear," meaning their wording was measured and their meanings evident, their purposes plain. These verses were either *muhkamat* (clear-cut verses) that came plainly, or *mutashabihat* (ambiguous verses) which were followed by clarification through the *muhkamat*, or the Messenger's clarification by word or deed, or they were manifest in their inimitability, by which they were challenged and could not be matched, or they were proofs and demonstrations.

It is apparent that His saying "clear" (*bayyinat*) is a confirmatory circumstantial clause, since the verses of Allah are never otherwise. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿and it is the truth, confirming﴾ [Fatir: 31]. That is: when the verses of Allah are recited to them while being characterized by what we have mentioned, they opposed them and argued against their invalidity, and that the truth was with them and not with the one who recites them, by a baseless doubt that no one argues with except one who lacks intellect. The content of their stated doubt is that they say to them: "We have a greater share than you in this world, so we are better than you in dwellings, better than you in provision, and better than you in appearance. Had we not been more favored by Allah than you, He would not have preferred us over you in this worldly life, and given us of its bounties and adornments what He did not give you."

So His saying: ﴿which of the two groups is better in position﴾ [Maryam: 73], meaning: which of us and you is better in position. "Maqam" according to Ibn Kathir's reading with a *dammah* on the *meem* means the place of residence, namely the dwellings and places in which they live. According to the majority reading, "maqam," with a *fathah* on the *meem*, means the place of standing, namely their place of standing, which is their homes and dwellings. It was said that it is the place of standing for great matters, but the first is the correct view.

His saying: ﴿and finer in assembly﴾, meaning: in gathering and meeting place. The interrogative in His saying ﴿which of the two groups﴾ is apparently an interrogative of affirmation, intended to lead the weak Muslims, who were in poverty and shabby appearance, to say: "You are better in position and finer in assembly than us." In any case, there is no disagreement that (p-484) their intended meaning by the aforementioned interrogative is that they, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh, are better in position and finer in assembly than the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that this is their proof that they are upon the truth and more honored by Allah than the Muslims. As for what appears in *al-Talkhis* and its commentaries, that the question with "ayyu" in the verse we are discussing asks about what distinguishes one of two participants in a matter that encompasses both, as is customary with "ayyu" regarding any error on their part, this is because they interpreted the noble verse with other than its correct meaning. The correct view is what we have mentioned, if Allah the Exalted wills. Their argument from their share in this worldly life to their share on the Day of Resurrection, and that Allah gave them in this world only because of their standing with Him and their deserving of that, is due to the feebleness of their minds. Allah the Exalted has mentioned this in several places in His Book:

• Like His saying, exalted is He, about them: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it. And since they are not guided by it, they will say, 'This is an ancient falsehood.'"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We tested some of them by means of others, that they might say, "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?" Is Allah not most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ [al-An'am: 53].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ [Saba': 35].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children ﴿is hastening for them into good things? Rather, they do not perceive﴾﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55–56].

• And His saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ [Maryam: 77].

• And His saying: ﴿He said, "I do not think this will ever perish. And I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a destination."﴾ [al-Kahf: 35–36].

• And His saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best.﴾ [Fussilat: 50].

And other verses besides these. All these verses indicate that, in their ignorance, they assume that Allah has given them their share of this world only because of His pleasure with them and their standing with Him, and that the matter in the Hereafter will be the same.

Allah, the Exalted, has refuted this claim of theirs in many verses of His Book, such as His saying, exalted is He, in this noble surah: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were better in furnishings and appearance﴾ [Maryam: 74]. The meaning: We destroyed many generations, that is, nations that existed before them, who had more share in this world than they did. So what did the adornment and provisions of worldly life they possessed avail them against Allah's destruction of them when they disobeyed and denied His messengers? Had share and portion in this world indicated Allah's pleasure and standing with Him, He would not have destroyed those before you, who were better in furnishings and appearance than you.

As for His saying in this noble verse: "how many" (*kam*), it is the informative *kam*, meaning the report of a large number, and it is in the place of an accusative as the object of "We destroyed," meaning: We destroyed many. And "min" (from) is explanatory of "kam." Every generation of people is a *qarn* (generation) for those after them, because they precede them. It was said they were called *qarn* from *iqtiran* (conjunction) in existence. "Ath-thath" (furnishings) is the goods of the house. It was also said it is the new of the bedding, and what is not new of it is called *al-khurthiyy*, with a *dammah* on the *kha'*, a silent *raa'*, and the *thaa'* with a light *yaa'* after it doubled. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Tusi cited for this distinction the verse of the poet:

*Long ago the time passed since Umm al-Walid was with us,*
*and the furnishings of the house became old goods.*

The well-known usage in Arabic is applying "ath-thath" to the goods of the house in general. Al-Farra' said: it has no singular. "Ath-thath" is also applied to all property: camels, sheep, slaves, and goods. Its singular is *athathah*. And "ta'assatha fulan" means: when someone acquired fine clothing (*riyash*), as al-Jawhari reported from Abu Zayd.

His saying "wari'an," according to the majority reading with *hamzah*, means: finer in appearance and bearing. It is a verb in the sense of a passive participle from *ra'a* (to see), the visual sense, and it means what the eye sees of their fine appearance and fine goods. Abu 'Ubaydah cited for this meaning a verse of Muhammad ibn Numayr al-Thaqafi:

*Did the camel-litters of the women grieve you the day they departed,*
*with the fine appearance of the goods?*

On the reading of Qalun and Ibn Dhakwan with a doubled *yaa'* without *hamzah*, some scholars said its meaning is the same as the first reading, except that the *hamzah* was changed to a *yaa'* and assimilated into the *yaa'*. Others said there is no *hamzah* in either of these two readings at all, but rather it is from *ray* (abundance), which is blessing and luxury, from their saying: "he is *rayyan* (replete) with blessing," and "she is *rayya* (abundant) from it." On this basis the meaning is: finer in blessing and luxury. The first is more apparent to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

The verses by which Allah refuted this claim of theirs are many, such as:

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is good for themselves. We only give them respite that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

• And His saying: ﴿And neither your wealth nor your children are that which will bring you near to Us in position, except for one who believes and does righteousness. For those will be a double reward for what they did, and they will be safe in the upper chambers.﴾ [Saba': 37].

• And His saying: ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this statement. We will progressively draw them in from where they do not know. And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [al-Qalam: 44].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and at once they were despairing.﴾ [al-An'am: 44].

Verses of this kind are very numerous, and we have already presented some of them.

As for the saying of the disbelievers which Allah related in this noble verse: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in assembly?﴾ (p-486), the apparent point of their mention of *maqam* and *nadi* is this: *maqam* is the specific dwelling place of each one of them, and *nadi* is the place where some of them gather with others. So when each of these is better for the disbelievers than its counterpart among the Muslims, this indicates that their share in this world is more abundant than the share of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) at that time. A parallel to this in Arab speech is the verse of the poet:

*Two days: a day of dwellings and gatherings,*
*and a day of marching against the enemies, returning in haste.*

*Maqamat* is the plural of *maqamah* in the sense of *maqam*, and *andiyah* is the plural of *nadi*, which is the assembly of a people. From this is His saying: ﴿And you commit in your *nadi* (gathering) what is evil﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29]. So *nadi* and *nadiy* are both applied to the assembly, and to the people sitting in it. Likewise *majlis* (sitting place) is applied to the people sitting. From the application of *nadiy* to a place is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*None of us stands up in our nadiy*
*to speak except with what is most known.*

And His saying here: ﴿and finer in assembly﴾.

From its application to a people is His saying: ﴿Then let him call his nadi﴾ ﴿We will call the guards of Hell﴾ [al-'Alaq: 17–18]. And from the application of *majlis* to the people sitting in it is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*For them is a gathering, with white-tipped mustaches,*
*humbled, equal, its free and its slaves alike.*

As for the clause in His saying: ﴿they are better in furnishings and appearance﴾, al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the place of an accusative as a descriptive modifier of "kam." Do you not see that if you omitted the word "they," you would have no choice but to put "better" in the accusative as a qualifier? End quote. Abu al-Baqa' followed al-Zamakhshari in this. Abu Hayyan, in *al-Bahr*, criticized him, saying that some grammarians stated that "kam," whether interrogative or informative, is not described and does not describe. He said: On this basis, "they are better" is in the place of a modifier of *qarn*, and the plural of the description of *qarn* is used in consideration of the meaning of *qarn*. This is the correct view in my opinion, not what al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' said. The comparative form in His saying: ﴿they are better in furnishings and appearance﴾ requires *min* (from), because it is stripped of addition and definiteness. However, it is omitted because the context indicates it. The estimate is: they are better in furnishings and appearance than them. This is in accordance with his saying in the *Khulasah*:

*And the comparative form, always join it with "min," explicitly or implicitly, if it is stripped.*

If it is said: where does the pronoun refer to in this noble verse, in His saying: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieved say﴾? The verse [Maryam: 73]. The answer: it refers to the disbelievers mentioned in His saying: ﴿And man says, "When I die, will I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ the verse [Maryam: 66], and His saying: ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein kneeling﴾. Thus said al-Qurtubi. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 75:

﴿Say: "Whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend his term extensively, until, when they see what they are promised, either the punishment or the Hour, they will know who is worse in position and weaker in forces."﴾

Regarding the meaning of this noble verse, there are two well-known interpretations among the scholars, and each of them is supported by the Qur'an.

The first: Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet ﷺ in this noble verse to say these words as a supplication of mubahala (mutual imprecation, a prayer in which two parties call down God's curse upon the liars among them) between himself and the polytheists. The explanation of its meaning: Say, O Prophet of Allah ﷺ, to these polytheists who claimed that they are better than you, and that the proof of this is that they are better than you in station and finer in assembly: "Whoever is in error, that is, in disbelief and straying from the path of truth, from us and from you, the Most Merciful will extend his term extensively," that is, the Most Merciful will grant him a long respite in what he is in, so that He may lead him on gradually through respite, and he dies upon that and does not turn back from it, but persists in it until he sees what Allah promises him. This is either a punishment in this world at the hands of the Muslims, as in His saying: ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands﴾ [al-Tawbah: 14], or by other than that; or the punishment of the Hereafter if they die while in that disbelief. According to this interpretation, the imperative form indicated by the lam in His saying "fa-l-yamdud" (let him extend) remains on its original meaning, and accordingly it is the lam of supplication for granting respite in error to the one who is astray from both parties, until he sees the evil he is promised while he is in the worst state of disbelief and straying. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir restricted themselves to this interpretation, and it is the apparent sense of the imperative form in His saying "fa-l-yamdud." A parallel to this meaning in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿Then whoever argues with you about it after knowledge has come to you, say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then let us earnestly pray and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 61]; because according to this interpretation, in both verses there is a supplication for evil upon the one who is astray from both groups. Likewise His saying concerning the Jews: ﴿So wish for death, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 94], in "al-Baqarah" and "al-Jumu'ah," according to those who say that the intended meaning of the wishing (tamanni) is a supplication for death upon the liars from both groups; this is the choice of Ibn Kathir, but the apparent sense of the verse does not support it.

The second interpretation: the imperative form in His saying "fa-l-yamdud" is intended to convey information about the sunnah (established way) of Allah concerning those who are astray. According to this, the meaning is: Allah has established the custom that He grants the one who is astray a respite and gives him time, so that He leads him on gradually through that, until he sees what he is promised, while he is in heedlessness, disbelief, and error.

This interpretation is supported by many verses, such as His saying: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is good for them; We only give them respite that they may increase in sin﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 178], and His saying: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the doors of everything until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 44], as we mentioned shortly before, some of the verses indicating this.

Among what supports this interpretation is what Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, who said: In the reading (harf) of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): "Say: Whoever is in error, then Allah will increase him in error." Ended. This was said by the author of al-Durr al-Manthur, and such a thing is of the category of tafsir (exegesis), not of the category of recitation (qira'ah).

If it is said, according to this interpretation: What is the point of using the imperative form with the meaning of a report? The answer: al-Zamakhshari answered this in his al-Kashshaf. He said in his explanation of His saying: ﴿fa-l-yamdud lahu al-Rahmanu madda﴾, i.e., "the Most Merciful has extended for him," meaning He gave him respite and granted him a long life. It was expressed in the form of a command to indicate that this is obligatory, and that it is certainly going to happen, like the commanded act that is carried out, so that the excuses of the one who is astray are cut off, and it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough that whoever would be mindful might have been mindful therein?﴾ [Fatir: 37]. The end of the relevant point from him. In my view, the most apparent of the opinions regarding His saying: ﴿until, when they see what they are promised﴾ is that it is connected to what precedes it and what follows it, and the meaning is: "Let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension, until, when he sees what he is promised, he knows that the matter is contrary to what he used to assume."

Al-Zamakhshari also said: The "hatta" (until) in this verse is the one after which sentences are narrated, and he cited in evidence the coming of a conditional sentence after it.

His saying: "ma yu'adun" (what they are promised): the word "ma" is the object of "yu'adun" (they are promised). His saying: ﴿either the punishment or the Hour﴾ is an apposition (badal) from the object which is "ma." The word "man" in His saying: ﴿they will know who is﴾ — some scholars said: it is a relative pronoun in the accusative position as object of "ya'lamun" (they know); according to this, "'alima" here is of the type of knowledge by acquaintance (irfaniyyah), which transitions to one object. Some people of knowledge said: "man" is an interrogative, and the mental verb which is "ya'lamun" is suspended by the interrogative. This is more apparent in my view.

His saying: ﴿worse in position and weaker in forces﴾ is in opposition to their saying: ﴿better in station and finer in assembly﴾; because their station is their place and their dwelling, and "nadiyy" is the assembly that gathers the notables of their people, their helpers and their supporters, and "jund" (forces) are the helpers and the aides. So the stated opposition is evident. A verse of the Book of Allah has indicated the use of "sharr makanan" (worse in place), and what is intended is the attribution of evil to the person, not to the place, and that is His saying: ﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before." So Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said: "You are worse in position"﴾ [Yusuf: 77 in some numbering; cited here as 72 in the source]. So the comparative of place in evil here, the apparent meaning is that what is intended by it is his preferring his brothers in evil over himself in what they attributed to him of the evil of theft, not the place itself. Except that what is intended is the figurative place, i.e., "you are worse in standing with Allah, exalted is He."

His saying in these mentioned verses: "maqaman" (station), "nadiyyan" (assembly), "athathan" (furnishings), "makanan" (place), and "jundan" (forces), each one of them is a tamyiz (specification) transferred from the agent, as he indicated in the Khulasah (the Alfiyyah) with his saying:

"The agent, in meaning, let it be put in the accusative after an elative (af'al) of preference, like: 'You are higher in dwelling.'"

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 76:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance, and the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in return.﴾

His saying, exalted and high is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance﴾ [Maryam: 76] is evidence for preferring the second opinion regarding the preceding verse, and that the meaning is: whoever is in misguidance, Allah increases him in misguidance, and whoever is guided, Allah increases him in guidance. The verses indicating this meaning are many:

• such as His saying concerning misguidance: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5];

• and His saying: ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed their hearts because of their disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa': 155];

• and His saying: ﴿That is because they believed, then disbelieved, so their hearts were sealed﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 3];

• and His exalted saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 110], to the end of the verse;

as we have previously mentioned many verses indicating this meaning.

He also said concerning guidance: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Muhammad: 17]. He said: ﴿It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers that they might increase in faith along with their faith﴾ [al-Fath: 4]. He said: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ to the end of the verse [al-'Ankabut: 69]. He has combined the two in other verses,

• such as His saying: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [al-Isra': 82];

• and His exalted saying: ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing. And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them﴾ to the end of the verse [Fussilat: 44];

• and His exalted saying: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added to them filth upon their filth, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124–125],

as its clarification has already passed.

As for His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in return﴾ [Maryam: 76], its clarification has already passed in the surah of "al-Kahf" [p. 490].

If it is said: The apparent meaning of the verse is that the word "khayr" (better) in His saying ﴿better with your Lord in reward﴾ and ﴿better in return﴾ is a comparative form, and the apparent meaning is that the one being compared against is the reward of the disbelievers. What supports this is what the author of al-Durr al-Manthur said: "Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying ﴿better with your Lord in reward﴾, meaning: better reward than the reward of the polytheists, ﴿and better in return﴾, meaning a better destination than their destination to the Fire." In Arabic, the known rule is that the comparative form requires the participation of the one being compared against, while the quality of being "better" is completely negated from the reward of the polytheists and from their return, so they do not share in that with the Muslims such that the Muslims could be preferred over them.

The answer is: al-Zamakhshari, in his al-Kashshaf, attempted to answer this question with what in summary amounts to: it is as if it were said, "Their reward is the Fire, and the Garden is better than it," following the manner of the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Hazim:

*"The Tamim became angry that 'Amir should be slain on the day of al-Nisar, so they were pleased with the sword at al-Saylam."*

So his saying "they were pleased with the sword at al-Saylam" means they were satisfied by the sword, i.e., there is no satisfaction for them with us except the sword, by which they are slain.

Its parallel is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

*"And cavalry, against which I advanced with cavalry, whose greeting among them is a painful blow."*

That is, there is no greeting among them except the painful blow.

And the saying of another:

*"A she-camel whose cud is the journey, which she chews, a camel that pastures in the early hours when the riding camels have gone with their heavy gait."*

It means: this she-camel has no cud that she brings up from her stomach and chews except the journey. On this meaning, the intended sense is: they have no reward except the Fire, and by considering it as a reward in this sense, the reward of the believers is preferred over it. This is the summary of al-Zamakhshari's answer, along with our clarification of it.

Its author, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, said: What appears to me in the verse is another answer closer than this, namely that we have previously established that the Qur'an and the authentic Sunnah indicate that the disbeliever is rewarded in this world for his good deed. So if he is dutiful to his parents, relieves one in distress, hosts a guest, or maintains ties of kinship, seeking thereby the Face of Allah, then Allah rewards him in this world, as we have previously mentioned the indication of the verses for it, and the hadith of Anas in Sahih Muslim. So this reward of his, which returns to him from his deed in this world, is what Allah prefers over the reward of the believers in the verse. This is clear and has no difficulty. And Allah knows best.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 77:

(p-491) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated through more than one chain, "from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: 'I came to al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi seeking a debt he owed me. He said: "I will not give you anything until you disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ)." I said: "No, not until you die and are resurrected." He said: "And will I be dead and then resurrected?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed, I will have wealth there, and I will pay you back." So this verse was revealed: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾'"

Some people of knowledge said: his saying ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾ was intended as mockery of the religion and of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (may Allah be pleased with him). The apparent meaning is that he claimed he would be given wealth and children, reasoning by analogy from this world to the Hereafter, as we have explained in the verses that indicate this,

• such as His saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat: 50],

• and His saying: ﴿Do they think that what We provide them with of wealth and children is [a sign of] Our hastening to them with good? (the verse)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55-56],

• and His saying: ﴿And they said, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ [Saba': 35],

and other verses, as its clarification has already been presented. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this word as "wa-wuldan" (وَوُلْدًا), with a damma on the second waw and a sukun on the lam. The rest read it with a fatha on both the waw and the lam (وَوَلَدًا). Both are dialectal forms with the same meaning, like al-'urb and al-'arab, and al-'udm and al-'adam. Among the Arabs' uses of al-wuld (وُلْد) with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam, as in the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, is the saying of al-Harith ibn Hillizah:

"Indeed I have seen people who multiplied wealth and offspring"

and the saying of Ru'bah:

"Praise be to Allah, the Mighty, the One alone, who has not taken any offspring, nor has any offspring been taken by Him."

Some scholars of Arabic claimed that walad (وَلَد) with a fatha on the waw and lam is singular, and that wuld (وُلْد) with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam is its plural, like asad (أَسَد) with a fatha, which is pluralized as usud (أُسُد) with a damma and then a sukun. The apparent view is that this is not correct. Among what shows that wuld with a damma is not a plural is the saying of the poet:

"So would that so-and-so had been in his mother's womb, and would that so-and-so had been the offspring of a donkey."

Because "wuld" in this line has a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam, and it is definitively singular, as you see.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 78 (part 1 of 4):

Allah's saying: ﴿Has he attained the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?  No!﴾.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, in this noble verse refuted the statement of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi (p-492) that he would be given wealth and children on the Day of Resurrection, by means of the proof known among the dialecticians (jadaliyyun) as al-taqsim wa al-tardid (division and disjunction), among the usulis (scholars of legal theory) as al-sabr wa al-taqsim (examination and division), and among the logicians (mantiqiyyun) as the disjunctive conditional syllogism (al-sharti al-munfasil).

The structure of this great proof is composed of two principles. The first is the restriction of the attributes of the subject to a means of restriction, which is what is termed division (taqsim) by the usulis and the dialecticians, and the disjunctive conditional by the logicians.

The second is the selection of those restricted attributes, the nullifying of what is false among them, and the retaining of what is sound among them, as you will see clarified, Allah willing. This last is what is termed "sabr" (examination) by the usulis, "tardid" (disjunction) by the dialecticians, and, among the logicians, the exception (istithna') in the disjunctive conditional.

The correct division in this noble verse restricts the attributes of the subject to three, and the correct examination nullifies two of them and validates the third. By this, al-'As ibn Wa'il's claim that he will be given wealth and children on the Day of Resurrection is silenced.

As for the manner in which the attributes of the subject are restricted to three: we say, your statement that you will be given wealth and children on the Day of Resurrection—your basis for it is necessarily one of three things:

The first: that you have attained knowledge of the unseen and know that your being given wealth and children on the Day of Resurrection is among what Allah has written in the Preserved Tablet.

The second: that Allah has given you a covenant regarding this, for if He has given you a covenant, He will not break it.

The third: that you said this as a fabrication against Allah, without any covenant or any attainment of the unseen.

Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the first two in His saying: ﴿Has he attained the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ [Maryam: 78], nullifying both by the particle of denial. There is no doubt that both of these two divisions are false, because the aforementioned al-'As had not attained the unseen, nor had he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful. Thus the third division is determined, namely that he said this as a fabrication against Allah. Allah has indicated this division, which is the actual case, by the particle of rebuke and repulsion, which is His saying: "Kalla" (No!), meaning: since it necessarily follows that the matter is not as he claims—he had not attained the unseen, nor had he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, but rather he said it as a fabrication against Allah. For if either of them were established, it would not warrant the repulsion of his statement, as you see. This proof by which He refuted the claim of Ibn Wa'il is the very same proof by which He refuted the claim of the Jews that "the Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days," in Surat al-Baqarah. In that place He explicitly stated the division that is the truth, namely that they said that falsely without knowledge.

In al-Baqarah the division of attaining the unseen, mentioned in Maryam, is omitted, because its mention in Maryam indicates its intent in al-Baqarah. Likewise, their lying, which He stated explicitly in al-Baqarah, is not stated explicitly in Maryam, because what is in al-Baqarah clarifies what is in Maryam, since the Noble Qur'an explains some of it by others. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They say, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." Say, "Have you taken a covenant with Allah, so that Allah will not break His covenant? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]. So the attributes here are the three attributes mentioned in Maryam, as we have explained. What has been omitted from them is indicated by its mention in Maryam. Taking a covenant is mentioned in both al-Baqarah and Maryam together. The lying about it against Allah is stated explicitly in al-Baqarah by His saying: ﴿Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and it is alluded to in Maryam by the particle of rebuke, which is "Kalla." Attaining the unseen is stated explicitly in Maryam and omitted in al-Baqarah, because what is in Maryam indicates the intended meaning in al-Baqarah, as we have explained.

* *

Matters related to this noble verse.

The First Matter

Know that this proof, which is sabr and taqsim, is repeated in the Noble Qur'an. We have now mentioned two examples of it, one in al-Baqarah and the second in Maryam, as we have explained just above. Al-Suyuti, in al-Itqan, in his discussion of the dialectic of the Qur'an, mentioned only one example of sabr and taqsim. The content of the example he mentioned, in brief, is what is contained in His saying: ﴿eight pairs: of the sheep two, and of the goats two﴾ [al-An'am: 143] and the following verse. It is as if Allah is saying to those who forbade some females, such as the bahira and the sa'iba, but not others, and forbade some males, such as the hami, but not others: your forbidding some of what is mentioned but not others is either caused by an intelligible cause or is ta'abbudi (a matter of pure devotion). If it is caused by a cause, then the cause in the forbidden females is either femaleness, and in the forbidden males is maleness, or the cause in both is the being formed in the womb and its containing both. These are the divisions by which it is possible to claim that the ruling is attached to them. Then, after restricting the attributes by this division, we return to examining the mentioned divisions, that is, testing them so that the sound may be distinguished from the false. We find them all false by sound examination. For if the cause were maleness, it would require the forbidding of every male, while you permit some males. This indicates the invalidity of causing by maleness, because of the defect of breaking the rule (naqd), which is non-universality (adam al-ittirad). If the cause were femaleness, it would require the forbidding of every female, as we mentioned before. If the cause were the womb's containing both, it would require forbidding all. To this invalidation He pointed by His saying: ﴿Say, "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain?"﴾ [al-An'am: 144], meaning: if the cause were maleness, every male would be forbidden; if femaleness, every female would be forbidden; if the womb's containing both, all would be forbidden. If it were ta'abbudi, it would require that Allah enjoined it on you without an intermediary, since no messenger came to you with it. This indicates that it is also false, and He pointed to its invalidity by His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you?﴾ [al-An'am: 144]. Then He made clear that such forbidding without evidence is among the most heinous injustice, and that it is a fabricated lie and misguidance, by His saying: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the unjust people.﴾ [al-An'am: 144]. Then He affirmed the absence of prohibition in that by His saying: ﴿Say, "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine—for indeed it is impure—or an abomination over which something other than Allah has been invoked."﴾ [al-An'am: 145].

The summary is that the invalidation of all the mentioned attributes is evidence for the invalidity of the mentioned ruling, as we have explained. Among the examples of sabr and taqsim in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur: 35]. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: the matter does not fall outside one of three situations by correct division. The first: that they were created from nothing, meaning without any creator at all. The second: that they created themselves. The third: that a creator other than themselves created them. There is no doubt that the first two are false, and their falsity is self-evident, as you see, so there is no need to establish evidence for it, since it is clear. The third is the truth about which there is no doubt: that He, exalted is He, is their Creator, the One deserving that they worship Him alone, exalted is He.

Know that the logicians, the usulis and the dialecticians each use this proof for a purpose other than the purpose of the others in using it, except that its use among the dialecticians is more general than its use among the logicians and usulis.

* *

The Second Matter

Know that the dialecticians' aim from this proof is knowing the sound and the false among the attributes of the subject of dispute. It consists, according to you, of two matters: the first is restricting the attributes of the subject, and the second is nullifying what is false among them and validating what is sound absolutely. Sometimes all of them are false, so the invalidity of the ruling resting on them is established, like the aforementioned verse ﴿Say, "Has He forbidden the two males"﴾ [al-An'am: 144]. Sometimes some are false and some sound, like the verses of Maryam, al-Baqarah and al-Tur, whose explanation of this proof we have already presented in each of them. This proof is more beneficial and more fruitful in the method of the dialecticians than in the method of the usulis and the logicians.

* *

The Third Matter

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 78 (part 2 of 4):

Know that *sabr wa taqsim* (sifting and division, *al-sabr wa'l-taqsim*) among the legal theorists (*usuliyyun*) is used for one specific thing: deducing the *'illah* (effective cause) of a legal ruling by the method of *sabr wa taqsim*. The governing conditions of this method among the legal theorists are two. The first is confining the attributes of the original case that is being analogized from (*al-asl al-maqis 'alayh*) by one of the methods of confinement (*hasr*), some of which we will mention, God willing. The second is eliminating whatever is not suitable to be the *'illah* by one of the methods of elimination (*ibtal*), some of which we will also mention, God willing. Some have added a third condition, which is the consensus that the ruling of the original case is in general rationally motivated (*mu'allal*) and not purely devotional (*ta'abbudi*). The majority do not stipulate this last condition. The upshot is that this proof, according to the legal theorists, is composed of two things: the first is confining the attributes of the locus (*al-mahall*), and the second is eliminating what is not suitable to be the *'illah*. If both the confinement and the elimination are certain (*qat'iyyayn*), then it is a certain proof (*dalil qat'i*). If both are speculative (*zanniyyayn*), or one of them is speculative, then it is a speculative proof (*dalil zanni*).

An example in which both the confinement and the elimination are certain is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur: 35]. This is because confining the attributes of the locus to the three divisions is certain beyond doubt, for they were either created from nothing, or they created themselves, or a creator other than themselves created them, and there is no fourth possibility whatsoever. The elimination of the first two divisions is certain beyond doubt, so it is established that the third is true beyond doubt. It has been omitted from the verse because it is evident. Thus the indication of this sifting and division upon the worship of God alone is certain beyond doubt. Yet the example of this verse as an instance of the certain form of this proof is valid only according to the meaning intended by the dialecticians (*al-jadaliyyun*), not the legal theorists. This is because the intent is to illustrate the certain form of this proof, even in its more general sense, and the certain form of it admits no disagreement. As for the speculative form, the scholars differ concerning it because of the differing speculations of the mujtahids when they examine the issues. They have disagreed about *riba* (usury) in many things, such as apples and the like, and *nawra* (depilatory) and the like, because of their disagreement over the elimination of what is not suitable. One says: "This is an attribute whose elimination is valid." Another says: "It is not suitable, so its elimination is necessary." This is like their statement, for example, in confining the attributes of wheat, which is the original case, the prohibition of usury applying to it, when one wants to analogize maize to it, for example. It must be either that the 'illah of the prohibition of usury in wheat is measure (*al-kayl*), or food (*al-ta'm*), or staple sustenance and storability (*al-iqtiyat wa'l-idikhar*), or both of these, and the prevalence of subsistence on it, or monetary value and ownership (*al-maliyya wa'l-milkiyya*). The Malikī says: "Other than staple sustenance and storability is invalid," and claims that the proof of its invalidity is the absence of consistency (*'adam al-ittirad*), which is the counter-example (*al-naqd*). The Hanafī and the Hanbalī say: "Other than measure among those attributes is invalid, and measure is the 'illah on which the ruling depends." They support this with hadiths such as the hadith of Hayyan ibn Ubayd Allah in al-Hakim, in which, after mentioning the six items for which usury is prohibited, it says: "And likewise everything that is measured or weighed," and with the sound hadith in which it says: "And likewise the balance (*al-mizan*)," as we have previously set out in full in surah al-Baqara, in the discussion of the verse on usury.

Al-Shafi'i says: "Other than food is invalid, and the 'illah for the prohibition of usury in wheat is food." He supports this with the hadith of Ma'mar ibn Abd Allah in Muslim: "Food for food, like for like," the hadith in full. This has also been previously clarified in al-Baqara. This type of analogy, in which the mujtahids differ over the 'illah, is what is known among the legal theorists as analogy of a composite original (*murakkab al-asl*), and he alluded to it in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* with his words:

"If they differ over two 'illahs, the original becomes composite according to those who came before."

He alluded to the composite attribute (*murakkab al-wasf*) with his words:

"A composite attribute, when the opponent denies that this attribute exists in the original being followed."

The composite analogy, in its two mentioned types, does not establish the proof against the opponent, contrary to some of the dialecticians. And as for the view that its rejection (*radd*) in relation to the opposing opponent is the preferred one, he alluded to it in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* with his words:

"Its rejection is void, and it is said it is accepted; and there is a reported disagreement concerning its precedence."

The pronoun in his saying "its rejection" (*wa radduhu*) refers to the composite in both of its types. This is the truth. So the proof is not established by the statement of al-Shafi'i that the 'illah for the prohibition of usury in wheat is food, against the Hanafī and the Hanbalī who say it is measure, in the reverse manner, and so on. However, with regard to the mujtahid and his followers, his aforementioned speculation is a valid proof for him and his followers.

Know that confining the attributes of the locus has several methods. Among them is that the confinement is rational, as we have already mentioned concerning the verse ﴿Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur: 35], and like your saying: "Either the Prophet (ﷺ) was knowing of this matter to which he is calling the people, or he was not knowing of it," as will be clarified. So the attributes of the locus are confined to these two matters, since there is no third possibility whatsoever, because there is no intermediary between a thing and its contradiction, as is known.

Among them is that the aforementioned confinement is indicated by consensus. Some of the legal theorists gave an example of this with the compulsion of a mature virgin into marriage according to those who hold this view, for the 'illah of compulsion is either ignorance of the benefits, or virginity. If the objector says: "Where is the proof that the attributes are confined to these two matters?" it is answered that it is the consensus that the ruling is not rationally motivated by anything other than these two. Thus, if the one providing the proof claims the confinement of the attributes of the locus, and the objector says: "Where is the proof of the confinement?", the one providing the proof says: "I have searched thoroughly for the attributes of the locus and found nothing other than what I mentioned," or he says: "The default is the absence of what you mentioned." The correct view is that this suffices for establishing the confinement. If the objector says: "I know of an additional attribute that you did not mention," it is said to him: "Specify it." If he does not specify it, his objection falls. If he specifies an additional attribute beyond those mentioned by the one providing the proof, the confinement of the one providing the proof is invalidated merely by the objector's presenting the additional attribute, unless the one providing the proof demonstrates that it is not suitable to be an 'illah, in which case its existence and non-existence are then equal. The statement of one who says that his saying "I searched and found nothing other than this" does not suffice is contrary to the verification of the matter. Al-Shinqiti alluded to this method among the methods of the 'illah in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* with his words:

"Sifting and division is a fourth type, in which the one who combines confines the attributes in it."

"And what is not suitable for the 'illah is invalidated, so what remains becomes clear in its specification."

"The objector to the confinement, in repelling it, comes forward: 'I searched, and after my search I found nothing.'"

"Or the absence of what is other than it is the default, and there is no room in the confinement for a speculative basis."

"It is certain if both are established for certainty, and the speculative and other than it are known to be speculative."

"The authority of the speculative is according to the majority, with respect to the one who examines and the one who debates."

"If the objector presents an additional attribute, he fulfils it, without the explanation fulfilling the aim."

"The certainty of the one who performs sifting, when it is made definite, and the matter in its invalidation is ambiguous."

His saying in these verses "with respect to the one who examines and the one who debates" applies where the debater does not claim an 'illah other than his own. If he does claim one, then the 'illah of one of them is not a proof against the other, as we have clarified just before, and as he indicated by his aforementioned saying "its rejection is void..." and so on.

When the confinement of the attributes of the locus is established, then the elimination of those that are not suitable has well-known methods. Among them: demonstrating that the attribute is purely incidental (*tardi mahd*), either in relation to all rulings, like length and shortness, or whiteness and blackness, or in relation to the particular ruling under dispute regarding its establishment or negation, like maleness and femaleness in relation to the matter of manumission (*al-'itq*). For there is no difference in the rulings of manumission between a male and a female, because maleness and femaleness, with respect to it, are two incidental attributes. Yet they are not incidental in other matters, such as inheritance, testimony, judgeship, and the guardianship of marriage, for the male in these is not like the female. It is known that an attribute is incidental, that is, that it has no bearing on the 'illah at all, by inductive examination of the sources and origins of the Shari'a, either absolutely, or in some chapters but not others, as we have previously mentioned.

An example of eliminating the incidental attribute in all rulings is what came in some narrations of the hadith concerning the one who had intercourse during Ramadan. In some of the narrations he is described as a bedouin (*a'rabi*), and in some of them it says that he came beating his chest and plucking his hair. The established principle in the principles of jurisprudence is that an example (*al-mithal*) is not objected to, since its purpose is to explain the principle, and the supposition and mere possibility suffice for it, as he alluded to in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* with his words:

"The matter does not object to the example, since supposition and possibility suffice for the purpose."

So when you know this, know that his being a bedouin, and his coming beating his chest and plucking his hair, are attributes of the locus in this ruling. These are attributes that must be eliminated, and the obligation of expiation (*kaffara*) must not be rationally motivated by them, because they are incidental attributes from which attaching the ruling to them yields no benefit whatsoever. So the bedouin and others are equal in this, and whoever came calmly and with dignity, and whoever came beating his chest and plucking his hair, are equal in this as well.

An example of elimination by the attribute being incidental only in the chapter in dispute and not in others is the hadith: "Whoever frees his share in a slave, and he has wealth that reaches the value of the slave, the slave is to be valued upon him at a fair price, and he gives his partners their shares, and the slave is freed for him..." the hadith, which is agreed upon (*muttafaq 'alayh*) from the hadith of Ibn Umar, and which we have already cited in surah al-Isra' and al-Kahf. So the word "male slave" in this hadith is an incidental attribute. Therefore whoever frees his share in a female slave is likewise, because it is known from inductive examination of the Shari'a that maleness and femaleness, with respect to manumission, are two incidental attributes, on which the rulings of manumission do not depend, even though maleness and femaleness are not incidental in matters other than manumission, such as inheritance and testimony, as previously mentioned. In the terminology of the legal theorists, the incidental attribute is that which is known from the Shari'a to be disregarded and not taken into account, because there is no benefit whatsoever in attaching the ruling to it, so it is devoid of suitability (*munasaba*). Among the methods of elimination, after the confinement is established, is that no suitability appears for the attribute. Suitability, in the terminology of the legal theorists, is that attaching the ruling to the attribute results in a benefit. So the absence of the aforementioned suitability is one of the methods of its elimination in the method of sifting, although the absence of apparent suitability in the attribute does not invalidate it in some other methods, other than sifting, such as indication by allusion (*al-iyma'*), according to the more correct view, and concomitance (*al-dawaran*). So there are three states:

The first: that suitability appears. Its appearance is indispensable in the method of sifting and in the method of suitability and suggestion (*al-munasaba wa'l-ikhala*).

The second: that neither suitability nor its absence appears. This suffices in concomitance and in indication by allusion according to the correct view.

The third: that the absence of suitability appears, so the attribute is incidental, as previously mentioned shortly before.

Among the methods of elimination after the confinement is established is that the attribute is nullified even though it is suitable for the disputed ruling. The nullification occurs by the independent sufficiency of the attribute that remains in attaching the ruling, apart from the other, in a case on which there is consensus. This was related by al-Fihri. An example of this is the statement of al-Shafi'i: "Measure, staple sustenance, and the like are attributes that are nullified with respect to the prohibition of usury in a handful of wheat, because it is neither measured nor eaten as a staple owing to its small quantity. So the 'illah for the prohibition of usury in it is food, because the 'illah of food is independently sufficient for the ruling, apart from the other attributes, in this case." The intention is merely illustration, not disputing the examples.

And among the methods of refutation, after the restriction (hasr) has been established, is that the attribute which the one presenting the proof (al-mustadill) has retained is transitive (muta'addiyan) from the locus of the ruling (mahall al-hukm) to something else, while the attribute which the objector (al-mu'taridh) wants to retain is restricted (qasir) to the locus of the ruling. The author of al-Diya' al-lami' said: "This resembles the conflict (ta'arud) of the transitive and restricted effective causes ('illah muta'addiyah wa qasirah)." This is as he said. An example of it is the disagreement of the imams, may God have mercy on them, regarding the effective cause ('illah) of the expiation (kaffarah) for deliberately breaking the fast during the day of Ramadan. Some of them say: the effective cause in this is specifically intercourse (jima'). Others say: the effective cause in this is the violation of the sanctity of Ramadan (intihak hurmat Ramadan). So, the attribute that the cause is attached to in this ruling being intercourse requires that it not extend beyond the locus of the ruling to something else, so there is no expiation except in intercourse specifically. And its being, in this ruling, the violation of the sanctity of Ramadan requires that it extend from the locus of the ruling to something else, so the expiation becomes obligatory for eating and drinking deliberately during the day of Ramadan, by the common factor (jami') of the violation of the sanctity of Ramadan in all of them, whether intercourse, eating or drinking. Thus this attribute is preferred over the other because it is transitive, while the other is restricted to the locus of the ruling. Our aim is illustration, not the discussion of examples. What we have mentioned does not preclude that someone may come and say: the effective cause is intercourse, with other preferring factors for his cause. In Maraqi al-Su'ud he pointed to the aforementioned methods of refutation with his words:

"Refute what appears as a mere sweeping (tard), and refute what is not suitably connected to it, the dismissed (al-munkhazil).
Likewise, by nullification (al-ilgha'), even if it is suitable, and the attribute he has chosen extends (yata'adda)."

This is the summary of the statement of the jurists of legal theory regarding what they intend by this proof, which is the sabr and taqsim (examination and division).

* *

The Fourth Issue

Know that the purpose of this proof as mentioned by the logicians (al-mantiqiyyun) differs from its purpose according to the jurists of legal theory (al-usuliyyun) and the dialecticians (al-jadaliyyun). Division according to the logicians occurs only in attributes between which there is mutual exclusion (tanafin) and repulsion (tanafur). This division is what they call the disjunctive conditional (al-shartiyy al-munfasil). Their purpose in mentioning those mutually exclusive attributes is to infer the absence of some of them from the presence of others, and the presence of some from the absence of others. This is what they call "the istithna' (exceptive inference) in the disjunctive conditional." The particle of istithna' among them is "lakinna" (but). The mutual exclusion among the said attributes is limited by reason to three divisions:

Because it is either in both existence and non-existence together, or in existence only, or in non-existence only, and there is no fourth at all.

If it is in both existence and non-existence together, it is, according to them, the disjunctive conditional known as the "real" (haqiqiyyah). It is "mani'at al-jam' wa al-khuluw" (preventing both combination and absence together). It is composed only of two contradictories (naqidayn), or of a thing and the equivalent of its contradictory. Its rule is that its two terms cannot be combined together, nor can they be absent together; rather, one of them must exist and the other be absent. Their non-combination is because of the repulsion and opposition between them in existence, and their non-absence is because of the repulsion and opposition between them in non-existence. Its four modes are productive, as when you say: "The number is either even or odd." If you say: "But it is even," it produces that "it is not odd." If you say: "But it is odd," it produces that "it is not even." If you say: "But it is not even," it produces that "it is odd." If you say: "But it is not odd," it produces that "it is even." The rule of its syllogism is that it returns to inferring the existence of the contradictory or its equivalent from the non-existence of the contradictory or its equivalent, or the reverse of this.

If the repulsion and opposition between its two terms is in existence only, then it is "mani'at al-jam'" (preventing combination), which permits absence (al-khuluw). In it the restriction of the attributes is not required, and it is composed only of a proposition and something more specific than its contradictory (akhass min naqidiha). Its rule is that its two terms cannot be combined because of the repulsion and opposition between them in existence, and there is no obstacle to their both being absent, since there is no opposition or repulsion between them in non-existence. From the syllogism of "mani'at al-jam'" two modes are productive and two are sterile. Its example is your saying: "The body is either white or black." The istithna' of the very identity of each of the two terms produces the contradiction of the other, unlike the istithna' of the contradiction of one of them, which produces nothing. If you say: "The body is either white or black, but it is white," it produces: "So it is not black." If you say: "But it is black," it produces: "So it is not white." Unlike if you say: "But it is not white," which does not produce the negation or affirmation of the other term, because what is not white may be black, and may be not black but red or yellow. Likewise, if you say: "But it is not black," it does not entail the negation or affirmation of the other term, because what is not black may be white, and may be not white because it is red, for example.

This is a concise summary of this proof according to the logicians.

The Fifth Issue

Know that this proof has historical effects, and we will mention here, God willing, some of them.

Among them: it is reported in history that this great proof was the first cause of weakening the great ordeal (mihnah) upon the Muslims regarding their creed, namely the claim that the Qur'an is created (khalq al-Qur'an). The ordeal of the claim that the Qur'an is created arose in the days of al-Ma'mun, intensified greatly in the days of al-Mu'tasim, and continued in that state in the days of al-Wathiq, and throughout that history it stood firmly on its legs.

It is well known what occurred in it of the killing and torture of some eminent scholars, and the compulsion of some of them to flatter by speech out of fear.

It is well known also what befell the master of the Muslims in his time, "the Imam Abu 'Abd Allah Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal" — may God cover him with His vast mercy and reward him on behalf of Islam and the Muslims with goodness — of severe beating during the days of al-Mu'tasim. It is reported that the first historical source for the weakening of this ordeal and the restraint of its excess is this great proof.

Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi said in Tarikh Baghdad, in the discussion of the biography of "Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad":

"Muhammad ibn al-Faraj ibn 'Ali al-Bazzaz informed us; 'Abd Allah ibn Ibrahim ibn Masi informed us; Ja'far ibn Shu'ayb al-Shashi narrated to us; Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Shashi narrated to me; Ibrahim ibn Munabbih narrated to me, saying: I heard Tahir ibn Khalaf say: I heard Muhammad ibn al-Wathiq, who is called al-Muhtadi billah, say: My father, whenever he wished to kill a man, would bring us to that assembly. A shaykh, dyed with henna and shackled, was brought, and my father said: 'Admit Abu 'Abd Allah and his companions' — meaning Ibn Abi Du'ad. He said: The shaykh and al-Wathiq were brought into his prayer area, and he said: 'Peace be upon you, O Commander of the Faithful.' He said to him: 'May God not grant you peace.' He said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, how badly your teacher (mu'addib) educated you! God the Exalted said: "When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it, or return it" [al-Nisa': 86]. By God, you have not greeted me with it, nor with anything better than it.' Ibn Abi Du'ad said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, the man is a speaker (mutakallim).' He said to him: 'Speak to him.' He said: 'O shaykh, what do you say about the Qur'an?' The shaykh said: 'You have not been fair to me' — meaning that the questioning was his right. He said to him: 'Ask.' The shaykh said to him: 'What do you say about the Qur'an?' He said: 'It is created.' He said: 'Is this something that the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali and the rightly guided caliphs knew, or something they did not know?' He said: 'Something they did not know.' He said: 'Glory be to God! Something the Prophet ﷺ did not know, nor Abu Bakr, nor 'Umar, nor 'Uthman, nor 'Ali, nor the rightly guided caliphs? Did you know it?!' He said: So he was embarrassed, and said: 'Excuse me, and let the question stand as it is.' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What do you say about the Qur'an?' He said: 'It is created.' He said: 'Is this something the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr, 'Umar and the rightly guided caliphs knew, or did not know?' He said: 'They knew it, but they did not call people to it.' He said: 'Did what sufficed them not suffice you?!'"

He said: "Then my father stood up, entered the private chamber, lay on his back, placed one of his legs over the other, and said: 'This is something the Prophet did not know, nor Abu Bakr, nor 'Umar, nor 'Uthman, nor 'Ali, nor the rightly guided caliphs. Did you know it? Glory be to God! Something the Prophet, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, may God be pleased with them, and the rightly guided caliphs knew, and did not call people to it; did what sufficed them not suffice you?'"

Then he called 'Ammar the chamberlain and ordered him to remove the shackles from him, to give him four hundred dinars, and to permit him to return. Ibn Abi Du'ad fell from his eyes, and he did not test anyone after that. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 19, verse 78 (part 4 of 4):

Ibn Kathir mentioned this story in his *Tarikh* (History), citing al-Khatib al-Baghdadi. After finishing its narration, he said: "al-Khatib mentioned it in his *Tarikh* with a chain of narration that includes some unknown transmitters." End of quote.

This story finds support in what al-Khatib and others mentioned: that al-Wathiq repented of saying that the Qur'an was created.

Ibn Kathir said in *al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya* (The Beginning and the End): al-Khatib said: Ibn Abi Du'ad had gained control over al-Wathiq and had induced him to be severe in the *mihna* (the inquisition), and he called people to say that the Qur'an was created. He said: It is said that al-Wathiq retracted this before his death. 'Abd Allah ibn Abi'l-Fath informed me: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Hasan related to us: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn 'Arafa related to us: Hamid ibn al-'Abbas told me, from a man, from al-Muhtadi, that al-Wathiq died after having repented of saying that the Qur'an was created.

In any case, this story has remained well known among the scholars and sound as a proof, and in it is the silencing of the opponent with a stone.

The essence of this story, by which this shaykh, who was shackled with chains and whom they wanted to kill, silenced Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad with a stone, is this great proof, which is *al-sabr wa'l-taqsim* (systematic division and elimination). The shaykh mentioned would say to Ibn Abi Du'ad: "Your statement that you call people to, by correct division, cannot be free of one of two matters: either the Prophet ﷺ and his rightly guided caliphs knew it, or they did not know it, and there is no intermediate state between knowledge and non-knowledge, so there is no third possibility at all." Then he returned, through correct elimination, to the two aforementioned possibilities and showed that correct elimination reveals that Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad is not in either case.

As for the first case, that the Prophet ﷺ and his companions knew it and left the people alone without calling them to it, then Ibn Abi Du'ad's call to it contradicts what the Prophet and his companions practiced, which was not calling to it, and he would have been content with what they were content with.

As for the second case, that the Prophet ﷺ and his companions did not know it, then Ibn Abi Du'ad cannot claim that he knows it while they did not know it. Thus his error is evident in either case. For this reason he fell in the eyes of al-Wathiq, and al-Wathiq left the testing of the scholars because of it. This great proof was thus the first historical source for the weakening of this great inquisition, until God removed it completely at the hand of al-Mutawakkil, may God have mercy on him. In this there is a great historical virtue for this proof.

Among the historical effects of this proof is what some historians mentioned: that 'Abd Allah ibn Hammam al-Salouli was denounced to 'Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad by an informer. Ibn Ziyad brought the informer into a place near his assembly, then called Ibn Hammam al-Salouli and said to him: "What led you to say such and such about me?!" Al-Salouli said: "May God set the Amir right; by God, I said nothing of that." Ibn Ziyad then brought out the informer and said: "This one told me that you said that." Ibn Hammam was silent for a moment, then said, addressing the informer:

You are a man: if I entrust you alone with a secret, you betray it, and if you say a word without knowledge,
then you are, regarding the matter that was between us, in a position between betrayal and sin.

Ibn Ziyad said: "You have spoken the truth." And he expelled the informer.

The essence of these two verses, by which Ibn Ziyad expelled the informer and did not harm al-Salouli because of them, is this great proof mentioned. It is as if he were saying to him: "Your statement cannot be free of one of two matters: either I entrusted you with a secret and you disclosed it, or you said it about me as a lie." Then he returned, by elimination, to the two aforementioned cases and showed that the informer commits what is not fitting in either case. For if he entrusted him with a secret and he disclosed it, then he is a betrayer of him; and if he said it about him as a lie and slander, then the matter is clear.
